he realm of psychology has been shaped by the profound insights of numerous
visionaries, and among them stands the towering figure of Carl Gustav Jung.
Renowned for his ground -breaking contributions to the understanding of human
behaviour, Jung’s analytical psychology has left an indelible mark on the field (Samuels,
Shorter, & Plaut, 1986). This paper, titled “Unravelling the Depths of the Psyche: A Review
of Carl Jung’s Analytical Psychology,” embarks on a journey through the intricate corridors
of Jung’s theories, aiming to illuminate the profound implications they hold for our
comprehension of the human psyche.

Jung’s analytical psychology represents a departure from the prevailing schools of thought
in his era, offering a holistic and encompassing approach to the complexities of the human
mind (Jung, 1933). In an age dominated by Freudian psychoanalysis, Jung dared to delve
into the deeper layers of the unconscious, introducing concepts that have since become
integral to the broader landscape of psychology.
The significance of this exploration lies not only in its theoretical richness but also in its
practical implications for individuals and practitioners alike. Jungian concepts such as the
collective unconscious, archetypes, and individuation have resonated far beyond the
confines of academia, influencing diverse fields ranging from psychotherapy to literature
and art (Von Franz, 1964).
As we embark on this scholarly expedition, it is imperative to unravel the enduring
relevance of Jung’s theories and their impact on our understanding of human behaviour. By
navigating through the intricacies of analytical psychology, we aim to discern the threads
that connect the individual to the collective unconscious, offering a nuanced perspective on
the intricate tapestry of the human psyche.

Background on Carl Jung
Early Life and Education
Carl Gustav Jung was born on July 26, 1875, in Kesswil, a small village in Switzerland, to
Paul Achilles Jung, a rural pastor, and Emilie Preiswerk Jung (Jung, 1961). From an early
age, Jung displayed an intense curiosity about the mysteries of the human mind and a deep
interest in exploring the complexities of human nature.
Jung’s educational journey began at the Humanistisches Gymnasium in Basel. He then
pursued his studies at the University of Basel, where he initially studied medicine. In 1900,
he completed his medical degree, and his doctoral dissertation, “On the Psychology and
Pathology of So-Called Occult Phenomena,” reflected his early interest in the intersection of
psychology and the occult (Jung, 1902).
Early Career and Collaboration with Freud
Jung’s professional career took a significant turn when he entered the world of psychiatry. In
1900, he started working at the Burghölzli Psychiatric Hospital in Zurich, where he would
later become the director. It was during this time that he encountered Sigmund Freud’s
work, and their ensuing collaboration profoundly influenced the trajectory of Jung’s career
(Stein, 1998).
Jung became an active member of the psychoanalytic movement and served as the first
president of the International Psychoanalytical Association. However, philosophical
differences, particularly regarding the role of the unconscious and the interpretation of
dreams, led to a parting of ways between Jung and Freud in 1913 (Samuels, Shorter, &
Plaut, 1986).

Analytical Psychology and Key Concepts
The split with Freud marked the beginning of Jung’s development of analytical psychology,
a holistic approach that went beyond the confines of traditional psychoanalysis. Jung
introduced several groundbreaking concepts that would shape the landscape of psychology:
• Collective Unconscious: Jung proposed the existence of a collective unconscious, a
reservoir of shared memories and experiences that transcends individual
consciousness. Archetypes, universal symbols, were central to this concept (Jung,
1959).
• Archetypes: Jung identified and explored archetypes, universal symbols that are part
of the collective unconscious. These archetypes, such as the Hero, the Shadow, and
the Anima/Animus, play a crucial role in shaping human experiences and narratives
(Von Franz, 1964).
• Psychological Types: Jung’s theory of psychological types distinguished between
introversion and extraversion, and he introduced four primary functions: thinking,
feeling, sensation, and intuition (Jung, 1921). This laid the foundation for personality
typologies, influencing subsequent personality assessments like the Myers -Briggs
Type Indicator (MBTI).
• Individuation: Jung emphasized the process of individuation, a lifelong journey
toward integrating various aspects of the self to achieve wholeness and self -
realization (Jung, 1933).
Later Career and Legacy
Jung’s influence extended far beyond the academic realm. He continued to write prolifically,
exploring topics such as religion, mythology, and alchemy. His notable works include
“Psychological Types,” “The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious,” and “Man and
His Symbols” (Jung, 1964).

Later Career and Legacy
Jung’s influence extended far beyond the academic realm. He continued to write prolifically,
exploring topics such as religion, mythology, and alchemy. His notable works include
“Psychological Types,” “The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious,” and “Man and
His Symbols” (Jung, 1964).
Carl Jung passed away on June 6, 1961, leaving behind a profound legacy. His theories
continue to influence not only psychology but also fields such as literature, art, and
philosophy. Jung’s emphasis on the spiritual dimensions of the psyche and the
interconnectedness of individuals with the collective unconscious has sparked on -going
debates and discussions in the field of psychology. His ideas remain integral to the broader
understanding of the human mind and behaviour (Whitmont, 1969).
Collective Unconscious and Archetypes
Central to Carl Jung’s analytical psychology is the concept of the collective unconscious, a
reservoir of shared memories, experiences, and symbols that transcends individual
consciousness. Unlike the personal unconscious, which contains an individual’s unique
experiences, the collective unconscious represents a deeper, universal layer common to all
humanity. It is a vast and timeless repository that houses archetypes, fundamental symbols
and themes ingrained in the human psyche (Jung, 1959).
The Collective Unconscious as a Repository of Universal Experiences:
The collective unconscious serves as a storehouse of inherited, universal experiences that
shape human thoughts, emotions, and behaviours. Jung believed that these shared
experiences, though not consciously known, influence our perceptions, dreams, and cultural
expressions. Archetypes, as manifestations of the collective unconscious, play a pivotal role
in connecting individuals to the broader human experience (Von Franz, 1964).

Jung believed that these shared
experiences, though not consciously known, influence our perceptions, dreams, and cultural
expressions. Archetypes, as manifestations of the collective unconscious, play a pivotal role
in connecting individuals to the broader human experience (Von Franz, 1964).
Exploring Archetypes and Their Roles:
• The Hero Archetype: The Hero embodies the journey of self -discovery and
transformation. Often facing challenges and overcoming adversity, the Hero
symbolizes the quest for personal growth and the triumph of the human spirit (Jung,
1964).
• The Shadow Archetype: The Shadow represents the unconscious and repressed
aspects of an individual. It embodies the darker, hidden side of the self that is often
projected onto others. Confronting the Shadow is crucial for personal development
and achieving balance (Whitmont, 1969).
• The Anima/Animus Archetypes: The Anima (in men) and Animus (in women)
represent the feminine and masculine aspects within individuals, respectively.
Integrating these elements is essential for achieving a harmonious and balanced
personality (Jung, 1959).
• The Wise Old Man/Woman Archetype: Symbolizing wisdom, guidance, and
knowledge, the Wise Old Man or Woman archetype represents the deep reservoir of
insights that comes with experience and maturity (Von Franz, 1964).
Examples of Archetypes in Myths, Dreams, and Cultural Symbolism:
• Myths: In Greek mythology, the Hero archetype is embodied by figures such as
Hercules, who undertakes epic quests and faces formidable challenges. The Shadow
archetype is evident in characters like Medusa, representing the darker aspects that
heroes must confront (Jung, 1964).
• Dreams: Dreams often feature archetypal symbols.

• Dreams: Dreams often feature archetypal symbols. For instance, encountering a
helpful guide in a dream may represent the Wise Old Man/Woman archetype
providing guidance (Whitmont, 1969).
• Cultural Symbolism: The Hero archetype is pervasive in cultural symbols like King
Arthur in medieval literature or contemporary superheroes in modern cinema. The
Shadow archetype is reflected in cultural fears and taboos, manifesting in stories of
monsters or villains (Jung, 1933).
Jung’s concept of the collective unconscious and its archetypes offers a profound lens
through which to understand the universality of human experiences. By recognizing these
archetypes in myths, dreams, and cultural symbolism, we gain insight into the enduring
impact of shared symbols that shape the narratives of our individual and collective psyches.
The exploration of archetypes provides a gateway to understanding the deep currents that
flow beneath the surface of human consciousness.
Psychological Types
Jung’s Theory of Psychological Types: Navigating the Spectrum of the Human Psyche.
Defining Psychological Types:
At the heart of Carl Jung’s analytical psychology lies the theory of psychological types, a
framework that seeks to elucidate the fundamental ways in which individuals perceive and
interact with the world. Jung proposed that these psychological types arise from innate
preferences in the way individuals direct their energy, take in information, make decisions,
and engage with the external world (Jung, 1921).
The Four Dichotomies:
• Introversion/Extraversion:
➢ Introversion: Individuals with a preference for introversion focus inward,
gaining energy from reflection and solitude.
➢ Extraversion: Those inclined towards extraversion draw energy from external
stimuli and social interactions (Jung, 1959).

text:
The Four Dichotomies:
• Introversion/Extraversion:
➢ Introversion: Individuals with a preference for introversion focus inward,
gaining energy from reflection and solitude.
➢ Extraversion: Those inclined towards extraversion draw energy from external
stimuli and social interactions (Jung, 1959).
• Thinking/Feeling:
➢ Thinking: Individuals who lean towards thinking make decisions based on
logic, objectivity, and rational analysis.
➢ Feeling: Those preferring feeling make decisions based on values, empathy, and
personal considerations (Jung, 1921).
• Sensation/Intuition:
➢ Sensation: Individuals oriented towards sensation rely on concrete, factual
information acquired through the five senses.
➢ Intuition: Those with an intuition preference focus on patterns, possibilities, and
the underlying meanings of information (Jung, 1933).
• Judging/Perceiving:
➢ Judging: Individuals with a judging preference prefer structure, organization,
and decisiveness.
➢ Perceiving: Those inclined towards perceiving favor flexibility, adaptability,
and spontaneity (Jung, 1959).
Practical Application and Implications:
Jung’s theory of psychological types has found widespread application, particularly through
the development of the Myers -Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI), a widely used personality
assessment tool. The MBTI operationalizes Jung’s theory by categorizing individuals into
one of 16 personality types based on their preferences across the four dichotomies (Von
Franz, 1964).
Self-Understanding:
The theory of psychological types offers individuals a framework for understanding their
own preferences, strengths, and potential areas for growth. It provides a language for
articulating differences in communication, decision -making, and problem -solving styles
(Jung, 1933).
Interpersonal Dynamics:
In interpersonal relationships, awareness of psychological types can enhance communication
and collaboration.

(Jung, 1933).
Interpersonal Dynamics:
In interpersonal relationships, awareness of psychological types can enhance communication
and collaboration. Understanding the diverse ways in which people approach tasks and make
decisions fosters empathy and cooperation (Whitmont, 1969).
Career Development:
The MBTI is often used in career counseling to help individuals identify professions and
work environments that align with their personality preferences. It provides insights into
preferred work styles, team roles, and leadership approaches (Stein, 1998).
Team Building:
In organizational settings, knowledge of psychological types is utilized for team -building
exercises. Recognizing and valuing the diversity of personality types within a team can
enhance overall performance and creativity (Samuels, Shorter, & Plaut, 1986).
Education and Training:
In education, understanding psychological types can inform teaching strategies. Tailoring
instructional methods to accommodate different learning styles can contribute to more
effective and engaging educational experiences (Jung, 1964).
While acknowledging that individuals may exhibit a range of behaviors and preferences in
different contexts, Jung’s theory of psychological types and its practical applications offer a
valuable framework for navigating the intricacies of the human psyche and fostering
personal and interpersonal growth.
Individuation
Individuation: The Journey Towards Self-Realization
Concept of Individuation:
Individuation, a central concept in Carl Jung’s analytical psychology, represents the lifelong
process of becoming the person one is meant to be, achieving a sense of self -realization and
wholeness. Jung proposed that individuation involves the integration of unconscious
elements into conscious awareness, leading to a harmonious and authentic self (Jung, 1933).
author: Samindar J. Vibhute; B. Suresh Kumar

Jung proposed that individuation involves the integration of unconscious
elements into conscious awareness, leading to a harmonious and authentic self (Jung, 1933).
Stages and Processes of Individuation:
Self-Reflection and Self-Awareness:
The journey toward individuation begins with self -reflection and increased self -awareness.
Individuals engage in introspective practices, exploring their values, beliefs, and motivations
(Whitmont, 1969).
Confrontation with the Shadow:
Individuation requires acknowledging and confronting the Shadow —the unconscious and
often repressed aspects of the self. This involves accepting and integrating the darker, less -
known facets, leading to a more complete self-understanding (Jung, 1959).
Encounter with Archetypes:
Archetypes, universal symbols embedded in the collective unconscious, play a significant
role in the individuation process. Individuals may encounter archetypal figures or symbols in
dreams and visions, offering guidance and insight (Von Franz, 1964).
Integration of Anima/Animus:
Another crucial step involves integrating the anima (in men) or animus (in women),
representing the feminine and masculine aspects within the individual. This integration leads
to a more balanced and complete personality (Jung, 1921).
Encounter with the Collective Unconscious:
The individuation process often involves tapping into the collective unconscious, connecting
with shared human experiences and archetypal images that transcend personal history (Jung,
1959).
Achievement of Wholeness:
As individuals progress through the stages of individuation, they move towards a state of
wholeness. This entails recognizing and reconciling the various aspects of the self, leading
to a more authentic and integrated personality (Jung, 1933).

Achievement of Wholeness:
As individuals progress through the stages of individuation, they move towards a state of
wholeness. This entails recognizing and reconciling the various aspects of the self, leading
to a more authentic and integrated personality (Jung, 1933).
Importance of Integrating Conscious and Unconscious Elements:
Balancing Opposing Forces:
Individuation involves reconciling opposing forces within the psyche, such as conscious and
unconscious elements, creating a dynamic equilibrium. This balance fosters psychological
well-being and resilience (Stein, 1998).
Enhancing Self-Understanding:
Integrating unconscious elements provides individuals with a deeper understanding of their
motivations, fears, and desires. This heightened self -awareness contributes to making more
informed and authentic life choices (Whitmont, 1969).
Facilitating Personal Growth:
The individuation process is inherently linked to personal growth. By embracing the full
range of experiences and emotions, individuals cultivate resilience and develop a greater
capacity for coping with life’s challenges (Jung, 1959).
Spiritual Development:
Individuation is not solely a psychological process; it has spiritual dimensions. As
individuals explore the depths of their psyche, they may experience a sense of connection to
something greater than themselves, contributing to a more profound and meaningful life
(Von Franz, 1964).
In essence, individuation is a transformative journey that involves self -discovery, self -
acceptance, and the integration of all aspects of the self. By embracing both the light and
shadow within, individuals embark on a path towards wholeness, fulfilling their unique
potential, and achieving a profound sense of self-realization.

Dream Analysis
Jung’s Approach to Dream Analysis: Unlocking the Symbolic Language of the
Unconscious
Jungian Dream Analysis:
Carl Jung regarded dreams as the “royal road to the unconscious,” emphasizing their
profound role in revealing the hidden aspects of the psyche. Jung’s approach to dream
analysis differs significantly from Freud’s, as he considered dreams not only as wish -
fulfillment but as messages from the unconscious striving to guide individuals towards self -
discovery and individuation (Jung, 1933).
Significance of Dream Analysis:
Accessing the Unconscious:
Dreams, according to Jung, provide a direct portal to the unconscious mind. Through
symbols, images, and narratives, the unconscious communicates insights, fears, desires, and
unresolved issues (Jung, 1959).
Archetypal Symbolism:
Jungian dream analysis focuses on archetypal symbolism, exploring universal symbols and
themes shared across cultures and human experiences. These symbols, drawn from the
collective unconscious, carry profound meanings that transcend personal history (Von Franz,
1964).
Integration and Individuation:
Dream analysis plays a crucial role in the individuation process by helping individuals
become aware of and integrate unconscious elements. By decoding dream symbolism,
individuals gain insights into unresolved conflicts and unexplored aspects of the self (Jung,
1933).
Symbolism and Themes in Jungian Dream Analysis:
Archetypes:
Dreams often feature archetypal figures such as the Hero, the Shadow, the Wise Old
Man/Woman, and the Anima/Animus.

Symbolism and Themes in Jungian Dream Analysis:
Archetypes:
Dreams often feature archetypal figures such as the Hero, the Shadow, the Wise Old
Man/Woman, and the Anima/Animus. These archetypes symbolize fundamental human
experiences and challenges (Whitmont, 1969).
Animals and Mythical Creatures:
Animals and mythical creatures in dreams may represent instinctual or primal aspects of the
psyche. Their characteristics and behaviors offer insights into the dreamer’s emotional and
psychological state (Jung, 1959).
Journey and Transformation:
Dreams frequently incorporate themes of journey or transformation, symbolizing the
ongoing process of personal growth and individuation. These dreams often feature symbolic
landscapes, paths, or obstacles (Stein, 1998).
Conflict and Resolution:
Conflict in dreams may manifest as confrontations with archetypal adversaries or symbolic
representations of internal struggles. Resolution in dreams can symbolize the resolution of
real-life challenges or internal conflicts (Jung, 1964).
Case Examples of Dream Interpretation:
Example 1: The Chasing Dream
Dream: The dreamer finds themselves being pursued by a menacing figure through a
labyrinthine forest.
Interpretation: Jung might interpret the pursuer as the Shadow, representing repressed
aspects of the dreamer’s personality. The forest symbolizes the unconscious, and the dream
suggests a need to confront and integrate these shadowy aspects for personal growth
(Whitmont, 1969).
Example 2: The Flying Dream
Dream: The dreamer experiences the sensation of flying freely through the sky, unburdened
and exhilarated.
Interpretation: In Jungian terms, flying dreams often symbolize transcendence, liberation,
and a connection to the spiritual or higher self.

Example 2: The Flying Dream
Dream: The dreamer experiences the sensation of flying freely through the sky, unburdened
and exhilarated.
Interpretation: In Jungian terms, flying dreams often symbolize transcendence, liberation,
and a connection to the spiritual or higher self. The dream suggests a desire for personal
freedom and a sense of expansiveness in the dreamer's waking life (Jung, 1959).
Example 3: The Encounter with a Wise Guide
Dream: The dreamer meets a wise old man who imparts guidance and wisdom.
Interpretation: The wise old man archetype often appears as a guide offering valuable
insights. In this dream, the figure may represent the dreamer's inner wisdom, signaling a
need to pay attention to intuitive insights and inner guidance (Von Franz, 1964).
In Jungian dream analysis, the personal context of the dreamer, their emotions, and their
associations to dream symbols are crucial for accurate interpretation. The goal is not only to
decipher the dream's meaning but also to uncover its relevance to the dreamer's
psychological journey and the pursuit of self-realization (Jung, 1933).
Complex Theory
Complex Theory: Unraveling the Threads of Psychological Dynamics
Definition of Complexes:
In the realm of Jungian psychology, a complex is a core pattern of emotions, memories,
perceptions, and desires organized around a central theme. Complexes are intricate and
influential, shaping an individual's thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Carl Jung proposed
that these complexes are formed through personal experiences, often with roots in
childhood, and are deeply entwined with the broader collective unconscious (Jung, 1959).
Influence of Complexes on Thoughts and Behaviors:
• Emotional Charge: Complexes carry a potent emotional charge, influencing how
individuals react to situations and people.

Carl Jung proposed
that these complexes are formed through personal experiences, often with roots in
childhood, and are deeply entwined with the broader collective unconscious (Jung, 1959).
Influence of Complexes on Thoughts and Behaviors:
• Emotional Charge: Complexes carry a potent emotional charge, influencing how
individuals react to situations and people. They can evoke intense emotions, such as
fear, anger, or desire, and shape the interpretation of experiences (Whitmont, 1969).
• Autonomous Nature: Complexes have a semi -autonomous nature, operating
independently of an individual's conscious control. They can intrude into
consciousness unexpectedly, leading to emotional reactions that may seem
disproportionate to the immediate situation (Jung, 1933).
• Impact on Perceptions: Complexes influence perceptions, coloring how individuals
interpret events and interact with others. They act as filters through which
individuals process information, affecting their worldview and responses (Stein,
1998).
Origins of Complexes:
• Personal Experiences: Complexes often originate from significant personal
experiences, particularly those that carry emotional weight. Traumatic events,
unresolved conflicts, or impactful relationships can contribute to the formation of
complexes (Jung, 1921).
• Archetypal Influences: Jung posited that certain archetypal themes in the collective
unconscious also contribute to the development of complexes. These archetypal
patterns shape individuals' experiences in a way that transcends personal history
(Von Franz, 1964).
• Ancestral and Cultural Influences: Complexes can be influenced by cultural and
familial factors. Patterns of behavior and emotional responses passed down through
generations contribute to the shaping of individual complexes (Jung, 1959).
Process of Integrating and Resolving Complexes:
• Conscious Awareness: The first step towards integration is becoming consciously
aware of the complex.

text:
• Ancestral and Cultural Influences: Complexes can be influenced by cultural and
familial factors. Patterns of behavior and emotional responses passed down through
generations contribute to the shaping of individual complexes (Jung, 1959).
Process of Integrating and Resolving Complexes:
• Conscious Awareness: The first step towards integration is becoming consciously
aware of the complex. This involves recognizing the recurring patterns of thought,
emotion, and behavior associated with a particular theme (Whitmont, 1969).
• Exploration and Reflection: Individuals explore the origin and significance of the
complex through reflection, often with the assistance of psychotherapy or self -
analysis. Understanding the roots of the complex contributes to the integration
process (Jung, 1933).
• Acceptance and Integration: Acceptance of the complex, without judgment, is
crucial. Integration involves acknowledging the presence of the complex without
being overwhelmed by its emotional charge. This allows for a more balanced and
conscious engagement with the associated themes (Jung, 1921).
• Transformation: The process of integration often leads to the transformation of the
complex. What was once a source of emotional turmoil may evolve into a source of
wisdom, resilience, or personal growth (Stein, 1998).
• Active Engagement: Engaging actively with the complex involves using its energy
constructively. This may include creative expression, finding positive outlets for
emotions, or channeling the complex's influence towards personal development
(Samuels, Shorter, & Plaut, 1986).
• Psychological Well -Being and Complex Integration: Integrating and resolving
complexes is integral to psychological well -being. It fosters a more conscious,
balanced, and authentic engagement with oneself and the external world. By
unraveling the threads of complex dynamics, individuals can move towards greater
self-awareness, resilience, and a more fulfilling life journey (Jung, 1959).

Alchemical Studies and Symbolism
Jung's Alchemical Studies and Symbolism: A Journey of Psychological Transformation
Jung's Interest in Alchemical Symbolism:
Carl Jung's fascination with alchemy extended beyond its historical and chemical aspects; he
saw in alchemical symbolism a rich source of psychological insight and symbolism. Jung
viewed alchemy as a precursor to modern psychology, suggesting that alchemists were
engaged in a symbolic exploration of the transformation of the psyche (Jung, 1953).
Relevance to Psychological Transformation:
Philosopher's Stone as Individuation:
Jung identified parallels between the alchemical process of transmuting base metals into
gold and the psychological journey of individuation. The Philosopher's Stone, a central
concept in alchemy representing perfection and enlightenment, became a metaphor for the
realization of the self through the individuation process (Whitmont, 1969).
Integration of Opposites:
Alchemical symbolism frequently involves the union of opposites, such as the marriage of
the sun and moon or the conjunction of masculine and feminine elements. Jung interpreted
these as representations of the integration of conflicting aspects within the individual, a
crucial aspect of psychological transformation (Jung, 1959).
Alchemy as a Symbolic Language:
Jung considered alchemy a symbolic language through which unconscious contents could be
expressed and explored. The alchemical quest for transformation mirrored the psychological
journey of confronting and integrating unconscious material (Jung, 1953).

Alchemy as a Symbolic Language:
Jung considered alchemy a symbolic language through which unconscious contents could be
expressed and explored. The alchemical quest for transformation mirrored the psychological
journey of confronting and integrating unconscious material (Jung, 1953).
Alchemical Symbolism and the Process of Individuation:
• Nigredo (Blackening): In alchemy, the nigredo represents the initial stage of
decomposition and putrefaction. Psychologically, this can be seen as the
confrontation with the Shadow —the dark, unconscious aspects of the self.
Individuation begins with acknowledging and working through these darker elements
(Von Franz, 1964).
• Albedo (Whitening): The albedo phase involves purification and cleansing.
Psychologically, this corresponds to a process of self -reflection and gaining clarity.
The individual starts to differentiate between the conscious and unconscious
elements, working towards a more refined and purified state (Jung, 1959).
• Citrinitas (Yellowing): Citrinitas symbolizes the emergence of a new awareness and
understanding. Psychologically, this stage corresponds to gaining insight into the
deeper layers of the unconscious and achieving a more balanced and harmonious
state of being (Whitmont, 1969).
• Rubedo (Reddening): The final stage, rubedo, signifies the culmination of the
alchemical process. It represents the integration of opposites, the realization of the
Philosopher's Stone, and the attainment of wholeness through individuation (Jung,
1953).
Role of Symbolism and Mythology in Understanding the Human Psyche:
• Archetypal Symbols: Jung believed that symbols and myths are expressions of
universal archetypes embedded in the collective unconscious. These archetypal
symbols provide a common language that transcends cultural and individual
differences, offering insights into fundamental aspects of the human psyche (Jung,
1964).
author: Samindar J. Vibhute; B. Suresh Kumar

text:
Role of Symbolism and Mythology in Understanding the Human Psyche:
• Archetypal Symbols: Jung believed that symbols and myths are expressions of
universal archetypes embedded in the collective unconscious. These archetypal
symbols provide a common language that transcends cultural and individual
differences, offering insights into fundamental aspects of the human psyche (Jung,
1964).
• Myth as a Collective Dream: Jung considered myths as collective dreams that
reflect shared human experiences and aspirations. Exploring myths allows
individuals to tap into the collective unconscious and gain a deeper understanding of
universal themes and patterns (Von Franz, 1964).
• Connection to Individuation: Symbolism and mythology play a crucial role in the
individuation process by providing a framework for understanding and integrating
unconscious material. Myths often mirror the stages of psychological transformation
and offer guidance for individuals on their journey towards self -realization (Jung,
1933).
In summary, Jung's exploration of alchemical symbolism illustrates his belief in the
transformative power of symbols and mythology. Alchemy, as a symbolic language,
provides a metaphorical roadmap for the individuation process, guiding individuals through
the stages of self-discovery and integration. The broader study of symbolism and mythology
enriches our understanding of the human psyche, offering profound insights into the
universal patterns and archetypes that shape the human experience.
Critical Evaluation
Critical Assessment of Jung's Theories:
Strengths:
• Holistic Approach: Jung's emphasis on a holistic approach to psychology,
considering the whole person and the interconnectedness of the psyche, has been a
strength. This approach paved the way for a more inclusive understanding of human
behavior beyond the confines of individual experiences (Samuels, Shorter, & Plaut,
1986).
• Concept of the Collective Unconscious: The concept of the collective unconscious,
with its archetypes and universal symbols, has resonated across disciplines.
author: Samindar J. Vibhute; B. Suresh Kumar

text:
This approach paved the way for a more inclusive understanding of human
behavior beyond the confines of individual experiences (Samuels, Shorter, & Plaut,
1986).
• Concept of the Collective Unconscious: The concept of the collective unconscious,
with its archetypes and universal symbols, has resonated across disciplines. It
provides a framework for understanding shared human experiences and offers a
language to explore the depths of the psyche (Jung, 1959).
• Individuation Process: Jung's concept of individuation, with its focus on personal
growth, self-realization, and the integration of the unconscious, has been influential
in the realm of psychotherapy and self-help. It encourages individuals to embark on a
journey of self-discovery and transformation (Jung, 1933).
• Symbolism and Mythology: Jung's exploration of symbolism and mythology as
vehicles for understanding the human psyche has enriched the field. The recognition
of archetypal patterns in symbols and myths contributes to a deeper comprehension
of the collective dimensions of the unconscious (Von Franz, 1964).
Weaknesses:
• Lack of Empirical Evidence: One of the main criticisms of Jung's theories is the
limited empirical evidence supporting many of his concepts. The reliance on
subjective experiences and the lack of rigorous scientific validation has led some to
question the scientific robustness of Jungian psychology (Whitmont, 1969).
• Complexity and Lack of Operationalization: Jung's theories, with their intricate
concepts such as the collective unconscious, archetypes, and individuation, can be
challenging to operationalize and measure. This complexity poses difficulties in
empirical research and practical applications (Stein, 1998).
• Ambiguity in Archetypal Concepts: Jung's concept of archetypes and their
interpretation can be seen as somewhat vague and subjective.
author: Samindar J. Vibhute; B. Suresh Kumar

text:
This complexity poses difficulties in
empirical research and practical applications (Stein, 1998).
• Ambiguity in Archetypal Concepts: Jung's concept of archetypes and their
interpretation can be seen as somewhat vague and subjective. Different analysts may
interpret archetypes differently, leading to a lack of precision in the application of
these concepts (Jung, 1964).
• Overemphasis on Symbolism: Some critics argue that Jung's emphasis on
symbolism and archetypal interpretations might lead to overemphasis on the
subjective aspects of the therapeutic process, potentially neglecting other crucial
dimensions such as environmental influences and behavioral patterns (Samuels,
Shorter, & Plaut, 1986).
Controversies and Debates:
Jung and Freud Split:
The split between Jung and Freud, his former mentor, was a significant controversy. Their
differing views on the nature of the unconscious and the role of sexuality led to a parting of
ways, with Jung pursuing his own theories (Jung, 1933).
Esoteric and Mystical Associations:
Jung's interest in esoteric and mystical subjects, such as alchemy and astrology, has been a
point of controversy. Some critics argue that these associations might undermine the
scientific credibility of his work (Jung, 1953).
Archetypal Interpretations:
The subjective nature of archetypal interpretations in Jungian analysis has sparked debates
within the psychological community. Critics question the universality of archetypes and
their relevance across diverse cultures (Jung, 1959).
Limited Integration with Other Psychological Approaches:
Jungian psychology has sometimes been criticized for its limited integration with other
psychological approaches. The emphasis on symbolic and depth psychology may exclude
insights from cognitive, behavioral, or neuroscience perspectives (Whitmont, 1969).
author: Samindar J. Vibhute; B. Suresh Kumar

text:
Limited Integration with Other Psychological Approaches:
Jungian psychology has sometimes been criticized for its limited integration with other
psychological approaches. The emphasis on symbolic and depth psychology may exclude
insights from cognitive, behavioral, or neuroscience perspectives (Whitmont, 1969).
In conclusion, while Jung's theories have made significant contributions to the field of
psychology, they are not without their criticisms and controversies. The strengths lie in their
holistic and inclusive nature, providing a framework for exploring the depths of the human
psyche. However, challenges arise from the lack of empirical evidence, complexity, and the
subjective nature of certain concepts. The ongoing debates reflect the diversity of
perspectives within the field and underscore the need for continued critical evaluation of
Jung's work.
CONCLUSION
In conclusion, Carl Jung’s contributions to analytical psychology have left an enduring
imprint on our understanding of the human psyche. His revelations about the collective
unconscious and archetypes have illuminated the universal symbols that underpin shared
human experiences. The concept of individuation, emphasizing a transformative journey
toward self-realization, remains a guiding principle for personal growth. Jung’s insistence on
integrating conflicting elements within the self -advocates for psychological harmony,
resonating in contemporary approaches to well -being. His exploration of symbolism and
mythology has deepened our comprehension of the collective dimensions of the
unconscious. Even today, Jung’s theories continue to be relevant, influencing therapeutic
practices, self -help methodologies, and interdisciplinary studies. His holistic approach,
transcending the boundaries of psychology, has enriched fields such as literature, art,
philosophy, and cultural studies. In essence, Jung’s legacy endures as a beacon, providing
profound insights into the intricate depths of the human experience and shaping the evolving
landscape of psychology.

Future Directions
Future Directions in Jungian Psychology: Bridging Tradition and Modernity
Neuroscientific Exploration:
Future research could explore the neural correlates of Jungian concepts, such as the
activation of archetypal symbols or the brain mechanisms involved in the individuation
process. This integration of neuroscience with Jungian psychology could bridge the gap
between the subjective and the neurobiological aspects of the psyche (Whitmont, 1969).
Cultural Adaptation and Diversity:
Adapting Jungian concepts to diverse cultural contexts could be a fruitful area of
exploration. Investigating how archetypes manifest and are interpreted across different
cultures would contribute to a more inclusive understanding of the collective unconscious
(Jung, 1964).
Technological Applications:
Incorporating Jungian principles into modern technology, such as virtual reality or artificial
intelligence, could open new avenues for therapeutic interventions. Virtual environments
designed with archetypal symbolism might offer unique tools for exploring the unconscious
(Stein, 1998).
Integration with Positive Psychology:
Integrating Jungian psychology with positive psychology could provide a more
comprehensive framework for well -being. Exploring how concepts like individuation
contribute to resilience, life satisfaction, and positive growth could enhance therapeutic
interventions (Jung, 1933).
Quantitative Approaches:
Applying quantitative research methods to Jungian concepts, such as developing
standardized measures for archetypal patterns or assessing the effectiveness of Jungian -
informed interventions, would strengthen the empirical foundation of analytical psychology
(Samuels, Shorter, & Plaut, 1986).

Quantitative Approaches:
Applying quantitative research methods to Jungian concepts, such as developing
standardized measures for archetypal patterns or assessing the effectiveness of Jungian -
informed interventions, would strengthen the empirical foundation of analytical psychology
(Samuels, Shorter, & Plaut, 1986).
Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration:
Collaborating with other disciplines, such as philosophy, anthropology, or sociology, could
enrich the understanding of Jungian concepts in a broader cultural and societal context.
Interdisciplinary research may uncover new connections and applications for Jungian
psychology (Jung, 1959).
Exploration of Shadow in Group Dynamics:
Investigating the role of the Shadow in group dynamics and intergroup relations could
provide insights into societal conflicts and contribute to conflict resolution strategies.
Understanding how collective Shadows manifest and interact could have implications for
social harmony (Von Franz, 1964).
Jungian Approaches in Organizational Psychology:
Applying Jungian principles in organizational psychology could enhance leadership
development, team dynamics, and workplace well -being. Concepts like archetypal
leadership styles or organizational Shadow dynamics might offer valuable perspectives for
organizational psychologists (Jung, 1921).
Mindfulness and Jungian Practices:
Exploring the integration of mindfulness practices with Jungian approaches could enhance
therapeutic interventions. Mindfulness techniques may complement Jungian concepts,
fostering greater self-awareness and facilitating the individuation process (Jung, 1953).
Digital Platforms for Self-Exploration:
Developing digital platforms or applications that incorporate Jungian principles for self -
exploration and personal development could make these concepts more accessible to a wider
audience. Interactive tools might guide individuals on their journey toward self -realization
(Jung, 1933).

In navigating future directions, the integration of Jungian psychology with modern research
methodologies, technology, and diverse cultural perspectives holds promise for both
enriching the tradition of analytical psychology and expanding its applications in
contemporary psychology.

著名精神病学家 、 心理学家 、 个体心理学 （individual psychology）创始人阿尔弗雷德  •  阿德勒 于 20 世纪二三十年代
创立的一种心理治疗方法。该疗法以个体的整体性 、 独
特性 、能动性和社会性为基础，主要通过对家庭结构 、出
生顺序 、 早期记忆 、 梦境 、 认知错误以及行为目标等内
容的分析，使来访者意识到心理问题产生的根源在于童年
早期的适应不良，认识到因自身存在缺陷和不足而渴望
相互合作，以形成一种具有社会兴趣且行之有效的应对实
际问题的生活方式。阿德勒逝世之后，后继学者系统化
阿德勒心理治疗，丰富该疗法的理念和技术，完善该疗法
的步骤和程序，强化评估手段和诊断工具，发展出多种治
疗模式，扩大其应用领域，将其发展成为一项专业性的心
理服务项目。

text:

伊德相比，阿尔弗雷德  •  阿德勒更可能成为真正的现代

疗师所取得的成就都应将功劳归功于阿德勒的个体心
理学。 ”
1　阿德勒心理治疗的初步发展
阿德勒心理治疗是以阿德勒个体心理学原理为理论
基础的一种心理治疗方法。个体心理学并非是基于个体
层面理解的心理学，而是从社会文化视角探讨心理发展动
力以及心理疾病成因的心理学体系。阿德勒的个体心理
学理论体系包括身体缺陷 、 自卑感 、 补偿机制 、 生活风
格、 社会兴趣 、 创造性自我等主要概念。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
阿德勒的个体心理
学理论体系包括身体缺陷 、 自卑感 、 补偿机制 、 生活风
格、 社会兴趣 、 创造性自我等主要概念。个体心理学认
为，个体因器官缺陷而引起心理自卑，自卑感推动着个体
的心理发展，促使个体追求优越，进而形成生活风格，并通
过自身创造性力量处理生活问题。由身体缺陷引起的错
误认知，致使个体在面对社会情境时缺乏勇气和应对策略，
最终产生某种心理失调。因此，个体心理学并不把个体的
心理症状看作是某种疾病，而是强调个体因身体缺陷而缺
乏生活的勇气，无力面对生活问题时造成的心理冲突。

维也纳贫民区开设私人诊所，从事神经症的临床治疗活动。

1.2　阿德勒心理治疗的初步发展
阿德勒逝世之后，阿德勒学派的发展重心转移至美国。
Ansbacher 和 Dreikurs 成为阿德勒学派的主要领导者。 Ansbacher 的主要贡献在于全面总结阿德勒的理论思想，为临
床实践的开展提供扎实的理论基础。 而 Dreikurs 更擅长临
床实践与应用推广工作。他系统概括出阿德勒心理治疗
的治疗步骤，提出儿童治疗的主要内容，发展出阿德勒学
派的家庭疗法。

text:
2　阿德勒心理治疗的迅速发展
20 世 纪 80 年代 ～ 90 年代，阿德勒心理治疗经历快速
发展时期。该疗法在治疗方法 、 治疗模式 、 治疗范围 、
评估手段 、 诊断工具以及实践领域等方面均取得突破性
进展，并发展成为一项专业性的心理服务项目。
2.1　治疗模式日趋多元
随着精神分析学派的不断分化和演变，以及以人为中
心治疗 、认知 -行为治疗 、家庭治疗 、后现代主义心理治
疗流派的兴起，阿德勒心理治疗吸收这些流派的相关技术，
形成多元化的治疗方法。 Manaster 等  214 指出 ： “ 在 心理
治疗过程中，阿德勒学派方法不排斥任何技术，只要技术
适合理论和来访者就可以运用到治疗中。实际上，在治疗
干预时，治疗师是可以自行选用技术的。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
实际上，在治疗
干预时，治疗师是可以自行选用技术的。 ”根据不同的治
疗目标和具体的治疗情境，阿德勒学派治疗师将治疗手段
分为策略 、 技术和方法三个等级。策略是针对治疗的整
体目标和终极目标，即发展社会兴趣和形成健康的生活风
格而言的。技术是为策略服务的，主要是对个体的生活风
格进行理解和分析，即对家庭氛围 、出生顺序 、早期记忆 、
梦境 、 错误行为目标以及认知错误等内容进行解析。在
实际治疗过程中，治疗师采用名目繁多的治疗方法，大致
可以分为动力学方法 、人本主义治疗方法和认知 -行为治
疗方法等。个体心理学脱胎于精神分析学，强调早年经验

author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
个体心理学脱胎于精神分析学，强调早年经验
阿德勒心理治疗的回顾及展望 —吴　杰等
30 Medicine and Philosophy,Oct 2022,Vol. 43,No. 19, Total No. 702
对人格发展的重要影响，其早期的治疗方法具有浓厚的精
神分析色彩。其动力学方法主要有梦的解析 、 重构早期
记忆 、 分析家庭动力系统等。个体心理学以人的健康发
展和主观经验为研究对象，倡导用整体论和现象学的方法
来研究人，注重人的整体性和创造性，强调自我发展的主
动性和选择性，关注人的价值意义，从而体现浓厚的人本
主义色彩。其人本主义治疗方法主要有鼓励和共情。个
体心理学强调在患者自己的意识经验框架内理解患者的
重要性，在心理治疗中尝试去阐明个体如何知觉和体验世
界。其认知 −行为治疗方法包括矛盾法 、反建议法 、按钮
技术 、家庭作业等。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
其认知 −行为治疗方法包括矛盾法 、反建议法 、按钮
技术 、家庭作业等。
早期的阿德勒心理治疗主要面向个体 、 以一对一的
形式展开。为了适应不同类型的治疗对象，后继学者发展
出多种多样的治疗模式。 Dreikurs 深入研究家庭结构，分
析家庭动力因素，创建出阿德勒学派家庭疗法 （Adlerian
family therapy）；Bitter 和 Manaster 等 通过父母学习小组 、
家庭教育计划 、 生活风格团体等多种方式进一步发展该
学派的家庭疗法。 Sonstegard 和 Bitter 将社会建构理论与
短程治疗的相关理念整合进阿德勒理论中，发展出阿德勒
学派团体疗法 （Adlerian group therapy）207。 Bitter 等  将阿
德勒心理治疗和短程治疗有机结合，提出阿德勒学派短程
疗法 （Adlerian brief therapy ）。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
Bitter 等  将阿
德勒心理治疗和短程治疗有机结合，提出阿德勒学派短程
疗法 （Adlerian brief therapy ）。当前，阿德勒学派短程疗法
主要有三种模式 ： 即 Nicoll 和 Bitter 创立的阿德勒学派短
程疗法 、 Nystul 建立的问题解决咨询模式 （problem-solving
counseling）以 及 Slavik、 Sperry 和 Carlson 提出的阿德勒学
派高效疗法 （efficient Adlerian therapy ）163。此外， Kottman
等 还将阿德勒理论和游戏疗法进行有效整合，发展出阿
德勒学派游戏疗法 （Adlerian play therapy）。
2.2　治疗范围不断扩大
阿德勒心理治疗最初用于治疗各种神经症，后来发展
到预防问题儿童的不良行为，现今已扩展到治疗各种心理
障碍如焦虑症 、 抑郁症 、 品行障碍 、 饮食障碍 、 人格障
碍等。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
在阿德勒学派看来，个体患有心理障碍是无力应对
生活问题的表现，这些个体面对生活困难时犹豫不决，常
常体验到失败和挫折感，由此而出现的心理应激症状都是
个体在避免失败或者避免做出糟糕决定时出现的内部需
要。在临床治疗中，治疗师鼓励患者，使其意识到自己被
扭转的知觉，以发展出有效的应对策略，来改变原有的错
误信念和不良行为。阿德勒心理治疗虽然作为一种心理
治疗形式，在治疗心理障碍方面取得很多成果；但同时它
也是心理预防与心理保健的有效手段，其主要功能在于促
进个体的身心健康发展。该疗法指出，所谓的心理疾病只
是个人在成长中体会到失败和挫折，心理治疗应该帮助个
人清除掉成长中的各种障碍，朝着正常的水平发展。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
该疗
法的教育功能还体现在，它注重引导和教育个体克服自卑
感，改变错误的行为动机，修正他们的错误目标和观点，发
展出有效应对现实问题的生活模式。
与阿德勒心理治疗范围同步发展的是应用领域的不
断拓展。在这一阶段，阿德勒心理治疗被应用到学校教育 、
特殊教育 、 教牧咨询 （pastoral counseling）、 生涯发展咨询
等领域。在学校教育中，阿德勒学派通过指导教师与儿童
建立平等合作的师生关系，增加儿童的归属感和认同感，
发展他们的社会兴趣，提高他们的自我觉察能力，帮助其
识别错误的行为目标，来消除不良行为 。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
在特殊教育领
域中，阿德勒学派通过关注家庭的动力系统，挖掘个体的
早期生活经验，调动家庭成员的积极性，促进家庭成员交
流沟通，指导父母发展有效的教养方式，帮助儿童获得积
极的心理感受和情感体验，以养成良好的行为习惯，促进
其心理健康发展 。教牧咨询基于宗教真理综合运用各
种心理学方法来治疗信仰障碍和心理障碍。教牧咨询吸
收阿德勒学派的整体意识观和能动意识观，认为宗教信徒
的心理是一个有机整体，鼓励宗教信徒挖掘自我价值和
内在潜能，通过自身努力能够修复破碎的心灵 。生涯发
展领域的著名学 者 Savickas 将阿德勒心理治疗应用于
生涯发展咨询中。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
生涯发
展领域的著名学 者 Savickas 将阿德勒心理治疗应用于
生涯发展咨询中。他通过使用生活风格访谈技术，收集个
体关于家庭结构 、早期经验 、人格特征等方面的信息，以
此来了解和分析个体的职业目标 、 职业偏好和职业调适
能力。
2.3　加强心理诊断
准确的心理诊断和心理评估是科学 、 高效地进行心
理治疗的基石。由于阿德勒心理治疗在这方面缺乏针对
性的研究，治疗师们通过发展符合自身特点的评估方法或
者使用已有诊断工具来弥补这方面的不足。 Powers 等
认为，阿德勒心理治疗既要使用和其他治疗模式相同的一
般诊断方法，还需要发展出符合该疗法的特殊诊断方法，
即生活风格访谈技术。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
Powers 等
认为，阿德勒心理治疗既要使用和其他治疗模式相同的一
般诊断方法，还需要发展出符合该疗法的特殊诊断方法，
即生活风格访谈技术。指出要完成一个全面的一般诊断
必须涵盖鉴别信息 、 呈现问题 、 背景资料 、 当前技能 、
治疗期待以及临床观点这六个方面的内容。在一般诊断
结束之后，治疗师才与来访者共同制定治疗方案。治疗方
案包括危机管理 、 医学干预 、 短期目标 、 长期目标和辅
助服务等内容。特殊诊断也被称为 “生活风格访谈 ”，作
为阿德勒学派特有的诊断技术，是一个半结构化的过程。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
特殊诊断也被称为 “生活风格访谈 ”，作
为阿德勒学派特有的诊断技术，是一个半结构化的过程。
在生活风格访谈中，咨询师搜集关于来访者十个方面的信
息：身体状况 、出生顺序 、童年记忆 、对性的认识 、角色
榜样 、 生活的意义 、 父母的影响 、 社会交往 、 学校经历
以及邻居的作用。
此外，还有研究者使用各种诊断工具对心理症状进行
有效鉴别。 Maniacci 等  将精神病诊断标准引入治疗中，
发展出基于阿德勒学派理论的五轴诊断系统 ：轴Ⅰ为防御
倾向或者保护机制，轴Ⅱ为生活风格，轴Ⅲ为器官自卑，轴
Ⅳ为负面生活事件，轴Ⅴ为生活任务。治疗师借助此系统
可有效鉴别和诊断心理障碍患者关于器官自卑和生活风
格方面的信息。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
治疗师借助此系统
可有效鉴别和诊断心理障碍患者关于器官自卑和生活风
格方面的信息。 Maniacci 等  提出将心理测验应用到阿
德勒心理治疗中的两条原则 ： （1）符合心理测验的设计和

Medicine and Philosophy,Oct 2022,Vol. 43,No. 19, Total No. 702 31
目的； （2）符合阿德勒学派理论。在此原则之下，治疗师们
使用自编的量表，如《生活风格量表》 （life-style inventory）、
《早期记忆测验》 （early memory test ）、 《社会兴趣量表》
（social interest scale ）等，收集关于个体家庭结构 、 早年经
历等方面的信息；或者使用已有心理测验工具，如《韦克斯
勒成人智力量表》 （Wechsler adult intelligence scale）和《罗夏
墨迹测验》，来考察个体运用生活常识解决现实问题的能
力，分析个体的自卑情结和补偿方式。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
这些评估工具适用
于不同的治疗对象和不同的治疗模式。评估工具的产生
和使用是心理治疗专业化发展的必然要求，反过来又进一
步提高了阿德勒心理治疗的专业性和科学性。
2.4　重视培训督导
阿德勒心理治疗专业化的重要标志包括期刊杂志的
创办 、协会的成立以及伦理道德标准的颁布等。《个体心
理学杂志》的创办为阿德勒心理治疗的研究提供平台。关
于治疗的一系列重要问题，如界定阿德勒学派，确定治疗
师的角色，限定治疗时间 、 怎样看待治疗过程，如何评估
治疗效果等，均通过这一平台展开广泛而又深入的探讨，
这极大地推动阿德勒心理治疗理论与临床实践的发展。
阿德勒学派协会的成立为阿德勒心理治疗的实践工作制
定更为严格的实践标准。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
阿德勒学派协会的成立为阿德勒心理治疗的实践工作制
定更为严格的实践标准。现今，美国 、加拿大 、英国 、澳
大利亚 、 巴西等地都已成立阿德勒学派协会。协会的职
能包括宣传 、 指导 、 监督与培训。各地协会向公众传播
有关阿德勒学派的理论和实践知识，为治疗师提供培训和
督导服务。监督工作涉及治疗师的培训 、 资质认定以及
执业监管。为加强治疗师的执业监管，各地协会还颁布相
关伦理准则 、 治疗师担负的责任 、 保密原则 、 评估手段
的运用等多个方面的信息，对实践工作中的具体事宜提出
明确的规定。协会的成立及其发挥的功能促使阿德勒心
理治疗在欧美各国发展成为一项专业性的心理服务项目。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
协会的成立及其发挥的功能促使阿德勒心
理治疗在欧美各国发展成为一项专业性的心理服务项目。
当前，芝加哥职业心理学阿德勒学院 （The Adler School of
Professional Psychology-Chicago）成为培训阿德勒学派治疗
师的主要阵营。一年一度的夏威夷夏季阿德勒短期训练
班，为各地阿德勒学派治疗师提供个人成长指导服务。
3　阿德勒心理治疗的当代发展
进入 21 世纪以来，心理治疗界呈现出多元发展与整
合发展的趋势。阿德勒心理治疗形成两条主要发展路线，
重视多元文化背景下的应用研究以及对治疗效果的研究。
3.1　形成两条主要发展路线
当前，心理治疗界正呈现出百家争鸣 、百花齐放的局
面。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
3.1　形成两条主要发展路线
当前，心理治疗界正呈现出百家争鸣 、百花齐放的局
面。由于治疗师个人背景 、 临床实践经验以及应用领域
的不同，阿德勒心理治疗在当代临床实践上亦表现出多取
向发展的趋势。在围绕阿德勒学派发展路线的问题上，特
别是针对是否要继续遵循阿德勒基本原理这一基本问题
上，学派内部出现激烈的争论，形成两大主要发展路线。
以旧金山阿尔弗雷德  •  阿德勒研究所的负责 人 Stein 为
首的少数学者，提出 “回归阿德勒 、重读阿德勒 ”的口号。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
以旧金山阿尔弗雷德  •  阿德勒研究所的负责 人 Stein 为
首的少数学者，提出 “回归阿德勒 、重读阿德勒 ”的口号。
斯特恩领导的经典阿德勒翻译项目 （classical adlerian translation project）团队，历 时 15 年时间，将阿德勒的著作重新
翻译 、 整理并编辑 为 12 卷《阿尔弗雷德  •  阿德勒的临床
著作选集》 （The Collected Clinical Works of Alfred Adler ）。他
们坚持阿德勒学派基本原理和治疗原则，形成经典阿德勒
学派路线 （classical Adlerian）。而 以 Bitter 为首的更多学
者则认为，只要符合阿德勒学派的基本框架和基本假设，
就可将之归入阿德勒学派范畴。他们坚持走理论整合与
技术折衷的发展路线，形成广义上的阿德勒学派路线。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
他们坚持走理论整合与
技术折衷的发展路线，形成广义上的阿德勒学派路线。他
们强调，面对心理学界的整合发展趋势，阿德勒学派唯有
表现出强大的整合性和包容性，充分吸收其他流派的理念
和技术，以此获得新的发展和突破，才能在心理治疗界占
据更为有利的位置。尽管学派内部针对发展路线问题的
看法存在较大分歧，然而临床工作者在实际操作中都很好
地遵循阿德勒学派的基本原理和操作原则。
3.2　注重多元文化背景
当代社会的多元文化特征十分明显，如何在治疗过程
中尊重不同文化与个体差异，这是当前心理治疗界关注的
主要问题。阿德勒学派主张男女平等 、人人平等，强调每
个人都生活在特定的社会环境中，只有在其生活的特殊背
景中理解每个人才有意义。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
阿德勒学派主张男女平等 、人人平等，强调每
个人都生活在特定的社会环境中，只有在其生活的特殊背
景中理解每个人才有意义。在实际治疗过程中，该学派治
疗师注重情境的差异性，参照个体的文化背景理解其认知 、
情绪和行为问题，并依据文化差异调整治疗方法。有研究
者指出，阿德勒学派心理学的特点和假设与许多少数族裔
团体的价值观相一致，该学派尊重不同人群在语言 、文化 、
地理位置等方面存在的差异，强调家庭内部成员的平等性，
重视家庭结构的积极作用 。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
La Guardia 等  就发现，阿
德勒学派所提倡的平等观 、 家庭气氛 、 合作意识 、 社会
兴趣意识 、生活风格等观点，以及在治疗中所运用的灵活
策略和多样方法，都有助于少数族裔美国家庭成员增进相
互理解 、凝聚家庭共识 、处理家庭矛盾 、融入当地文化。
此外，多元文化背景下的心理治疗发展还涉及到本土
化问题。阿德勒个体心理学虽然根植于西方个体文化背
景，但将社会性作为其理论发展的起点，强调家庭教育 、
社会文化因素对心理发展的促进作用，帮助个体发展合作
意识和社会兴趣，以此实现个人的生活意义和人生价值。
社会兴趣是个体心理学最为重要的概念，是指一种关心他
人与社会的潜能，也是一种目标实现的动力，能够引导个
体完善自身和追求更美好的社会 。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
社会兴趣是个体心理学最为重要的概念，是指一种关心他
人与社会的潜能，也是一种目标实现的动力，能够引导个
体完善自身和追求更美好的社会 。Croake 等 认为，社
会兴趣是个体心理学与东方文化最明显 、 最重要的共同
点，社会兴趣所提倡的 “积极关注他人 、为社会做出奉献 ”
的理念与东方文化相契合。然而该疗法是否能够应用到
我国心理治疗的实践中，其治疗效果又如何，这需要进一
步探索。令人欣喜的是，我们已看到，我国有研究者尝试
应用阿德勒疗法治疗个体的不良行为。如赵漪蓉  和胡
娜 研究发现，使用阿德勒学派游戏疗法，儿童能够学会
表达自己的情感需求，与父母和老师的关系得到改善，情

绪控制能力显著加强，攻击性行为明显减少，社会交往能
力也有所提高。李银春  在对大学生网络成瘾的实证研
究中发现，控制组 （不使用阿德勒取向团体辅导技术 ）和试
验组 （使用阿德勒取向团体辅导技术 ）的社会兴趣得分具
有显著差异，发展社会兴趣能够有效干预网络成瘾行为。
3.3　重视治疗效果
阿德勒心理治疗注重治疗的过程研究，而缺乏结果研
究。该疗法使用大量的心理治疗共同因素，有研究者认为
共同因素对心理治疗结果的贡献比专有成分更大。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
该疗法使用大量的心理治疗共同因素，有研究者认为
共同因素对心理治疗结果的贡献比专有成分更大。阿德
勒心理治疗与治疗结果的共同要素存在许多共同点，如强
调治疗关系 、 采用多样的治疗模式和灵活的治疗技术 、
关注治疗之外的因素和来访者因素 （如来访者自身的力量
和能力 ），以及在治疗过程中强化个体的积极信念及其主
观体验。阿德勒心理治疗与理性 −情绪治疗 、 认知 −行为
治疗 、家庭治疗 、建构主义治疗等流派存在较多的重叠。
例如， Sperry 认为，阿德勒心理治疗与认知 −行为治疗至
少存在三个共同点 ：（1）注重个体的认知因素，阿德勒学派
称为生活风格，认知治疗称为认知图式； （2）强调形成平等
合作的治疗关系； （3）认为治疗是重新教育与认知改变的
过程。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
这些因素使人们难以明确指出研究结果中阿德勒
心理治疗究竟做出哪些贡献，以致对它的有效性产生怀疑。
无怪 乎 Watkins 等会评论说 ： “ 尽管有大量的研究文献支
持阿德勒学派心理学理论的核心理念，但关注阿德勒心理
治疗效果的研究文献却很罕见且难以找到。 ”32 为了解
决这一关键问题，阿德勒学派可采用个别研究 、案例研究
或者质性研究方法，深入而有效地探讨治疗的结果，更好
地促进该疗法的发展。
4　评价与展望
相对于精神分析学派把人看作为病态的生物体，行为
主义把人等同于低等的动物，阿德勒学派主张恢复和弘扬
人的整体性 、独特性 、社会性和创造性。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
该学派认为，每
个人都是一个完整的不可分割的整体，都试图归属于某个
社会群体；每个人都有自由选择的权利，并对自己的行为
负责；每个人都从自己的主观经验出发认识世界，在特定
的社会背景中理解每个人如何应对生活问题。阿德勒心
理治疗摒弃传统的医学治疗模式，开启人文治疗模式的大
门，扭转心理治疗的发展方向。阿德勒心理治疗对以人为
中心治疗 、 存在主义治疗 、 理性 −情绪行为治疗 、 认知 −
行为治疗 、 叙事治疗等都产生直接或间接影响。不管后
来提出新的心理治疗方法的学者是否提及自己受惠于阿
德勒心理治疗，但我们都可以看到许多心理治疗方法与阿
德勒学派的观点和方法之间具有相似或相通之处。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
尽管
今天明确声称属于 “阿德勒学派 ”的治疗师人数并不多，
但阿德勒的观点和技术已经微妙而又悄无声息地渗入当
今许多治疗取向中，以至于我们 “不应问某人是否是阿德
勒学派，而应说某人隶属阿德勒学派的程度如何 ” 。
经过几代人的努力 、近百年的发展，阿德勒心理治疗
已经形成一套行之有效的治疗体系和相对成熟的操作流
程。该疗法在理论上具有某种发展的活力，也具有很强的
整合性，在技术上表现出折衷灵活性 ，既可以在多种环
境，如学校 、 私人诊所 、 住院和门诊环境中，也可以在多
种模式，如一对一 、家庭 、团体中发挥作用 。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
面对当前
心理治疗界出现的整合发展趋势以及阿德勒学派内部呈
现出的多元化局面，阿德勒学派研究者们依然清醒地看到，
该学派不能停滞不前，它必须向新的方向发展。研究者们
不断地进行各种尝试，努力将阿德勒心理治疗和当前盛行
的其他流派理论 、技术进行有效整合，如叙事治疗 、建构
主义治疗 、焦点短程治疗等。励骅等  指出， “阿德勒学
派的方法为整合不同的治疗形态和形式提供了一种稳固
的基础。 ” 这个稳固的基础即为 “ 在一个有组织的 、 连
贯的理论框架内，将所有关于人格理论 、精神病理学 、心
理治疗主要知识构成内在地整合起来，在这样一种统一模
式的指导下，治疗师可以更好地探求心理治疗原理 、程序
与方法的综合模式 ”  。
author: 吴杰; 郭本禹

text:
阿德勒心理治疗的最大贡献就
在于他提供了一个经受住了时间考验的综合理论，并为当
代许多心理治疗模式奠定了基础。

text:
卡伦·霍妮 ( Karen Horney ,1885 —1952)是著名的新精神分
析先驱 ,社会文化学派的重要代表人物。霍妮最初是因反对弗
洛依德关于女性心理的论述而扬名精神分析界 ,尽管如此 ,当她
发现“不可能区分出什么实质上是女性的时候 ,毅然放弃了探讨
‘女性本质’,转而研究一种能推动整个人类人格完善的理论即
神经症理论”[1 ]。霍妮本人关于神经症的著述很多 ,对其神经症
理论的总结得很困难 ,国内心理学界鲜有关于其神经症理论的
总结就是一个例证。对霍妮神经症理论的疏理总结 ,不仅有利
于我们能够系统的把握其思想 ,而且对于丰富咨询理论、启示临
床经验 ,对于建构和谐的社会文化都有重要的意义。
霍妮对神经症的论述抛弃了弗洛伊德的本能论 ,
author: 丁建略; 田浩

text:
而且对于丰富咨询理论、启示临
床经验 ,对于建构和谐的社会文化都有重要的意义。
霍妮对神经症的论述抛弃了弗洛伊德的本能论 ,从阻碍儿
童心理自由成长的环境因素着眼 ,以追求安全感、消除基本焦虑
的神经症驱力为线索 ,纵向地探讨了神经症的动态过程 [2 ] ,揭示
了神经症的心理历程 ,并最后回观了社会文化的和谐建构问题。
虽然霍妮的思想大致经历了三个阶段[3 ] ,神经症成熟理论的形
成也经历了一个过程 ,但这一理论线索贯彻了霍妮神经症研究
的始末。本文正是依据这一理论线索对霍妮成熟的体系化的神
经症理论进行述评。
1 　神经症的起源
霍尼认为 ,儿童的健康成长需要一个“温暖的氛围”,而家庭
是儿童得到这种氛围最重要、最基本的环境。
author: 丁建略; 田浩

text:
1 　神经症的起源
霍尼认为 ,儿童的健康成长需要一个“温暖的氛围”,而家庭
是儿童得到这种氛围最重要、最基本的环境。但是 ,父母由于自

的基本需要得不到满足 ,甚至感到威胁 ;儿童被迫接受一种外来
的强迫意愿 ;儿童不能真实的表达自己的情感等 ,这使儿童内心
产生一种排斥父母的力量 ,而儿童又因为弱小 ,渴望父母的满

症驱力。
2 　神经症的人际关系策略
由基本冲突导致的基本焦虑包含三种因素 :无助感、敌意、
孤立感。儿童必须作出三种相应的人际关系策略去缓解这三种
情感。霍妮把人际关系策略区分为趋众、逆众、离众。无助感迫
使儿童顺从他人 ,顺从他人可以缓解儿童的无助感。敌意导致
逆众的人际关系策略 ,孤立感导致离众人际关系策略。但由于
这三种人际关系策略本身是矛盾、不可协调的 ,会涉及到各不相
同的性格构成和行为取向 ,
author: 丁建略; 田浩

text:
孤立感导致离众人际关系策略。但由于
这三种人际关系策略本身是矛盾、不可协调的 ,会涉及到各不相
同的性格构成和行为取向 ,因此 ,儿童被置于强烈的内心冲突之
中。为了消除内心冲突 ,获得行为动力和整体感 ,个体会强调其
中一种人际关系策略使其成为主导倾向。这一过程具有强制
性 ,即个体必须通过强调一种人际策略来内心冲突。由基本焦
虑到主导倾向的形成过程霍妮称之为“转移”。但是 ,其它转移
倾向并没有消失 ,仍继续存在 ,主导倾向和非主导倾向的冲突为
神经症的进一步发展埋下了祸根。

需要指出的是 ,霍妮是根据神经症的动力原则来进行类型

3 　神经症的心理内防御策略
儿童采用人际关系策略试图来对付基本焦虑 ,然后使其中
一种策略占主导地位并抑制其他策略 ,以这种方式来处理各种
策略之间的冲突。然而 ,这种人际关系策略并没有给患者带来
宁静的内心世界。主导倾向和非主导倾向之间的冲突以及随之
相伴的无能、焦虑、软弱等感受迫使患者继续寻找进一步的防
御 ,即心理内防御策略。心理内防御策略启动的标志是理想化
形象的出现。
理想化形象为解决主导倾向和非主导倾向之间的冲突而产
生 ,它通过强化主导倾向的价值观、情感取向、行为方式来以绝
对的形式获得统一感。
author: 丁建略; 田浩

text:
理想化形象为解决主导倾向和非主导倾向之间的冲突而产
生 ,它通过强化主导倾向的价值观、情感取向、行为方式来以绝
对的形式获得统一感。但压抑的非主导倾向并没有消失 ,冲突
依然存在。为了获得更彻底的统一感和避免冲突带来的焦虑 ,
个体创造了更完美的理想化形象。它把由基本冲突导致的三种
性格结构整合进理想化形象的三个层面里 ,看成是丰富心灵的
几个和谐部分。在这里 ,对立面显得很调和 ,主导倾向和非主导
倾向所涉及的价值、信念、情感显得毫不冲突 ,相反被认为是种
种崇高品质的超级组合 ,使个体获得彻底的统一感。在这一过
程中 ,理想化形象代替真实自我成为各种意愿、动机、自我统一
感的动力来源 ,进一步疏离了真实自我 ,使自我实现的力量从此
趋向于实现理想化形象。
理想化形象是完美无暇的 ,
author: 丁建略; 田浩

text:
进一步疏离了真实自我 ,使自我实现的力量从此
趋向于实现理想化形象。
理想化形象是完美无暇的 ,实现它成为个体生活的全部意
义。个体一方面为理想化自我 (理想化形象随着神经症的发育
逐渐变成理想化自我)感到强烈的骄傲 ,并据此对别人提出神经
质的要求 ,按照自己的理想化自我要求受到相应的待遇 ,个体按
照理想化自我的“专横的应该”(tyrannical shoulds)来衡量一切 ,
形成了霍妮称之为的“骄傲系统”。另一方面 ,当现实自我无法
实现那些不具现实意义的理想化自我应该时 ,就会产生自我憎
恨 ,即理想化自我憎恨现实自我的软弱无能 ,其结果就是产生了
被鄙视的自我。自我憎恨及由理想化自我产生的内心冲突一旦
增长 ,个体就会加强对理想化自我的认同 ,
author: 丁建略; 田浩

text:
其结果就是产生了
被鄙视的自我。自我憎恨及由理想化自我产生的内心冲突一旦
增长 ,个体就会加强对理想化自我的认同 ,导致进一步的自我赞
美 (其结果是更强烈的自我憎恨和进一步的自我赞美) 。自我憎
恨和自我赞美成了一对不断恶性循环的冲突。为了应对由于理
想化自我而带来的这种额外内心冲突 ,个体启动了以行为和想
象来实现理想化自我的强迫性努力 ,即霍妮所谓的追求荣耀的
过程。这种追求往往以渴求绝对事物的形式出现 ,其具体内容
取决患者的主导倾向。骄傲系统的形成和追求荣耀的启动标志
着患者走到了自我疏离的尽头。
4 　神经症的最终表现
为了应对最初的基本冲突而采取的人际关系策略却引发了
主导倾向和非主导趋向之间的冲突 ,
author: 丁建略; 田浩

text:
4 　神经症的最终表现
为了应对最初的基本冲突而采取的人际关系策略却引发了
主导倾向和非主导趋向之间的冲突 ,为了消除这一冲突而启动
的理想化形象等一系列心理内策略却引发了自我疏离。神经症
患者在防御策略的指引下 ,每一次消除冲突的努力都进一步加
剧了冲突 ,促进了神经症的进一步恶化 ,造成个体与自我、与他
人关系的紊乱 ,并最终形成神经症的性格结构。
霍妮把由于防御性策略而形成的性格结构称之为保护性结
构。保护性结构虽然表面上极具整体感 ,精心构造貌似坚固 ,实
际上却极为脆弱和矛盾 ,患者时刻处于恐惧之中 ,不得不小心翼
翼应对内置冲突的性格结构 ,怕打破平衡、怕暴露冲突 ,怕精神
错乱等 ,
author: 丁建略; 田浩

text:
患者时刻处于恐惧之中 ,不得不小心翼
翼应对内置冲突的性格结构 ,怕打破平衡、怕暴露冲突 ,怕精神
错乱等 ,这都会引发各种各样的具体神经症 ,如偏执狂、强迫症、
人格衰竭等。霍妮区分了神经症的性格紊乱和神经症的临床症
状两个概念。霍妮认为 ,各种各样的具体神经症是神经症的临
床症状 ,它可以表现各异 ,但都是由神经症的性格紊乱决定的。
性格紊乱不一定引发具体的神经症症状 ,同样的性格紊乱也可
以引发不同的神经症临床症状。霍妮还区分了情景性神经症和
人格性神经症 ,前者是由于创伤性事件或由于外在的冲突性情
景缺乏处理能力而形成的暂时的不良反应方式 ,
author: 丁建略; 田浩

text:
霍妮还区分了情景性神经症和
人格性神经症 ,前者是由于创伤性事件或由于外在的冲突性情
景缺乏处理能力而形成的暂时的不良反应方式 ,后者是由于人
际关系紊乱伴随着人格的形成而形成的。
然而 ,并不是所有的人都能够成功的采用人际关系策略与
心理内防御策略应对神经症冲突的。神经症冲突持久得不到解
决就会产生无望感 ,一方面 ,它可能会使一部分人放弃对生活的
认真探索而转向生活的边缘 ,试图从某种刺激性行为 ,如过度抽
烟、酗酒、纵欲 ,中攫取幸福。这就会使神经症患者成为老烟枪、
酗酒狂、纵欲狂。另一方面 ,它也可能使神经症患者极具破坏
性 ,通过奴役、玩弄、挫败他人以求代偿自己的生活成为虐待狂。
author: 丁建略; 田浩

text:
另一方面 ,它也可能使神经症患者极具破坏
性 ,通过奴役、玩弄、挫败他人以求代偿自己的生活成为虐待狂。
5 　神经症的治疗
神经症的心理历程显示神经症是与他人关系、与自我关系
的紊乱的结果 ,因此 ,神经症的治疗过程是帮助患者建立良好的
人际关系 ,放弃理想化自我 ,坦然的接受现实自我。神经症的治
疗目的是由神经症的本质决定的。神经症本质上是与健康相悖
的异化 ,是真实自我的丧失 ,因此 ,神经症的最终治疗目的是帮
助患者获得内心独立和自由、自发的情感和行为、生命能量的充
分发挥。
霍妮指出 ,神经症患者都有受神经症驱力驱使维持现状的

霍妮认为 ,通过治疗达到一种完满的健康状态是不可能的。
完满的健康状态是机能充分或自我实现 [5 ]。它只是我们的一个
理想 ,它的价值就在于能够指导我们的治疗和生活。霍妮意识

6 　对霍妮神经症理论的评价
霍妮神经症理论是对弗洛伊德批判地继承 ,是弗洛伊德神
经症理论的重大新发展。弗洛伊德的传统精神分析认为 ,神经
症是由文明和本能的冲突引起的。在弗洛伊德看来 ,由于本能
需要释放而文明又压抑本能 ,这一冲突持久得不到解决最终导
致神经症。霍尼神经症的理论继承了“神经症是由得不到解决
的冲突引起的”这一思想 ,但是在引起神经症的具体冲突上 ,霍
尼从社会文化的理论视角出发得出了神经症是由基本焦虑引起
的结论。
author: 丁建略; 田浩

text:
但是在引起神经症的具体冲突上 ,霍
尼从社会文化的理论视角出发得出了神经症是由基本焦虑引起
的结论。
霍妮神经症理论对弗洛伊德的批判性继承还体现在 :她反
对弗洛伊德把神经症内驱力解释为力比多现象 ,但她继承了弗
洛伊德动力学思想[6 ] ,认为导致人格紊乱的神经症内驱力是追
求安全和克服焦虑 ;她反对弗洛伊德的机械进化论思想 ,但她继
承了进化论思想 ,承认儿童早期经验对神经症的影响的同时认
为神经症人格发育的方式是通过每一步制约下一步实现的 ;霍
妮批判弗洛伊德一味地以“过去解释现在”的历时方法 ,在承认

text:
Recent advances in the understanding of personality disorder and disturbed personality functioning have enabled us to
extend the clinical application of TFP to patients suffering from deficits in self-functioning and interpersonal functioning at different levels
of severity. The range of severity spans from, at the mildest level of
severity, neurotic level of personality organization, and with increasing
levels of severity, high-borderline organization, mid-borderline organization and, finally, at the level of most extreme severity, low-borderline
level of organization (Caligor, Kernberg, Clarkin, & Yeomans, 2018).
The enhanced application of TFP is called TFP extended (TFP-E).
In this article we provide an overview of recent developments of
three central aspects of the TFP-E approach: (1) a model of personality
pathology (object relations theory), (2) the assessment of levels of severity of personality organization, and (3) the basic principles of TFP-E as
applied to the individual patient with a particular level of personality pathology severity. Whereas other articles in this series discuss the
application of TFP-E to various patient groups and treatment settings,
this overview focuses on the individual treatment format for adults
with various levels of severity of personality organization.
RECENT ADV ANCES IN THE PSYCHOTHERAPY FIELD
Advances in TFP have occurred in a context of advances in the wider
psychotherapy field.

Whereas other articles in this series discuss the
application of TFP-E to various patient groups and treatment settings,
this overview focuses on the individual treatment format for adults
with various levels of severity of personality organization.
RECENT ADV ANCES IN THE PSYCHOTHERAPY FIELD
Advances in TFP have occurred in a context of advances in the wider
psychotherapy field. Whereas the randomized clinical trial continues
to be dominant in assessing the impact of a particular intervention, it is
now commonly recognized that the randomized clinical trial based on
the selection of patients on the basis of individual Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) diagnoses, including individual
personality disorder diagnoses, has serious limitations (Norcross &
Wampold, 2018). More precisely, within the criteria-defined DSM categorical system, multiple comorbid conditions and varying levels of
severity assure substantial patient heterogeneity that influences treatment outcome. Future research must capture this patient complexity as
related to treatment outcome.
In contrast, the DSM-5 alternative model for personality disorders
(AMPD; American Psychiatric Association, 2013) attempts to address
the issue of heterogeneity and severity by defining the core of personality pathology as dysfunction in self functioning and other functioning
(Clarkin, Caligor, & Sowislo, 2020) and construction of a severity rating for each patient.

In contrast, the DSM-5 alternative model for personality disorders
(AMPD; American Psychiatric Association, 2013) attempts to address
the issue of heterogeneity and severity by defining the core of personality pathology as dysfunction in self functioning and other functioning
(Clarkin, Caligor, & Sowislo, 2020) and construction of a severity rating for each patient. This approach is in line with conceptualizations of
personality pathology as a large general factor of dysfunction (Sharp

190 CLARKIN, CALIGOR, AND SOWISLO
et al., 2015), similar to our construct of borderline organization (Kernberg, 1984). Some have gone a step further in addressing heterogeneity,
noting that every patient is unique, and that treatment must be per -
sonalized and address the individual in his/her environmental context
(Wright & Woods, 2020).
The manualized treatment approach with the goal of encoding clear
and consistent guidelines and procedures for the treatment of every
diagnostic condition is not only daunting but redundant given the multiple comorbidities among patients. Instead, Barlow, Allen, and Choate (2004) have suggested a transdiagnostic approach in which there
are common therapeutic approaches to domains of functioning such
as the various manifestations of anxiety. To further refine the match
between the patient and the particular treatment approach, precision
medicine has been applied to psychotherapy with attempts to match
patients to specific treatments when multiple approaches are available
(DeRubeis et al., 2014).
author: John F. Clarkin; Eve Caligor; Julia Sowislo

text:
To further refine the match
between the patient and the particular treatment approach, precision
medicine has been applied to psychotherapy with attempts to match
patients to specific treatments when multiple approaches are available
(DeRubeis et al., 2014). This approach would use patient characteristics
beyond the diagnosis per se to guide treatment selection (Keefe et al.,
2020). Others (Norcross & Lambert, 2018) have summarized the work
of successive review groups on empirically based psychotherapy relationships; moving beyond the examination of specific treatment techniques, they underscore the empirically supported importance of the
therapist–patient relationship to treatment outcome.
Advances in psychoanalytic thinking about personality functioning
and dysfunction have also contributed to the overall development of
TFP-E. The development and articulation of the Psychodynamic Diagnostic Manual (PDM-2; Lingiardi & McWilliams, 2017) is an example
of contemporary developments in psychodynamic approaches to the
description and assessment of personality pathology. Where TFP-E
remains somewhat discrepant with much of the larger psychoanalytic
world is the TFP-E model’s emphasis on patient assessment, definition
of treatment goals, and active pursuit of transference themes in the
patient’s everyday life and with the therapist.
These advances in the overall world of psychotherapy development
combined with our own theoretical, clinical, and research experience
have resulted in major refinements in our assessment and treatment of
the heterogeneity of patients who meet criteria for personality disor -
ders.
author: John F. Clarkin; Eve Caligor; Julia Sowislo

text:
These advances in the overall world of psychotherapy development
combined with our own theoretical, clinical, and research experience
have resulted in major refinements in our assessment and treatment of
the heterogeneity of patients who meet criteria for personality disor -
ders. We highlight the following: Our clinical assessment of the patient
is consistent with the DSM 5’s AMPD but focuses specifically on the
level of personality organization, diagnosed using the clinical Structural Interview or a semistructured interview, the Structured Interview
of Personality Organization—Revised (Clarkin, Caligor, Stern, & Kernberg, 2016). Our treatment manuals are principle-driven, rather than
describing procedures in lockstep fashion, with the aim of assisting the

clinician in applying the principles flexibly to the individual patient
in different clinical situations and phases of treatment. The degree to
which the treatment is structured from the beginning varies with the
level of personality organization, as does the progression of levels of
interpretation of the dominant object relations (Clarkin et al., 2020).
Our extensive clinical and research experience with the assessment
and treatment of a wide range of patients with personality pathology
has led to the following two-faceted formulation: (1) the complexity of
the individual patient goes beyond the assessment of traits and categorical diagnoses of personality disorder, and (2) the treatment of these
complex individuals must be flexible and adapted to the level of per -
sonality organization and environmental condition of the patient.

text:
This
interaction of patient complexity/severity and treatment flexibility is
captured in our current conceptualization of levels of personality organization as matched to the process of therapeutic interpretation within
a carefully constructed treatment frame (Clarkin, Caligor, & Sowislo,
in press). In the next sections, we describe the theoretical model, the
nosology and assessment, the treatment, and related clinical research.
Recent modifications, refinements, and advances in TFP are woven into
this description.
OBJECT RELATIONS MODEL OF PERSONALITY PATHOLOGY
The model of personality pathology and levels of personality organization is based upon the clinical and theoretical writings of Otto Kernberg (Kernberg, 1975, 1984), along with recent reformulations with colleagues and related empirical work (for a summary see Horz- Sagstetter
et  al., 2018). This model predates and has been a contributor to Criterion A of personality pathology in the recently published DSM-5
AMPD (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
The concept of identity and its healthy or maladaptive development
is the cornerstone of the object relations theory model of personality
functioning and disorder. Object relations theory refers to a group of
psychodynamic models that view the internalization of early patterns of
relating as central to psychic development and function.1 Early and continuing interactions between the developing infant, child, and adolescent contribute to accumulating mental representations of self and others that are affectively charged. Assisted by a supportive interpersonal
environment with a predominance of positive affect, the individual with
normal identity formation possesses a core sense of self that is relatively
stable, coherent, and realistic across different situations.
author: John F. Clarkin; Eve Caligor; Julia Sowislo

text:
Assisted by a supportive interpersonal
environment with a predominance of positive affect, the individual with
normal identity formation possesses a core sense of self that is relatively
stable, coherent, and realistic across different situations. This central
concept of self enables the individual to experience a cognitive-affective
G4949.indd 191G4949.indd 191 5/19/2021 11:36:10 AM5/19/2021 11:36:10 AM
192 CLARKIN, CALIGOR, AND SOWISLO
connection with others that is nuanced and well modulated. In contrast,
failures in normal identity formation can lead to various levels of identity pathology, described as high-, mid-, and low-level borderline organization (Clarkin et al., 2020). These failures of normal identity formation are characterized by a sense of self and others that is superficial,
unstable, and often distorted, accompanied by affects that are predominantly negative and poorly modulated. Failure of identity formation
reflects the impact of splitting-based defenses, which dissociate mental
states and representations of self in relation to other colored by positive
affect from those colored by negative affect states, interfering with normal integrative processes and with identity consolidation.
NOSOLOGY: LEVELS OF PERSONALITY ORGANIZATION
The nosology that flows from this model combines dimensions of
severity of pathology of internal object relations as described, with
tendencies related to affiliation (introversion vs. extraversion), while
providing a prototypic classification of personality pathology across
four levels of personality organization. The four levels of personality
organization are characterized by different levels of identity integration, quality of object relations, defensive functioning, management
of aggression, and moral values.

treatment planning, and clinical process. This object relations model
of levels of personality organization has influenced the DSM-5 AMPD
(American Psychiatric Association, 2013). This dimensional model
describes personality disorders along two dimensions, namely level
of personality functioning (Criterion A) and pathological personality
traits (Criterion B).

EXTENDED TREATMENT MODEL
The TFP-E treatment model can be articulated at a general level on
the basis of its treatment focus, that of promoting identity integration,
and its intervention strategies, which combine structure and limitsetting with psychodynamic exploration. Recent advances have elaborated how, within the framework of these general principles, strategies

of intervention must be differentially applied according to patient
severity and phase of treatment. Our extensive clinical and research
experience with narcissistic personality organization and borderline
personality organization patients has made it clear that patients do not
enter treatment with the same capacity for change. Patients at different
levels of personality organization experience crucial differences in their
perception of self and others and their level of affect regulation in daily
interactions, informing their experience of the treatment setting and
of the therapist. In addition, it is our clinical observation that patients
begin treatment in different phases of their severe personality disorder.

The natural history of borderline personality disorder involves more
impulsivity, affect dysregulation, and self-destructive behavior in the
20s and less self-destructive behavior but more depression and continued social dysfunction in the 30s and 40s. These factors require sophisticated initial assessment and individual case formulation.
Model of Change
The overall aim of TFP is to reduce patients’ symptoms and inter -
personal difficulties manifested in work/profession and friendship/
intimacy deficits. This aim is accomplished through focus on the
patient–therapist relationship, which exposes and provides opportunity to modify the mental representations of self and others that drive
the patient’s experience and maladaptive behavior. Because patients
at a neurotic level of organization and those at the borderline level of
organization differ in terms of cognitive biases and affective dysregulation, the TFP-E treatment approaches to these two groups of patients
vary accordingly.
For patients at the neurotic level of personality organization, transference manifestations are subtle, the distortions in self-other representations are nuanced, and affect regulation is generally evident but variable in conflict situations. In contrast, for patients at a borderline level
of organization, transference manifestations are intense and dominated
by primitive elements, self-other representations are characterized by
sharp division of positive and negative evaluations, and affective reactions are extreme.

In contrast, for patients at a borderline level
of organization, transference manifestations are intense and dominated
by primitive elements, self-other representations are characterized by
sharp division of positive and negative evaluations, and affective reactions are extreme. From a psychoanalytic object relations view, the predominance of highly charged negative affect states is seen as driving
the activation of splitting- based defenses and related dissociative processes. In particular, negative affective experience invades and colors
representations of self and others, and these representations are dissociated from positive affective experience. These dynamics interfere

Consistent with the dominance of negative affect in the object relations model of personality pathology, the treatment model posits a central role for affect activation and increasing affect containment in the
therapeutic process (Caligor, Diamond, Yeomans, & Kernberg, 2009;
Levy et  al., 2006). This model acknowledges the necessity of affect
arousal in the treatment setting, made safe by the containing structure
provided by the treatment frame and contract. The structured treatment setting provides opportunity to examine, clarify, confront, and
modify extreme mental representations and related affects activated in
the emotionally “hot” experience of others. This approach is consistent
with current understanding of primitive affects and their contribution
to numerous forms of psychopathology (Panksepp & Biven, 2012).

Patient Assessment and Treatment Selection
The goal of the initial clinical assessment of an individual with suspected personality pathology is to understand current symptoms and
difficulties, to diagnose the level of personality organization, to provide
feedback to the patient, and to negotiate a treatment plan.
The assessment of levels of personality organization by using the
clinical Structural Interview (Kernberg, 1981) or the semistructured
interview Structured Interview of Personality Organization—Revised
(STIPO-R; Clarkin et al., 2016; Stern et al., 2010) enables the clinician
to diagnose the patient’s level of personality organization, essential
for treatment formulation and determination of the parameters treatment. Empirical support for this typology was found by using an
advanced latent structure model known as finite mixture modeling
to identify subgroups of patients with borderline personality disor -
der (Lenzenweger, Clarkin, Yeomans, Kernberg, & Levy, 2008).

public health systems in many countries provide funding for only one

Principal Intervention Strategies and Techniques
Key features of the TFP-E treatment model include: (1) framing the
treatment with a verbal contract, (2) an interventional stance characterized by concerned technical neutrality on the part of the therapist, (3)
focus on disturbed interpersonal behaviors both in the patients’ relationship with the therapist and in extra-therapy current relationships,
(4) use of a sequential process of interpretation to modify the patients’
mental representations of self and others, leading to (5) changes in the
patients’ current interpersonal world of work and intimate/love relations (see Table 2).
Treatment Frame. Following a thorough assessment, the TFP therapist
shares the diagnostic impression, focusing on identity and personality functioning and linking this to the patient’s presenting complaint.
Next, patient and therapist jointly identify treatment goals, focusing
on improving concrete aspects of self and interpersonal functioning.
Specific goals function as the “north star” of the treatment and help to
avoid separation of treatment from the patient’s day-to-day functioning. Before the therapy formally begins, the TFP therapist articulates
a verbal treatment agreement, or “treatment contract,” with the prospective patient in which the responsibilities of both therapist and
patient are stated, and a discussion of each participant’s responsibilities evolves. The treatment agreement establishes the treatment frame
along with the necessary conditions for treatment, while providing
a degree of structure needed for effective treatment of individuals
with personality pathology.

who is not omniscient but helpful.
Technical Neutrality. The basic stance of a TFP therapist is therapeutic
neutrality, that is, the stance of a neutral observer, not taking sides in
relation to the patient’s internal conflicts, and from this position fostering the patient’s observation and understanding of her own conflicts. In essence, the therapist allies herself with the patient’s capacity
for self-observation. Encouragement by the therapist of the patient’s
capacity to articulate, observe, and reflect on her own conflicts is a
major treatment goal, as reflection decreases reflex action and increases
self- observation in times of stress.
Technical neutrality does not imply a passive or noncommittal attitude
toward the patient on the part of the TFP therapist. Rather, while maintaining a neutral, nonjudgmental stance in relation to the patient’s conflicts, the TFP therapist manifests active interest and curiosity in relation
to the patient as an individual, seeking to understand the patient’s experience in depth. By maintaining technical neutrality, the therapist protects a strategic position that allows for clarification and interpretation of
dominant active transference paradigms that arise in the treatment.
Interpretive Process. The process of interpretation, as it is contained
within the structure of the treatment frame, most defines TFP . Four
discernable levels of intervention in the interpretive process have been
described (Caligor et al., 2009; Clarkin et al., 2020). These levels take on
individual detail and characteristics with each patient.

In the first phase of interpretation, the therapist works with the patient
to elaborate the dominant object relation activated in the session,

to further patient affective reactions toward the therapist. The therapist next transforms these reactions into words, putting language to the
patient’s dominant experience of himself in relation to the therapist in

patient’s dominant experience of himself in relation to the therapist in

experience me as bullying you, while you feel diminished, helpless,
and angry”). This process, when done well, results in the patient feeling
understood by the therapist, while promoting affect containment and
enhanced affect regulation in the moment.
The second phase in the interpretive process involves observing and
identifying role reversals between self and object representations within
the object relation dyad articulated in the first phase. These reversals
are often enacted, most evident in the patient’s behavior, while remaining dissociated from his dominant conscious experience. For example,
while the patient perceives himself as a bullied victim in the hands of
an aggressive, powerful other, the patient comes to aggressively attack
and bully the therapist. In this process, the patient still sees himself in
the familiar role of victim, while, without reflection and largely without
awareness, behaves as victimizer and attacker. An alert therapist points
out these role reversals, helping the patient to tolerate awareness of
dissociated (typically aggressive) aspects of his behavior and experience, and then inviting him to reflect upon their possible meaning. (“I
understand that you feel bullied by me. At the same time, I wonder
if you can step back for a moment and consider that your behavior,
raising your voice and berating me, might leave me feeling bullied
as well.”)
