The therapist invites the patient to observe and reflect on the
polarized and contradictory aspects of the experience of the therapist
across time. (“I appreciate that you experience me right now as caring
and nurturing. At the same time, I remember that at the beginning of
the session I seemed a dangerous and aggressive bully.”) This level of
intervention calls attention to the discontinuous and polarized nature
of the patient’s experience in the transference, helping the patient to
appreciate that his experience is internal and subjective, in contrast to
material and concrete, and that subjective experience is constructed
and symbolic. (For example, it is not possible that the therapist is, in
fact, both the absolute best and the absolute worst as he has seemed at
different moments.)
In the fourth phase of interpretation, the therapist provides hypotheses about the meaning of the patient’s transference experience and the
anxieties and motivations driving the patient’s defenses. (“Perhaps you
need at this moment to see me as perfectly nurturing and caring. It is as
if you feel you must split off any possibility of negative feelings. As if
you fear your positive feelings might be swamped by even a hint of the
negative ones that were so powerful earlier in the session.”)
It is important to emphasize that the process of interpretation begins
at the cognitive-affective level that the individual patient brings to
the treatment. Patients at different levels of personality organization
bring different cognitive-affective capacities, coloring the quality of
their self/other representations and their capacity for affective integration and regulation, setting limits on both the speed and the degree of
change in the treatment.

A close examination of multiple treatment cases, including published cases (e.g., Clarkin, Petrini, & Diamond, 2019), provides detailed
information about the sequence of therapeutic challenges and patient
progression of change in TFP-E. The progression of patient change
depends upon the initial severity of the patients’ pathology and other

Initial contract setting is tailored to the level of the patients’ personality organization. The patient at a neurotic level of personality organization clearly sees herself/himself as having a problem and as in the role
of seeking assistance from an expert. This clear role delineation is less
salient with patients at a borderline level of organization. As the bor -
derline level of severity increases, there is more need for the TFP therapist to clearly articulate the respective roles of patient and therapist as
part of the treatment contract.

This clear role delineation is less
salient with patients at a borderline level of organization. As the bor -
derline level of severity increases, there is more need for the TFP therapist to clearly articulate the respective roles of patient and therapist as
part of the treatment contract. The treatment contract also introduces
the behavioral frame of the treatment, for example, being on time and
ready to discuss what is on his/her mind for all sessions and accepting
the need for volunteer or part-time work. Treatment will not begin until
patient and therapist have formed a treatment contract. With border -
line patients, internal acceptance of the contract and acceptance of what
the therapist has to offer typically emerge only after careful exploration, involving clarification and confrontation, of the patient’s attitude
toward the necessary conditions of treatment.
Once the treatment begins, with the patient having accepted the conditions of treatment in the form of the treatment contract, the patient’s
conflicts begin to test the treatment frame in ways that invite therapist
attention, clarification, and interpretation. The patient’s response to the
sequence of clarification, confrontation, and interpretation is a reflection of a test of the therapeutic alliance. As the severity of personality
organization increases, it is more likely that the patient’s initial response
to therapist interventions is negative rebuttal, dismissal, or silent resistance. This phase can last for several months or more (see Clarkin et al.,
2019), but in many cases even during this phase the patient begins to
show hints of affectionate attachment to the therapist, with an increasing receptivity to therapist interventions.
author: John F. Clarkin; Eve Caligor; Julia Sowislo

text:
This phase can last for several months or more (see Clarkin et al.,
2019), but in many cases even during this phase the patient begins to
show hints of affectionate attachment to the therapist, with an increasing receptivity to therapist interventions.
From case data, we can identify patients who demonstrate symptomatic, often behavioral improvements (e.g., beginning to do volunteer
work or working part time) but show no structural change (e.g., little
change in negative perceptions of self and others, little improvement in
friendships and intimate relations). The more complete change, including behavioral and structural change, seems to be related to pretreatment patient characteristics (e.g., lack of antisocial traits) and active,
emotional engagement with the therapist and the therapy. Different
domains of functioning change at different rates; patients at a border -

HETEROGENEITY IN THE THERAPIST–PATIENT MATCH:
THE ROLE OF PEER CONSULTATION
The psychotherapy research community has emphasized the need
for a treatment manual that carefully describes the treatment, to
ensure the treatment is actually being delivered, to make it possible
to rate therapist adherence and competence, and to enable faithful
replication of the treatment at different sites. These guidelines have
influenced our research and our clinical work.
author: John F. Clarkin; Eve Caligor; Julia Sowislo

text:
These guidelines have
influenced our research and our clinical work. In both, we utilize
weekly peer consultation in a group format looking at videotaped
therapy sessions. It is our observation that therapist adherence and
competence in TFP is not a trait phenomenon but rather varies somewhat from case to case. A very talented and competent therapist can
experience substantial difficulties in a particular case. This can happen in a number of ways, but, in general, it is related to the patients’
behavior and the transference– countertransference dynamic, wherein
the patient’s transference has the effect of drawing the therapist into
a collusion with the patient’s dysfunctional attitudes and behavior.
For example, one experienced therapist was drawn into the dismissive style of a borderline patient, and the therapist adopted that
style in return. An overriding role of peer consultation is to alert the
therapist to countertransference reactions that could be distorting the
treatment. Often such countertransferences are at least to some degree
outside of the therapist’s awareness, requiring the “third eye” of the
supervision group to be fully identified.
RECENT ADV ANCES FROM THE EMPIRICAL
EVIDENCE ON TFP
We are a group of medical college academics and practicing clinicians
who are focused on examining our psychotherapy efforts with empirical
methods. Our interests start with the pathology and treatment of the individual patient and expand to potential similarities between groups and
subgroups of patients that become evident in our data. We have taken
a systematic, stepwise approach to the empirical development of TFP
(Kazdin, 2004), and briefly summarize here our advances in this area.

Articulation of a Principle-Driven Treatment Manual
A beginning step was the development of a principle-driven treatment manual (Clarkin et al., 1999) based on principles of intervention

RECENT ADV ANCES IN TFP-E 207
used by senior clinicians working with seriously disturbed personality disorder patients as viewed on video recordings of actual sessions.
Every clinician knows that no two patients are alike even given the
same diagnosis, especially as the transference evolves over time. We
have attempted to advance the art of psychotherapy by writing principle-based treatment manuals because every patient–therapist treatment episode is unique. It is the task of the therapist to apply the TFP-E
principles to the unique and individual situation.
Our manuals have progressed from the first principle-driven
manual for TFP and the treatment of borderline personality disor -
der, to the current manual describing the object relations treatment
of patients with varying levels of disturbed personality organization
(Caligor et  al., 2018). This advance recognizes both the complexity
and uniqueness of every patient and the flexible application of the key
principles of TFP-E.

Treatment Development Study
The next step was a treatment development study funded by
National Institute of Mental Health (Clarkin et  al., 2001). Borderline
patients were treated in 1 year of TFP . The treatment was well received,
the dropout rate was low (19.1%), and none of the patients deteriorated
or were adversely affected by the treatment. Compared to the year
prior to treatment, patients experienced significantly fewer psychiatric
hospitalizations, fewer days of inpatient hospitalization, and a reduction in the number of suicide attempts. These results suggested that
TFP was effective in lowering health care costs incurred by emergency
room visits and hospitalizations. The reduction in hospitalizations also
provides room for the more normal development in the community for
the patient.
Randomized Clinical Trial
Based on these encouraging results we conducted a randomized
clinical trial in which TFP was compared to dialectical behavior ther -
apy (DBT) and a dynamically oriented supportive treatment (Clarkin
et al., 2007) delivered in individual treatment format over 1 year. Individual growth-curve analysis (Lenzenweger, Johnson, & Willett, 2004)
was used to investigate change in symptoms and domains of functioning over time. All three treatments showed significant change across
multiple domains after 1 year of treatment.

Individual growth-curve analysis (Lenzenweger, Johnson, & Willett, 2004)
was used to investigate change in symptoms and domains of functioning over time. All three treatments showed significant change across
multiple domains after 1 year of treatment. However, only TFP and

DBT were associated with improvement in suicidality, and only TFP
was significantly associated with improvement in impulsivity, irritability, and verbal and direct assault. Our impression from this first randomized controlled trial was that all three structured treatments were
effective with borderline patients with significant structural pathology,
but that TFP was unique in the reduction of aggression, possibly due
to the close examination of aggression in the patients’ transferences in
treatment.
We utilized a subsample from this study to further explore the patient
pretreatment predictors of change in three specific domains of functioning (aggression dyscontrol, global functioning, and anxiety/depression
and impulsivity; Lenzenweger et  al., 2012). Lower pretreatment levels of negative affect and aggression were associated with more rapid
clinical improvement in aggressive dyscontrol. Higher pretreatment
identity diffusion was associated with more rapid clinical improvement in global functioning. Lower initial levels of social potency were
associated with more rapid improvement in anxiety/depression and
impulsivity.
Randomized Controlled Trial in Different Setting
The next step in the empirical development of TFP was to evaluate
the effectiveness of TFP in a cultural setting different from that of the
original study in New York.

associated with more rapid improvement in anxiety/depression and

Randomized Controlled Trial in Different Setting
The next step in the empirical development of TFP was to evaluate
the effectiveness of TFP in a cultural setting different from that of the
original study in New York. Female borderline patients were randomized to 1 year of either TFP or treatment by community therapists experienced in the treatment of borderline patients in a two-site randomized
controlled trial conducted in Europe (Doering et al., 2010). The patients
treated with TFP showed many indications of superior improvement
over the patients in the comparison treatment: reduction in border -
line personality disorder criteria, reduction in suicide attempts, reduction in hospital treatment, and improvement in social and personality
functioning. The results of this study suggested to us that the specific
aspects of TFP as compared to treatment by local experts added to
patient improvement. However, we were still not capturing and measuring the specific effects of the interpretive process in TFP .
With the TFP focus on understanding and improving internal representations of self and others, we hypothesized that TFP would result in
changes in attachment organization and reflective functioning, which
is a measure of the capacity to understand the behavior of oneself and
others in terms of intentional mental states such as thoughts, feelings,
and beliefs (Levy et al., 2006).

to us that the interpretive process was enhancing the patients’ ability to

Neurocognitive Functioning
There is growing evidence that patients with borderline personality disorder manifest particular abnormalities in brain functioning
associated with distorted thinking about self and others (higher connectivity between limbic and midline structures), hyperreactivity to
negative stimuli (higher limbic activation; lower prefrontal activation),
and impulsivity (lower ventral striatum activation; lower ventral striatum-frontal connectivity; Gunderson, Herpertz, Skodol, Torgersen, &
Zanarini, 2018; Ruocco & Carcone, 2016; Skodol, 2018).
author: John F. Clarkin; Eve Caligor; Julia Sowislo

text:
In contrast to
the growing data on brain functioning in individuals with borderline
personality disorder, there is scarce data on the impact of treatment in
modifying brain functioning in these individuals. The hypothesized
mechanism of change in TFP is increased affect regulation achieved
through mentalization, that is, the growing ability of the patient with
borderline personality disorder to put momentary affect arousal, especially in social interactions, into a more benign and broader contextual
understanding (Levy et al., 2006). We hypothesized that as the gradual
analysis of the perception of self and others in TFP would modify the
extreme cognitive/affective perceptions, these changes would be consistent with changes in neurocognitive functioning.
In a pilot study with N=10 borderline patients manifesting prominent affect dysregulation treated in TFP for 1 year, we found changes
in brain functioning consistent with this hypothesis (Perez et al., 2016).
Patients exhibited significant change in behavioral and psychological domains over the course of 1 year of TFP , including a reduction in
affective lability, interpersonal sensitivity, and paranoia, and significant
positive changes in work functioning.
In a comparison of pretreatment and posttreatment functional magnetic resonance imaging scans, patients with borderline personality
disorder manifested relative increased activation in cognitive control
regions (right anterior–dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and right dor -
sal-lateral prefrontal cortex) and relative decreased activation in the left
inferior frontal gyrus and the left hippocampus.

SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS
The object relations model of personality functioning and pathology
and related development of TFP have both contributed to and benefited from recent advances in the field of psychotherapy and psychotherapy research on the personality disorders. Object relations theory
emphasizes both observable interpersonal behavior and the underlying
affectively charged mental representations of self in relation to others
that organize observed behavior.
author: John F. Clarkin; Eve Caligor; Julia Sowislo

text:
Object relations theory
emphasizes both observable interpersonal behavior and the underlying
affectively charged mental representations of self in relation to others
that organize observed behavior. This view is quite consistent with the
AMPD as defined by the DSM-5 and assessment of self–other functioning along dimensional lines of severity of dysfunction. Our approach
to treatment emphasizes the match of levels of personality pathology
with the process of interpretation in the context of the treatment structure. This approach is both transdiagnostic in the sense of focusing on
the core of personality dysfunction across the categories of personality disorder and also personalized for the individual patient. Whereas
randomized clinical trials pit alternative treatments against each other,
focusing on patients selected with specific personality disorder diagnoses, the approach of focusing on the relationship between patient
and therapist as an essential ingredient in all psychotherapy outcomes
(Norcross & Lambert, 2018) is quite consistent with the TFP approach to
examining and understanding the therapeutic relationship as a major
manifestation of the personality disordered patients’ core difficulties in
relating to others as a focus of needed change.
Since its initial articulation in 1999 (Clarkin et  al., 1999) TFP has
developed from an object relations treatment for patients with bor -
derline personality disorder to a specialized approach to individuals’
difficulties in self-functioning and functioning with others that is the
heart of personality pathology (Caligor et al., 2018).

difficulties in self-functioning and functioning with others that is the
heart of personality pathology (Caligor et al., 2018). A central theme
in our clinical research efforts is to advance both the science (i.e.,
empirically based group effects) and the art of long-term intensive

Extensive clinical experience with the individual treatment format in
delivering TFP has led to important modifications, including enhancing the treatment contract and structuring of the treatment, and placing emphasis on both the developing transference and the behavior
of the patient in his/her current daily life. The principles of TFP have
remained the same, but their application to a range of problems in
self-functioning and functioning with others has expanded. As other
articles in this special issue indicate, the principles of TFP are now
extending to other treatment formats (e.g., group and family formats),
and multiple treatment settings including inpatient, day hospital, and
medical environments.

text:
Introduction: Mentalization- based therapy (MBT) is an evidence- based treatment for borderline personality disorder (BPD)
and the second most studied psychotherapeutic intervention for this disorder. Despite its growing prominence, there is a lack of
focused reviews summarizing the evidence base from randomized clinical trials (RCTs). This review aims to address this gap and
highlight directions for future research.
Methods: This narrative review synthesizes findings from RCTs evaluating MBT for BPD. Building on the seven studies identified
in the Cochrane review by Storebø et al. (2020), we conducted an updated search to incorporate RCTs published to 1st April 2025,
expanding the evidence base to 14 trials. Eligible studies were assessed for effectiveness outcomes and methodological quality.
Results: While some trials report improvements in BPD symptoms and interpersonal functioning, significant limitations exist.
Research has largely focused on symptom reduction, despite concerns about the validity of categorical PD diagnoses. The trials
were predominantly conducted in European settings, involving primarily female participants, and did not sufficiently account
for BPD severity, comorbidities, or developmental stages. All identified RCTs were at high risk of bias, with significant issues
involving attention, attrition, and allegiance bias.
Conclusions: MBT shows promise, but methodological shortcomings and limited generalizability constrain its evidence base.
Future research should prioritize rigorously designed trials with diverse samples, assess core personality dysfunction using di -
mensional models, and explore adaptations for adolescents, older adults, and comorbid mental disorders to improve and broaden
the clinical utility of MBT for BPD.

1 | Introduction
Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a severe mental dis -
order characterized by instability of affects, behaviours and
interpersonal relationships (Leichsenring et  al.  2024). BPD is
furthermore associated with an increased risk of comorbidity,
severe functional impairments, high suicidal risk, intensive use
of treatment, poor treatment compliance and high societal costs
(Hastrup et al. 2019; Leichsenring et al. 2024 ).
Several evidence- based treatments that target core features
of BPD have been proposed, including mentalization- based
treatment (MBT). MBT represents the second most studied ap -
proach for BPD, only surpassed by dialectical behaviour therapy
(Storebø et  al.  2020). Mentalization was initially proposed by
Peter Fonagy (1989) and refers to the capacity to perceive and interpret oneself and others' behaviour in terms of underlying feelings, thoughts, needs, motives, desires and intentions (Bateman
and Fonagy  2010). Mentalizing is a dynamic psychological
2 of 18 Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy, 2025
capacity that has evolved in human evolutionary history as a
response to increasing social complexity.

text:
Mentalizing is a dynamic psychological
2 of 18 Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy, 2025
capacity that has evolved in human evolutionary history as a
response to increasing social complexity. Rather than being a
fixed trait, it involves state- and context- dependent processes
and is shaped by interactions with others (Allen et al.  2008; Hill
et al.  2023). Mentalization develops through early attachment
relationships and is considered a core aspect of normative de -
velopment (Fonagy and Target 1996). During early interactions,
caregivers are expected to respond sensitively to the infant's ex -
pressive behaviours, adapting to its needs and desires. Through
marked and contingent mirroring, caregivers signal their refer -
ential emotional displays, which help the child understand its
own and others' subjective experiences, and support the child in
internalizing emotional security, a sense of safety, trust, agency
and empathy (Beebe and Lachmann  2013). Engagement in in -
teractions with a mentalizing caregiver teaches the child that
information from others is reliable, relevant, safe to trust, can
be stored in memory and generalized to other contexts (Fonagy
and Allison  2014). This fosters an openness to learning, con -
ceptualized as epistemic trust, which facilitates the child's en -
gagement in joint attention, ‘we- mode’, and meaning- making
(Fonagy and Allison  2014; Fonagy and Target  1996; Sharp
et al. 2020).

This fosters an openness to learning, con -
ceptualized as epistemic trust, which facilitates the child's en -
gagement in joint attention, ‘we- mode’, and meaning- making
(Fonagy and Allison  2014; Fonagy and Target  1996; Sharp
et al. 2020).
Inadequate development of mentalizing abilities is theorized to
have significant negative consequences, potentially contribut -
ing to the emergence of various mental disorders. For exam -
ple, mentalizing is considered a central factor in the aetiology
of BPD, where childhood experiences with low parental men -
talizing may influence the quality of future interpersonal re -
lationships (Vogt and Norman  2019). BPD is associated with
impaired mentalization, epistemic mistrust, difficulties in
joint meaning- making and challenges in joint intentionality,
particularly in emotionally intense situations within close re -
lationships (Fonagy and Allison  2014). As a result, MBT has
centred its approach on therapeutic interventions aimed at en -
hancing the patient's capacity to mentalize within the context
of attachment relationships, such as the therapist–patient dyad.
Enhanced mentalizing is thought to improve emotion regu -
lation, interpersonal functioning, social cognition and cogni -
tive flexibility. The core of MBT interventions centres around
a not- knowing stance, curiosity, openness and empathy. MBT
targets mentalizing dysfunctions by utilizing interventions like
emphatic validation, clarification, elaboration, confrontation,
basic mentalization and relational mentalization (Bateman and
Fonagy 2016).

The core of MBT interventions centres around
a not- knowing stance, curiosity, openness and empathy. MBT
targets mentalizing dysfunctions by utilizing interventions like
emphatic validation, clarification, elaboration, confrontation,
basic mentalization and relational mentalization (Bateman and
Fonagy 2016).
Anthony Bateman and Peter Fonagy originally developed MBT
as a structured treatment for BPD, combining individual ther -
apy and group therapy within a day hospital setting, rooted in
mentalization- based theory. The original program consisted of
18 months of therapy (Bateman and Fonagy  2016). Since then,
MBT has been adapted and empirically tested in various set -
tings, with modifications to its scope, duration and target pop -
ulation. For example, MBT has been tailored to address specific
comorbidities, applied to adolescent populations and extended to
caregivers. More recent iterations of MBT have incorporated so -
cial contextual factors, emphasizing the importance of not only
working with individuals but also engaging with the broader
social networks, including families, peers and professionals
(Fuggle et al.  2024; Luyten et al.  2024). The growing interest in
the mentalizing approach has positioned mentalization as a crucial human capacity, extending its relevance to the understand -
ing of temporary or permanent impairments in mentalizing
across various psychopathologies (Sharp and Bevington  2022;
Luyten et al.  2020).

The most recent Cochrane review on the effectiveness of psychotherapy treatment for BPD (Storebø et al.  2020) included seven

less clear.

comes, such as anger, affective instability, chronic emptiness,
impulsivity, abandonment fears, identity disturbance, dissocia -
tion and psychotic- like symptoms. Thus, MBT's effectiveness in
these areas remains unknown.
The Cochrane review used a random- effects statistical model,
which is appropriate given the heterogeneity across studies but
tends to yield more conservative estimates to mitigate random
errors. Storebø et al. ( 2020) also applied a fixed- effects model,
assuming greater homogeneity between studies. Under this
model, MBT showed additional superiority over control inter -
ventions for BPD severity (beyond 12 months), psychosocial
functioning (at EOT) and depression (at EOT and in follow- ups
at 0–6 months and beyond 12 months).
In conclusion, Storebø et al.'s (2020) review provides a nuanced
picture of MBT's effectiveness. While the random- effects model
highlights some positive outcomes, fixed- effects analyses sug -
gest additional benefits. However, the limitations of these mod -
els and the overall methodological constraints in existing RCTs
underscore the need for further high- quality research.

1.2 | State- Of- The- Science: A Narrative Review
Previous reviews have examined the effectiveness of MBT for
BPD (e.g., Volkert et al. 2019; Wolfs 2024), generally supporting
its clinical utility. However, these reviews predate and/or do not
include several recent RCTs. Given MBT's clinical and theoret -
ical prominence, there is a need for an updated, focused review
summarizing the current evidence base from RCTs. RCTs are
considered the gold standard for evaluating the efficacy and ef -
fectiveness of psychological interventions. By minimizing biases
through random allocation, rigorous control groups, and stan -
dardized outcome measures, RCTs provide the most reliable
evidence for determining causality and assessing the impact
of therapeutic interventions (Bhide et  al.  2018). While several
non- randomized studies have highlighted the potential benefits
of MBT, only RCTs can robustly address critical questions re -
garding its effectiveness compared to other treatments or stan -
dard care. Focusing on RCTs ensures high- quality evidence to
evaluate MBT's effectiveness.

evaluate MBT's effectiveness. This approach also helps to (1)
enhance clinical relevance : By emphasizing controlled settings,
RCTs provide insights into how MBT performs under standard -

(2) enable comparisons across treatments : RCTs often include
direct comparisons between a given experimental intervention
and other therapeutic modalities, facilitating an understanding
of the relative or comparative benefits and (3) identify limita -

methodological challenges, guiding future research directions.
By narrowing the scope to RCTs, this review aims to provide
clinicians, researchers, and policymakers with a rigorous and
focused evaluation of MBT's current evidence base and point to
knowledge gaps relevant for future research.
To achieve this aim, a narrative state- of- the- science review de -
sign was utilized to synthesize current findings on the effec -
tiveness of MBT, with a focus on evidence derived from RCTs.
A state- of- the- science review is widely recognized for its ability
to provide a solid state of current knowledge within a specific
field or phenomenon (Sukhera 2022).

A state- of- the- science review is widely recognized for its ability
to provide a solid state of current knowledge within a specific
field or phenomenon (Sukhera 2022). This approach is particu -
larly valuable as it allows for the exploration of focused research
questions tailored to a specific audience, offering insights into
the current status of a particular therapeutic approach, its development and future directions (Sukhera 2022). In this review, the
state- of- the- science review design is employed to examine MBT
as a treatment modality specifically for BPD, synthesizing find -
ings from RCTs to assess its effectiveness and highlight areas
for future development. In addition to assessing the overall ef -
fectiveness of MBT, we also aim to examine the outcomes used
in the trials to measure effectiveness. By gaining an overview
of the outcomes assessed across the trials, we aim to identify
which variables of effectiveness have been explored and where
there are gaps in our knowledge, where further research is
needed to build a more comprehensive understanding of MBT's
impact.
While narrative reviews do not provide definite answers, the
design facilitates a nuanced discussion aimed at engaging prac -
titioners and researchers. The goal is to generate insights not
only into the current evidence base for MBT for BPD but also
into how research methodologies can be refined to better eval -
uate its impact. By offering a detailed and interpretive synthe -
sis of the evidence, the narrative review serves as a foundation
for establishing new perspectives and guiding future research
(Greenhalgh et al. 2018).

2 | Methods
2.1 | Search Strategy
The search strategy for this review was based on the compre -
hensive systematic review conducted by Storebø et  al.  ( 2020),
which examined psychotherapeutic interventions for BPD, in -
cluding MBT. To ensure the review includes the most up- to- date
4 of 18 Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy, 2025
evidence, we supplemented the studies identified by Storebø
et  al.  (2020) with an updated search for RCTs published from
January 2020 to 1 April 2025. The top- up search was conducted
in the following electronic databases:
• PubMed/MEDLINE
• PsycINFO
• Embase
The search strategy utilized a combination of keywords and
MeSH terms, including ‘mentalization- based therapy’, ‘border -
line personality disorder’, ‘randomized controlled trial’, and re -
lated terms.
2.2 | Eligibility Criteria
Studies were eligible for inclusion if they met the following
criteria:
1. The study was a randomized clinical trial.
2. The study evaluated the effectiveness of MBT in individ -
uals diagnosed with BPD based on established diagnostic
criteria (DSM or ICD).
3. The study reported quantitative outcomes.
Studies included in the Cochrane review were directly extracted
from the original publication, while newly identified studies
were screened by two reviewers for relevance and eligibility.

We identified 14 RCTs investigating the effectiveness of MBT

We will further elaborate on the strengths
and limitations of these studies and evaluate the quality of the
evidence.
The first RCT of MBT was conducted by Bateman and
Fonagy  (1999). Since then, MBT has been tested in various
settings and across different durations and levels of inten -
sity. Even though BPD is commonly associated with various
comorbid mental disorders, only three RCTs have specifi -
cally addressed this: one trial focused on MBT for BPD and
comorbid eating disorders (Robinson et  al.  2016), another
investigated MBT for BPD with co- occurring substance use
disorders (Philips et al.  2018) and a third tested MBT for BPD
and antisocial personality disorder (Mohajerin et  al.  2024).
Furthermore, only three RCTs to date have investigated the
effectiveness of MBT for adolescents with BPD pathology com -
pared to control treatments (Rossouw and Fonagy  2012; Beck
et al.  2020 ; Mohajerin et al.  2025), but additional studies are
currently underway (e.g., Remeeus et al.  2024). Additionally,
while substantial caregiver burden has been documented
among relatives of both adults (Bailey and Grenyer  2013)
and adolescents with BPD (Jørgensen, Storebø, Poulsen, and
Simonsen 2021), only one trial has targeted family members of
individuals with BPD (Bateman and Fonagy 2019 ).

To summarize, the results across the identified trials are
somewhat mixed. While several studies indicate positive out -
comes in MBT, the evidence base remains limited, particu -
larly for MBT in the context of comorbidities, adolescents and
family- focused interventions. The variability in trial designs,
sample sizes and use of outcomes further complicates drawing
definitive conclusions.
3.1 | Quality of the Evidence
The most recent Cochrane review summarizing the evidence for
psychological therapies for BPD (Storebø et  al.  2020) included
seven trials of MBT. Below, we will outline the risk of bias asso -
ciated with these trials based on the findings from the Cochrane
review. Additionally, since the publication of the Cochrane re -
view, seven additional trials have been conducted (Bateman and
Fonagy 2019; Beck et al. 2020; Carlyle et al. 2020; Juul et al. 2023;
Mohajerin et al.  2024; Mohajerin et al.  2025; Smits et al.  2020).

light the risk of bias we have identified for these trials.
Cochrane's tool for assessing risk of bias (Higgins et al. 2011 ) is
used to categorize trials into three categories: low risk of bias,
unclear risk of bias, or high risk of bias, according to guidelines
provided in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of
Interventions (Higgins et  al. 2024 ). The tool assesses several
types of bias, including selection bias, performance bias, detec -
tion bias, attrition bias, reporting bias and other biases (e.g., ad -
herence bias, attention bias, and allegiance bias).

3.2 | Overview of Outcomes
The outcomes (both primary and secondary) used to assess the
effectiveness of MBT for BPD are summarized in Table 3. A total
of 46 different measures were employed across trials, with 28
instruments used only once. Most of these measures focused
on symptoms related to BPD, anxiety, depression, other psycho -
pathological symptoms, as well as general and interpersonal
functioning.
4 | Discussion
This review included 14 RCTs of MBT for BPD and represents,
to the authors' knowledge, the most extensive review of MBT
to date.

4 | Discussion
This review included 14 RCTs of MBT for BPD and represents,
to the authors' knowledge, the most extensive review of MBT
to date. However, the findings on MBT's effectiveness remain
inconclusive, with substantial heterogeneity across studies and
significant limitations due to high risk of bias. Consequently,
there are critical areas requiring further investigation to opti -
mize MBT's clinical application and broaden its reach. Below,
we will outline key concerns and highlight future directions.
One striking finding of this review is the predominant focus
on symptom reduction as the primary outcome. While this
approach is common in psychotherapy research in general
(Cuijpers  2019), it becomes problematic given the limited va -
lidity and reliability of the diagnostic categories used to define
BPD symptoms. The overlap between personality disorders
(PDs) and common mental disorders (Krueger et al.  2014) further underscores the challenges in defining clear treatment tar -
gets and evaluating meaningful outcomes. As Cuijpers ( 2019,
276) aptly states, “So, if we do not yet really know what these
disorders are and how they should be defined, what should
be the targets of treatments and how can we measure their
outcomes?”

interpersonal functioning as the core distinguishing feature of
PD, future research in MBT should pivot away from individual,
categorically defined PDs to assess outcomes related to the core
of personality dysfunction, including outcomes of personality
and interpersonal functioning, such as the Level of Personality

Given that MBT aims to enhance
mentalizing capacity as the driving mechanism for improved
self and interpersonal functioning, these outcomes may better
capture the core of what MBTs seek to change than symptom
levels at a phenotypic level. Encouragingly, upcoming trials of
MBT are beginning to incorporate dimensional measures such
as the LPF (e.g., Hauschild et al. 2025).
Similarly, an important gap in the current MBT literature is the
relatively sparse assessment of mentalizing. While MBT is explicitly designed to improve mentalizing capacity and is proposed as
the core mechanism of change, few trials have directly measured
this. Addressing this gap by incorporating validated assessments
of mentalizing represents a crucial direction for future research.
Another key issue is the limited generalizability of MBT findings.
Most RCTs on MBT have been conducted on female- majority
samples. This gender homogeneity observed in the included
studies likely reflects current clinical realities where BPD is
more often diagnosed in women (Leichsenring et al.  2024), and
women are likewise more likely to seek and access mental health
care compared to men and people of other gender identities
(Seelman et al.  2017; Wendt and Shafer  2016).

Furthermore, most RCTs on MBT have been conducted in
European countries. Although two trials conducted in Iran
were included, these trials represent the only non- European
contributions and were both conducted by the same research
group. In both trials, MBT was not found to be more effective
than UP, with UP appearing more beneficial on certain out -
comes. However, due to methodological concerns, including
critical details that were omitted in terms of quality of MBT
training and adherence, and the limited number of studies
outside Europe, no firm conclusions can be drawn about the
effectiveness of MBT in non- Western contexts. These findings
do, however, underscore the importance of expanding MBT re -
search into more culturally and geographically diverse settings.

and caregiver involvement in MBT. Given the interpersonal na -

enhance treatment outcomes, yet research in this area remains
scarce (Guillén et al. 2021). Similarly, BPD frequently co- occurs
with other psychiatric disorders, including post- traumatic stress
disorder (PTSD), substance use disorders, and eating disorders.
However, the impact of these comorbidities on the effectiveness
of MBT remains poorly understood. Our review identified only
three RCTs that examined MBT in the context of BPD with co -
morbid conditions (Mohajerin et  al. 2024 ; Philips et  al.  2018;
Robinson et al. 2016). In addition, secondary analyses from ear -

clinical severity, operationalized through comorbidity (Bateman
and Fonagy  2013), as well as for those with BPD co- occurring
with antisocial personality disorder (Bateman et  al.

research should explore whether MBT requires adaptation for

Finally, negative outcomes of MBT, including potential adverse
effects, deterioration, treatment dropout and non- response, re -
main understudied. Psychotherapy research rarely investigates
unintended consequences, yet these are critical for evaluating
treatment safety and effectiveness (Cuijpers  2019; Linden and
Schermuly- Haupt 2014). Standardized reporting of negative outcomes in MBT trials would improve transparency and provide a
more balanced assessment of its risks and benefits. This concern
is amplified by the fact that several trials included in this re -
view reported no significant differences between MBT and comparator treatments on primary or secondary outcomes. While
participants in both treatment arms frequently demonstrated
meaningful clinical improvements, such as reductions in self-
harm, general psychopathology and interpersonal difficulties,
this raises important questions about the specific mechanisms
of change in MBT. In particular, it underscores the challenge
of disentangling MBT- specific effects from common therapeutic
factors.

statistical significance and treatment comparisons—is essen -

measures, alongside transparent reporting of both positive and
negative outcomes, will be crucial in refining our understanding

recognize that many of the methodological limitations identified
in MBT research are not unique to MBT but reflect broader challenges across BPD treatment trials. In fact, the Cochrane review
(Storebø et al. 2020) included 75 RCTs of psychological interventions for BPD, and found that, although BPD- specific treatments
tended to outperform non- specific comparators, every trial was
rated as having a high risk of bias due to problems in one or
more domains. This underscores that the entire evidence base
for BPD psychotherapies is methodologically underdeveloped.
Consequently, calls for more rigorous research should extend
beyond MBT to encompass the full spectrum of BPD- focused
treatments, prioritizing larger samples, blinded assessments,
standardized core outcomes, transparent reporting and care -
ful attention to treatment fidelity and allegiance. By addressing
some of the limitations regarding MBT trials to date, we can
move toward a more comprehensive and clinically useful un -
derstanding of its impact for people with BPD. Building on these
observations, we conclude by outlining several key directions to

5 | Limitations
This review focused exclusively on RCTs of MBT to provide a
more rigorous, structured and critical synthesis of the current
evidence. While this approach supports clearer conclusions re -
garding treatment outcomes under controlled conditions, it does
not capture valuable insights from non- randomized, naturalistic
or qualitative studies that can enrich understanding of real- world
implementation, therapeutic processes and patient experiences.

Introduction
Relational theorists have critiqued Freud’s drive theory, arguing that interpersonal factors—not intrapsychic drives—deﬁne mental life. For example, Greenberg (1991) calls for the “radical rejection of drive [theory]”
because “all motivation unfolds from our personal experience of exchange with others” (p. vii). Motivation theory certainly beneﬁts from this
Address correspondence to Jonathan Yahalom, M.A., Duquesne University, Psychology Department, 600 Forbes Avenue, 544 College Hall, Pittsburgh, PA 15282. E-mail:
yahalomj@duq.edu
396 JONATHAN YAHALOM, M.A.
reconceptualization: whereas motivation was once viewed as something
one has or does not possess, it is now understood as a dynamic process that is inﬂuenced by one’s relationship with another (Miller, 1994).
Yet this argument is not without consequences. Drive theory is pivotal
to psychoanalysis, and represents Freud’s ongoing attempt to secure a
solid philosophical foundation. Although psychoanalytic practice has unquestionably beneﬁted from the relational turn, it does not appear that
psychoanalytic theory (particularly of motivation) has beneﬁted as much
(Mills, 2005). This article maintains that the relational turn does have
a ﬁrm theoretical basis, albeit in the most unexpected source—Freud’s
drive theory.
The notion of drive is central to Freud’s conceptualization of psychoanalysis. From early formulations in his 1895 Project to the writings up
to his death, Freud was deeply occupied with investigating the nature
of drives and believed that it provided foundational concepts to the understanding of psychic life. Perhaps the most instructive text is Beyond
the Pleasure Principle (1920/2011; hereafter BPP), where Freud questions
the nature of pleasure and what it signiﬁes regarding the drives.

text:
Perhaps the most instructive text is Beyond
the Pleasure Principle (1920/2011; hereafter BPP), where Freud questions
the nature of pleasure and what it signiﬁes regarding the drives. In this
text, Freud follows the logical consequences of the pleasure principle to
make the surprising hypothesis that the goal of all organic life is death.
However much controversy this hypothesis has triggered, the text establishes deﬁnitive theoretical scaffolding for psychoanalytic theory: all
facets of psychic life are constituted by the pursuit of greater pleasurable
states, or, synonymously, the reduction of unpleasurable ones. Yet, this
deﬁnition fails to account for a fundamental dimension of human motivation. Freud’s notion of pleasure is remarkably quantitative and ignores
any qualitative dimension in this theoretical account.
This article postulates that quantitative and qualitative dimensions of
pleasure are each signiﬁcant and capture a different truth about pleasure.
The quantitative concept identiﬁes a fundamental nature concerning pleasure. In essence, this conceptualization of pleasure is unidimensional and
holds that all pleasures share a common form, which could be increased
or decreased in quantity. For example, this view of pleasure would postulate that the pleasures experienced in activities like walking and socializing are pleasurable because they share the same nature, and only differ
in the quantity of pleasure each activity brings. In contrast, the qualitative concept is multidimensional, attuned to different types (natures) that
are incomparable with and irreducible to each other. So, the pleasure
experienced in walking and socializing are both pleasurable, yet they
FREUD AND EPICUREAN PHILOSOPHY 397
may be pleasurable for different reasons. Hence, these two dimensions
of pleasure suggest that one cannot be equated with the other without
compromising precision about what one intends to describe about pleasure.

So, the pleasure
experienced in walking and socializing are both pleasurable, yet they
FREUD AND EPICUREAN PHILOSOPHY 397
may be pleasurable for different reasons. Hence, these two dimensions
of pleasure suggest that one cannot be equated with the other without
compromising precision about what one intends to describe about pleasure. This distinction is central to the arguments made in this article and
will be further elaborated in subsequent sections.
In what follows, I will argue that a qualitative dimension of pleasure
is presupposed in Freud’s quantitative description. To this end, I turn to
study Epicureanism, a school of ancient Greek philosophy that originated
around 300
B.C.E and ﬂourished for centuries after. Epicureanism was one
of the ﬁrst ancient schools to provide a theory of pleasure that is remarkably congruent with Freud’s deﬁnition. Moreover, Epicurean philosophy
was relational as well, simultaneously deﬁning psychic life in quantitative and qualitative terms. After a review of Epicureanism, I will turn to
Freud’s account of pleasure and situate it within the Epicurean tradition.
Those familiar with Freud’s writings may wonder why we should discuss
Epicureanism when he directly addresses other ancient philosophies. My
reasons for doing so will be articulated later. In general, however, I believe that a critical exploration of Epicureanism challenges our tendency
to equate classical drive theory with material reduction. This carries significant implications for contemporary psychoanalysis and its interpretation
of the drives.

Many commentators have pointed to similarities between ancient philosophy and psychoanalysis. Like Freud, ancient philosophers claimed
that their philosophical “truths” could improve the quality of life.

Epicurean Philosophy: A Relational Theory of Quantitative Pleasure
Many commentators have pointed to similarities between ancient philosophy and psychoanalysis. Like Freud, ancient philosophers claimed
that their philosophical “truths” could improve the quality of life. Henri
Ellenberger (1970) writes:
It is often overlooked that in the Greco-Roman era the adoption of a philosophy did not imply merely the acceptance of a certain doctrine. The
Pythagoreans, the Platonists, the Aristotelians, the Stoics, and the Epicureans, were not just adherents of “philosophical systems,” but members of
organized “schools,” also called “sects,” that imposed on them a speciﬁc
method of training and a way of life. (p. 41)
In ancient Greece, philosophical disciples were required to “convert” to
the way of life inspired by their philosophical vision. Philosophy was
not a form of speculation, but a practical exercise intended to transform
the lives of its followers. “Philosophy in the hands of the Hellenistic
398 JONATHAN YAHALOM, M.A.
thinkers,” writes Martha Nussbaum (1994), “no longer calmly contemplates the world: it plunges into the world, and becomes part of it”
(p. 36).
Ancient philosophies were generally devised to alleviate psychological
maladies and Epicureanism was no exception. Like other schools of the
time, Epicureanism required disciples to study its philosophy by living it.
In so doing, Epicureanism resembled a cult and its followers devoted the
entirety of their lives to the philosophy.

Ancient philosophies were generally devised to alleviate psychological
maladies and Epicureanism was no exception. Like other schools of the
time, Epicureanism required disciples to study its philosophy by living it.
In so doing, Epicureanism resembled a cult and its followers devoted the
entirety of their lives to the philosophy. Many facts we know about the
Epicurean tradition illustrate how devout its followers were: Epicureans
were known to wear rings depicting their philosophical god, Epicurus;
the Epicureans had their own publishing house to guarantee distribution
of their philosophy; and the Epicureans were exacting about how philosophy was to be learned by requiring followers to take residence in
“the Garden,” a commune where people would discuss and learn—or
embody—the Epicurean truth.
The groundwork for all of Epicurean theory is rooted in the notion of
ataraxia, the most desirable state of pleasure in organic life. The Epicureans argued that mental illness is caused by mistaken beliefs about
pleasure; experiences are commonly perceived to be pleasurable when,
in fact, they are not. To be sure, the Epicureans were not the ﬁrst to argue that people hold false beliefs about pleasure. Plato argued this in the
Republic, as did many others even earlier (see Gosling & Taylor, 1982).
But Epicurus was the ﬁrst who made pleasure central to the practice of
philosophy. For Epicurus, pleasure, or ataraxia, is an absolute state of
tranquility, a freedom from disturbance or agitation of the soul, which all
organic life strives to achieve. This quantitative deﬁnition holds that experiences that lead to greater psychical tranquility are more pleasurable
than ones that engender states of unrest. Yet this deﬁnition should not be
confused with apatheia, the Stoic form of pleasure meaning “not feeling.”

text:
This quantitative deﬁnition holds that experiences that lead to greater psychical tranquility are more pleasurable
than ones that engender states of unrest. Yet this deﬁnition should not be
confused with apatheia, the Stoic form of pleasure meaning “not feeling.”
Both are states of pleasure deﬁned negatively, yet the Epicureans do not
recommend abolishing feelings altogether. Ataraxia is a form of pleasure
to be sought and cultivated. Epicurus’ lesson was that pleasure is not the
satisfaction of desire but the cultivation of a psychological skill that eliminates pain. He taught that the perpetual ambition for additional forms
of pleasure is the reason for unsatisﬁed desires, thwarting one’s chance
at attaining pure pleasure. As such, Epicureans do not deny that things
like ﬁne foods and drink are pleasurable. There is nothing inherently
wrong in eating ﬁne foods and drinking ﬁne wine. Rather, the problem
stems from the way we are pained to continually fulﬁll our demands for
FREUD AND EPICUREAN PHILOSOPHY 399
such pleasures. Ataraxia refers to the careful control of desire, not the
elimination of pleasure per se. 1
Our knowledge of Epicurean philosophy comes from varied sources.
We know very little about the philosophy through its founder’s own
words, as the only existing texts are letters and brief aphorisms collected
by followers and historians. Epicurus (341–270
B.C.E.) lived after Plato and
Aristotle in the philosophically aware Grecian world. As mentioned before, in Athens he established a philosophical commune (“the Garden”)
that was a forerunner for the far-reaching Epicurean communities that
ﬂourished for centuries after his death.

text:
Epicurus (341–270
B.C.E.) lived after Plato and
Aristotle in the philosophically aware Grecian world. As mentioned before, in Athens he established a philosophical commune (“the Garden”)
that was a forerunner for the far-reaching Epicurean communities that
ﬂourished for centuries after his death. And because few primary works
survive, the most complete source of Epicurus’ teachings comes from a
devoted student, Lucretius. Titus Lucretius Carus was a Roman poet who
lived approximately between 99–55
B.C.E., two centuries after Epicurus
taught in Athens. In the didactic poem, The Nature of Things , Lucretius
presciently theorizes about a universe composed of “atoms,” the human
process of coping with fear of death, the development of societies, the
cause of war, the origins of language, and more. So predictive was it
of modern scientiﬁc thought, The New Yorker (Greenblatt, 2011) recently
published an article on the inﬂuence Lucretius’ poem has had on pioneers like Darwin, Francis Bacon, and Shakespeare, among others. And
although scholars once contested whether the poem accurately represents Epicurean philosophy, we now speak of Lucretius as a “translator”
of it (Clay, 1983, p. 17).
One way to approach Epicurean philosophy is to question why Lucretius presents it through poetry. A key tenet in Epicureanism is the
notion that philosophy—and, by extension, every mode of discourse—
ought to serve the attainment of ataraxia. Hence, the truth of philosophy is not valuable of itself, but as a means to achieve the Epicurean
end.
2 The same argument applies to poetry, which philosophers generally distrusted.

Epicurus wrote, “Empty is that philosopher’s argument by which no human suffering is
therapeutically treated. For just as there is no use in a medical art that does not cast out

distinctive for the way it positions its philosophy as important within—and not separate
from—a speciﬁc context that involves how one lives interpersonally.

discomfort of treatment.

their philosophy to the discipline of medicine, analogizing the philosopher to a surgeon who must anesthetize his or her patient prior to the
discomfort of treatment.
4 According to Epicurus, we have developed such
insatiable appetites that we have strayed from pursuing the true form of
pleasure. That is, we are confused in taking something as pleasurable
when, in fact, it is harmful to our mental health. What’s worse, when we
look around us, we ﬁnd that everyone else appears to desire the same
harmful things. Thus, Epicurean philosophy is at odds with conventional
living. This made their philosophy difﬁcult for individuals to accept fully.
It is difﬁcult to question the values around which our lives are organized,
making the Epicurean goal all the more challenging to achieve.
To address this challenge, Epicureans devised a three-step treatment
plan to achieve ataraxia.
5 Yet despite their generalized claim that psychic conﬂict stems from mistaken beliefs about pleasure, the Epicureans
approach is remarkably individualized, addressing the speciﬁc ways each
person developed his or her understanding of pleasure. We witness this
in Lucretius’ attempt to appeal to readers through poetry, as well as
Epicurus’ belief that the gods’ omniscience does not have much to do
with human experience. The Epicureans deprioritized abstract theory in
favor of concrete arguments that pertain to life as it is individually experienced. In this vein, one must remember that the subsequent review of
Epicureanism is tailored to ﬁt each individual.
The Epicurean argument begins by holding that, because most conventional pleasures lead to qualitatively greater forms of unrest, they must be
averted.

text:
Disciples are led to see that many
of the things we think are pleasurable are actually cause for despair. This
originates from the nature of our desires. Most often, our desires are limitless, and no amount of gratiﬁcation is sufﬁcient to end our hunger for
more. An example is the desire for power. As a politician (or any other individual who continually wants more) rises to power, Epicureans would
argue that no status will be enough to quell this thirst, therefore desire for
more leads to quantitatively greater insatiability and agony in an endless
pursuit. In comparison, Epicureans identify self-contained desires capable of complete satisfaction. Equanimity is one example. No additional
amount of equanimity will make life more valuable. Epicureans argue
that the resulting form of pleasure is self-contained and, unlike desires
for things like power, is actually pleasurable. In this argument, Epicureans introduce a qualitative dimension to their quantitative deﬁnition of
pleasure: not only is pleasure deﬁned by (quantitative) freedom from
disturbance of the soul, its fulﬁllment is possible only by recognizing a
(qualitative) distinction between limitless and self-contained desires.
After Epicureans distinguish between healthy and unhealthy desires,
the second step is to ﬁnd an explanation for how the latter desires originate. By this stage, the Epicurean disciple will have already gained awareness that some forms of pleasure are, in fact, not pleasurable at all. Now
begins a process of self-reﬂection where disciples are led to discover that
the source of their harmful desires arises from false belief.
According to Epicurus, false beliefs stand against our nature as human beings.
author: Jonathan Yahalom

text:
By this stage, the Epicurean disciple will have already gained awareness that some forms of pleasure are, in fact, not pleasurable at all. Now
begins a process of self-reﬂection where disciples are led to discover that
the source of their harmful desires arises from false belief.
According to Epicurus, false beliefs stand against our nature as human beings. The Epicurean philosopher will engage disciples through
reason to reveal that limitless desires are not constitutive of human nature whereas those leading to ataraxia are. Let’s reconsider the limitless
craving for power. The Epicurean argues that people crave power not
because it is inherent in being human, but because they are afraid of their
humanity. The desire for power arises as a defense, protecting individuals
from feelings of insecurity. What is the nature of insecurity? Epicureans
believe that no matter how different each individual is, every person is
fraught with the fear of his or her mortality.
The dread of death is so pervasive that Lucretius makes it central to
his poem. He writes: “the task that follows for me here in my verses to
explain and make the nature clear ... and toss that Dread of Death out
on its ear, since that’s what stirs the lives of mortals into such turmoil
from the very depths, and there is nothing that it does not soil” (2007,
402 JONATHAN YAHALOM, M.A.
p. 73). The Epicurean argument against death consists of three subarguments, each intending to prove that death should not trouble us. The
most convincing is known as the “symmetry argument,” which claims
that—just as existence prior to birth means nothing to us—we should
not be concerned about what occurs after. For the Epicureans, however
innocuous death is, we often live in attempt to divert our anxiety about
it.
author: Jonathan Yahalom
file_name: Freud and Epicurean Philosophy  Revisiting Drive Theory.pdf
source_document: Freud and Epicurean Philosophy  Revisiting Drive Theory.pdf

text:
The
most convincing is known as the “symmetry argument,” which claims
that—just as existence prior to birth means nothing to us—we should
not be concerned about what occurs after. For the Epicureans, however
innocuous death is, we often live in attempt to divert our anxiety about
it. Take for example the experience of romantic love. Lucretius (2007)
shows that too often individuals idealize their lovers due to a complex
fear of death: we idealize our lovers as immortal gods with the intention
of ultimately possessing them so that, by association, we may achieve
immortality (pp. 138–143). Romantic love, war, greed, revenge, and any
other limitless forms of desire arise as a means of avoiding the reality of
our transience. And no matter how much a follower denies fearing death,
it is the task of the Epicurean philosopher to reveal how pervasive it is.
However convincing this argument may (or may not) seem today, we
should emphasize Epicurus’ prescient account of the human psyche. Epicurus discovered that people feel and behave in certain ways in order
to divert themselves from something far more unsettling. This prototype of defense mechanisms was a novel way to understand human life.
Through this depiction, Epicureans were able to argue that many forms
of life serve as ways to psychically ward off threatening realities. As a
consequence, behaviors like greed and aggression are symptoms of an
underlying reality we choose not to confront.
Because desires lie deep within the human mind, Epicurean practice
goes further than merely providing an etiology of harmful desires. No
matter how much a person tries to live by Epicurean teachings, it is
likely that mistakes will be made and old habits will return. Hence, the
third step: Epicureans claim that followers must repeatedly experience
and live their philosophy.

gods, their unique position between animals and deities engendered a
human dilemma: each individual could either strive to be like the gods
or to succumb to a bestial life. Epicurean philosophy is centered on promoting the former, and encouraged disciples to become like gods despite
knowledge that it was not fully possible.
This interpersonal model is important for a number of reasons. First,
it signiﬁes that the Epicureans maintained a relational stance to their
approach that is compatible with a quantitative model of pleasure. The
Epicurean appreciation of friendship repositions their quantitative deﬁnition of pleasure within an interpersonal schema. As a form of tension
reduction, ataraxia is not an end in itself, but an end situated with another. Pleasure is still the quantitative reduction of “unpleasure,” yet it
can only be assessed within the interpersonal realm. This elevates friendship to a higher plane than wisdom, showing that no amount of theoretical knowledge outweighs interpersonal experience.
8 Such a concept
includes the Epicurean argument against fearing death, suggesting that
wisdom alone is insufﬁcient to achieve the aims of Epicurean philosophy;
the entire ediﬁce of one’s wisdom amounts to very little if it is not interpersonally situated. The import of relationships in Epicurean thought also
illuminates life in “the Garden”: one’s friendship with peers and teachers
is more important than devotion to an omniscient and unchallengeable
leader. In this light, Epicureans advocated a shift from uncritically accepting metaphysical truths to reclaiming the centrality of interpersonal
experience.

text:
The import of relationships in Epicurean thought also
illuminates life in “the Garden”: one’s friendship with peers and teachers
is more important than devotion to an omniscient and unchallengeable
leader. In this light, Epicureans advocated a shift from uncritically accepting metaphysical truths to reclaiming the centrality of interpersonal
experience.
Of course, friendships are made for different purposes and motivations. The Epicureans
would argue that relationships motivated by insecurity or other secondary gains are not
self-contained and would actually lead to more psychic discord. Epicurus wrote, “Every
friendship is worth choosing for its own sake, though it takes its origin from the beneﬁts
it confers on us” (1994, p. 37). Implicit in the Epicurean stance on friendship is that a
relationship may be an end in itself.
404 JONATHAN YAHALOM, M.A.
Epicureanism and Psychoanalytic Tradition
The prioritization of friendship in Epicurean philosophy is congruent
with the relational turn in psychoanalysis. Selfhood and psychopathology do not exist “inside” one’s mind, but rather are woven from the fabric
of one’s interpersonal environment (Sullivan, 1953). And so for Epicurus, the role of a philosopher is not merely to instruct, but to provide a
hospitable space where a disciple may feel safe and a relationship may
ﬂourish (Greenberg, 1986). The traditional epistemological view about
authority and objective knowledge is displaced in favor of knowledge
that is interpersonally situated and veriﬁed, as in an analysis (Orange,
2011). Finally, because relationships are the impetus of psychological
change, treatment must be individualized (Buechler, 2012).

The traditional epistemological view about
authority and objective knowledge is displaced in favor of knowledge
that is interpersonally situated and veriﬁed, as in an analysis (Orange,
2011). Finally, because relationships are the impetus of psychological
change, treatment must be individualized (Buechler, 2012). Yet although
Epicurean philosophy is congruent with many tenets in relational theory,
it also directly pertains to Freud and his theory of pleasure. In the subsequent sections, I argue that classical psychoanalytic theory is situated
within the Epicurean tradition, despite Freud’s failure to fully recognize
it. More immediately, I argue for the relevance of this analysis by tracing
the controversial history of Freud’s philosophical debts.
To my knowledge, Jacques Derrida is the only major scholar to begin
asking questions about the Epicurean inﬂuence in Freud’s work. In his
essay “My Chances,” Derrida (1984) explores the Epicurean notion of
parenklisis, the theory that all elements of the universe are subject to
indeterminacy, or chance. He wonders how the type of indeterminacy
fundamental to Epicurean philosophy is actually pervasive in Freudian
psychoanalysis, even though it purports to be a science of predictable
psychophysical forces and laws. The question is valuable in itself, but—
for the purposes of this article—Derrida also analyzes an illuminating
passage by Freud. Derrida turns to Freud’s early 1901 paper (“The Psychopathology of Everyday Life”) where Freud anecdotally describes an
instance of forgetting the name Gassendi, the 17th-century scholar famous
for reintroducing Epicureanism as an acceptable scientiﬁc and religious
theory.

Derrida turns to Freud’s early 1901 paper (“The Psychopathology of Everyday Life”) where Freud anecdotally describes an
instance of forgetting the name Gassendi, the 17th-century scholar famous
for reintroducing Epicureanism as an acceptable scientiﬁc and religious
theory. Freud (1901/1966) analyzes his own experience as follows:
Here is an example of name-forgetting with yet another and very subtle
motivation which its subject has explained himself: When I was examined
in philosophy as a subsidiary subject I was questioned by the examiner
about the teachings of Epicurus, and after that I was asked if I knew
who had taken up his theories in later centuries. I answered with the
FREUD AND EPICUREAN PHILOSOPHY 405
name of Pierre Gassendi, whom I had heard described as a disciple of
Epicurus while I was sitting in a cafe only a couple of days before. To
the surprised question how I knew that, I boldly answered that I had long
been interested in Gassendi. The result of this was a certiﬁcate magna cum
laude, but also unfortunately a subsequent obstinate tendency to forget the
name Gassendi. My guilty conscience is, I think, to blame for my inability
to remember the name in spite of all efforts; for I really ought not to have
known it on that occasion either. (p. 42)
Freud writes that he persistently forgets Gassendi’s name because he is
plagued by guilt of having lied about a longstanding interest in Gassendi
during his university examinations.

altogether. Or, more accurately, Freud forgets the disciple of Epicureanism just as he himself stands as a disciple.

We might say that Freud avoids credit to other philosophers because he
was so ambivalent about philosophy itself. In part this is due to Freud’s
belief that philosophy would threaten the scientiﬁc grounds of psychoanalysis. In his “Autobiographical Study” Freud (1935/1963b) writes:
I have on the contrary always remained in the closest touch with the analytic material and have never ceased working at detailed points of clinical
or technical importance. Even when I have moved away from observation,
I have carefully avoided any contact with philosophy proper ... . The large
extent to which psychoanalysis coincides with the philosophy of Schopenhauer ... is not to be traced to my acquaintance with his teaching. I read
Schopenhauer very late in my life. (p. 59)
Yet for all his efforts to gain distance from philosophy, BPP is his
most philosophical work. Derrida’s (1980/1987) careful reading of the
text shows how Freud’s philosophical debts return to haunt him. According to this reading, Freud’s book is ultimately a way for him to
engage with philosophy while simultaneously maintaining his distance.
Derrida is concerned to show how Freud’s “speculation” about the death
drive opens another possibility, antithetical to the pleasure principle that
dominated psychoanalytic theory. Though Derrida writes in light of his
deconstructionist agenda, it is a fascinating and delicate study of Freud’s
tense relationship with philosophy.
More recently, Alfred Tauber (2010) describes Freud as a “frustrated
philosopher.”

FREUD AND EPICUREAN PHILOSOPHY 407
contributed little to scientiﬁcally grounding psychoanalysis. Freud’s ambivalence towards philosophy is readily apparent in his writings. For example, in a well-known passage of BPP, Freud (1920/2011) turns to the
philosophy of Plato only to disparage his name as a “poet-philosopher,”
as one who does not validate or contribute to the objective demands
of empirical science (p. 95). There are also times where Freud turns to
philosophers only to situate them within his own psychoanalytic turf. For
example, in “The Economic Problem of Masochism,” the moment after
Freud discusses Kant’s categorical imperative as the apogee of morality,
he situates the theory within a psychoanalytic framework by claiming it is
“the direct heir of the Oedipus complex” (1924/1963c, p. 167). This is classic throughout Freud’s later works, all which appear to engage with philosophy while maintaining a psychoanalytic-”scientiﬁc” foothold. Hence,
despite Freud’s familiarity with the philosophical tradition, he rarely acknowledged his debts. This no doubt involves Freud’s relationship with
Epicurean thought, and raises questions about how psychoanalysis might
have beneﬁted had Freud acknowledged its inﬂuence.

Freud and Fechner: The Return of a Quantitative Theory on Pleasure
One exception to Freud’s philosophical ambivalence concerns his relationship with Fechner. Gustav Theodor Fechner, the 19th-century mystical philosopher and founder of experimental psychology, is cited both
very early in Freud’s development of psychoanalysis in his 1895 Project
and then in Freud’s speculations during the 1920s. Among other things,
Fechner is famous for his psychophysical theory that forces existing in
the mind are subject to the laws of physics. Fechner postulated that the
experiences of pleasure and “unpleasure” are rooted in psychophysical
states of stability or instability. We experience pleasure precisely because
forces in the mind approximate a state of equilibrium. Like the Epicureans, Fechner’s pleasure principle is the maxim that all organic life is
motivated to achieve pleasure by avoiding the instability associated with
psychophysical unrest. Fechner argued that the laws of the mind are subject to the same laws of the physical universe, giving rise to his second
postulation, the principle of constancy.
Henri Ellenberger helps elucidate the development of Fechner’s theory (and links it to his
nervous breakdown). According to Ellenberger (1993), Fechner appropriated his principle

Although Dufresne (2011) calls BPP “the Rosetta Stone of Freudian
theory” for the way he observes Freud’s return to the very principle he
had adopted in 1895 to ground psychoanalysis (p. 26), BPP is also noteworthy for the way Freud develops Fechner’s principle beyond Fechner’s
original formulation. In addition to claiming that all organisms strive towards stability, Freud claimed that existence itself is inherently unstable.
As a result, he said that the entirety of life is spent in search for an
impossible psychophysical state. Freud claimed that life itself is an annoying disturbance that diverts an organism’s ultimate drive towards stability. BPP concludes by speculating on the ultimate primordial drive, the
death drive, which Freud said is the organism’s desire to “die in its own
way,” and achieve the pleasure of complete imperturbability (1920/2011,
p. 78).

because death is the only state of absolute equilibrium.

devoted to true pleasure, without equating pleasure with death. How can
these two similar theories draw two very different conclusions?
Fechnerian psychophysics are actually quite different from Epicurean
ethics. For Epicureanism, ataraxia is a state that is sought and cultivated.
This involves a type of philosophical askesis, the repudiation of socially
conventional desire. As such, Epicureanism endorses an ethic, a way of
life that one must develop. For Fechner, in contrast, pleasure is understood as a common psychophysical process. It works indiscriminately,
whether we want it to or not. It might appear that the two traditions,
although both centered on a quantitative deﬁnition of pleasure, are actually describing different phenomena and reaching different conclusions.
But that simply overlooks the compatibility of the Epicurean state of
ataraxia with Fechner’s psychophysical universal theory. We might wonder whether there is, in fact, an alternative conclusion Freud might have
drawn. As suggested by Derrida, Freud’s symptom of forgetting the link
to Epicurus has serious implications for psychoanalytic theory. Although
articulating a quantitative perspective of pleasure, Freud’s forgetfulness
of Epicureanism ultimately amounts to neglecting to account for its qualitative features. To this end, I believe that Freud might have drawn other
conclusions, instead of the death drive, and possibly a theory of the
drives that is amenable to both qualitative and quantitative dimensions.

Toward an Interpersonal Theory of Drive
Many recognize that Freud’s bleak conclusion propelled psychoanalytic theory toward an even bleaker horizon (e.g., Brown, 1959/1985;
Ricoeur, 1970; Dufresne, 2011). Freud himself acknowledges this when he
writes that his theory has “unwittingly sailed into the harbor of Schopenhauer’s philosophy” (1920/2011, p. 87). To reference Schopenhauer, the
renowned philosophical pessimist, is to situate psychoanalysis in a similar
context of hopelessness and to put pleasure in a compromised position.
Freud conceived pleasure along individualistic lines, believing that his
investigations proved that the drives ultimately lead to a longing for independence from others so that one may die pleasurably, that is, alone.
Conceived in this way, the drives appear to leave no possibility for a
satisfactory interpersonal life. This is one reason why drive theory is justiﬁably interpreted as representing a type of psychoanalytic despair. Yet
410 JONATHAN YAHALOM, M.A.
although this conclusion seems consistent enough with Freud’s appropriation of Fechner, in what follows I suggest that this interpretation is
misguided. Moreover, Freud’s deﬁnition of the drives is actually more
congruent with relational theory than has been previously argued.
Freud believed that the death drive was the logical consequence of the
pleasure principle. This is what led Norman O. Brown to accuse Freud
of promoting a dialectical stage of despair.

Moreover, Freud’s deﬁnition of the drives is actually more
congruent with relational theory than has been previously argued.
Freud believed that the death drive was the logical consequence of the
pleasure principle. This is what led Norman O. Brown to accuse Freud
of promoting a dialectical stage of despair. Brown (1959/1985) writes,
“The psychoanalytical practitioners have good reason to draw back from
Freud’s ﬁnal instinct theory. The theory, as he left it, results in complete
therapeutic pessimism, and is therefore worse than useless for therapists”
(p. 81). Along with Paul Ricoeur (1970), who adopts a similar line of
reasoning, Brown was one of the few theorists who took the death drive
seriously enough to rescue it. Brown attempted to reconcile the death
drive by claiming that it is not opposed to, but compatible with existence
in the way that death substantiates life. For Brown, the greatest enemy
of life is not death itself, but the denial of death. Through recognizing
our drive towards death—that is, through confronting our mortality—
Brown says that we are redeemed in life by ceasing to escape the grip
of death. Thus, Brown (1959/1985) writes: “It is one of the sad ironies
of contemporary intellectual life that Freud’s hypothesis of an innate
death instinct [ sic], which has been received with horror as the acme
of pessimism, actually offers the only way out of the really pessimistic
hypothesis of an innate aggressive instinct” (p. 99). Along with Brown,
but for different reasons, I suggest that drive theory does not conclude
as bleakly as Freud originally believed.
Turning to Epicureanism reminds us that Freud’s quantitative deﬁnition
of pleasure does not entail that human existence must be lived alone.

recognition of this important difference would have rescued Freud from
