35). These mechanisms are an individual’s reaction
to an external object rejecting or depriving them, thus
protecting the individual from bad objects in a given
context. In a clinical context, Fairbairn advocated for the
dispossession of the client’s internalized bad objects
and subsequent supplementation with good objects. It is
critical that clinicians try to adapt to each client’s needs and
create an accepting environment for them, whether in a
short- or long-term treatment plan. In line with the general
goals of rehabilitation, therapeutic environments have
great potential to help an individual achieve psychological
growth and greater independence by providing a satisfying
and accepting space for the client.
Michael Balint
Michael Balint has made a huge contribution to
psychoanalysis and its application to psychotherapy and
general medicine (Ornstein
38). Because of his father, Balint
became interested in primary healthcare and began his study
of medicine. Balint had his first contact with psychoanalysis
due to his wife, Alice Szekely-Kovacs, whose mother was a
psychoanalyst. Both of them began studying psychoanalysis
seriously with Sandor Ferenczi and Hans Sachs during the
late 1910s to early 1920s. Although Balint’s professional
identity shifted from general practice to psychoanalysis
in 1926, he still believed that psychoanalysis had much
to offer the practicing physician (Johnson et al
39).
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
Both of them began studying psychoanalysis
seriously with Sandor Ferenczi and Hans Sachs during the
late 1910s to early 1920s. Although Balint’s professional
identity shifted from general practice to psychoanalysis
in 1926, he still believed that psychoanalysis had much
to offer the practicing physician (Johnson et al
39). Thus,
he started organizing lectures and seminars for general
practitioners to study the psychotherapeutic possibilities
and potentialities in their practices, evolving into the later
Balint Groups in London. Balint’s forty-year of study in
psychoanalysis mainly focused on the development of
object relations and the application of psychoanalysis,
specifically in the medical field. Based on his observation
of special changes that occur in a therapeutic relationship,
he built a unique interpretation of object relations theory
(Balint
7). His bold and innovative ideas have led the
revolutionary developments in object relations theories.
Balint7 proposed a new way to conceptualize the
psychodynamic structure involving three areas or levels.
The first is the oedipal or genital level, where conflicts
are centered around a three-party relationship. Anything
that happens at this level, whether related to the preoedipal or oedipal phase, involves at least two relevant
objects (the parents) in addition to the subject (the child;
Balint
7). Another key characteristic of the oedipal level is
that all the issues faced at this level are related to conflicts
in relationships among the three parties (i.e., the child
and parents). This conflict could be handled adequately in
psychotherapy because “adult language” used to interpret
these conflicts has the same meanings for both the analyst
and analysand (Mendez et al
40).
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
This conflict could be handled adequately in
psychotherapy because “adult language” used to interpret
these conflicts has the same meanings for both the analyst
and analysand (Mendez et al
40).
The second level, the basic fault level, has a marked
distinction from the oedipal level in terms of the usefulness
of language (Mendez et al
40). “ Adult language” loses its
conventional meaning when being used to describe
events that happen at this level. Analysands perceive the
interpretation of the analyst as meaningless. Events at this
level are based on a two-party mother-child relationship,
which constructs a more rare and primitive object relation.
The dynamics that drive the individual do not exist in the
format of either instincts or conflict. Rather, from Balint’s
perspective, it comes from a form of lacking, which derives
from the gaps between biological and psychological needs
and the care and love received during early development
phases (Balint
7).
The third level, the area of creativity, is a one-party
phenomenon characterized by the fact that no external
object is present (Balint
7). Balint 7 believed that it is the
level where an individual’s creative process occurs, such as
math, philosophy, and epiphany. Similar to the basic fault
level, it cannot be expressed by conventionally understood
means because of the primitive nature and the disorganized
“pre-objects” at this level (Mendez et al
40)
Unlike Freud, who believed that no object exists before
the beginning of extrauterine life, Balint 8 assumes an
immediate, primary object-relatedness based on clinical
observations.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
Based on this perspective, Balint
8 introduced
the notion of “primary love” to discuss things that happen
at a deep level. This concept refers to the withdrawal
of libido from a frustrating environment to reestablish
internal harmony and rediscover early care and support
(Mendez et al
40). Before birth, the infant and the uterine
environment are intertwined, creating an undifferentiated
early relationship with endless materials and harmony.
However, birth destroys this balance which becomes a
trauma, forcing the infant to start a new adaptation mode
of interacting with the environment and objects.
Balint
7 believed that the effectiveness of psychotherapy
depends on the analysand’s ability to regress to the
basic fault level and the analyst’s ability to create a
safe environment for that regression. Regression to
the basic fault level is the return to the primary status
before the development of the issue and is a way to find
a more appropriate and mature object relation. In other
words, it aims to seek a new start for clients to relearn
caring and love. Balint’s emphasis on the environment in
achieving positive outcomes in psychotherapy aligns with
the theoretical foundation of rehabilitation psychology.
The complex interaction between the individual and
the environment needs to be considered in every step
of rehabilitation services. Also, his conceptualization
of primary love seems to provide a new perspective on
understanding the psychosocial adaptation process of
disabilities. More importantly, the idea of regression could
potentially be applied in relevant adjustment counseling
practices. For instance, after acquiring a disability, the
individual may overgeneralize the impact of disability and
hold false assumptions regarding his or her capabilities to
achieve a successful life.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
More importantly, the idea of regression could
potentially be applied in relevant adjustment counseling
practices. For instance, after acquiring a disability, the
individual may overgeneralize the impact of disability and
hold false assumptions regarding his or her capabilities to
achieve a successful life. In order to get out of this basic
fault zone, rehabilitation practitioners could create a safe
environment and help the client regress into the past to reestablish primary love and uncover basic fault.
Harry Guntrip
The next object relations theorist to be discussed is
Harry Guntrip. His role was unique to object relations.
He made dramatic contributions in regards to the
coordination, synthesis, and expansion of other objectrelations theorists’ theoretical essences into a broad,
workable model. Guntrip, a former Congregational
minister, interacted with psychoanalysis as a patient
for the first time and soon started immersing himself in
practices and theoretical studies. During his membership
in the British Independent Group, Fairbairn and Winnicott
strongly impacted Guntrip’s work regarding interactions
between self and object. Instead of emphasizing the Oedipal
complex during the Phallic stage of development as other
Freud’s followers, Guntrip shifted attention to infancy and
infantile dependency (Mendez et al
40). He believed the
initial dependence on a stronger partner finally results in
a sense of meaningful independence. Rather than directing
and borrowing Klein’s “essential contributions” of object
splitting and the unconscious as an inner world, Guntrip
(1968) modified her conceptualization and suggested
that object splitting and aggression derive from perceived
failures and disruptions in nurturing.
Guntrip’s most important contribution to psychoanalytic
theory and practice is his study of regressed ego.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
Rather than directing
and borrowing Klein’s “essential contributions” of object
splitting and the unconscious as an inner world, Guntrip
(1968) modified her conceptualization and suggested
that object splitting and aggression derive from perceived
failures and disruptions in nurturing.
Guntrip’s most important contribution to psychoanalytic
theory and practice is his study of regressed ego. Individuals
with schizoid personality have experienced insufficient
mothering and provisions in early childhood, resulting in an
empathic failure in infancy and a certain amount of splitting
and withdrawal (Ehrlich, 2009
41). Guntrip 10 believed
that retreating into an inner world of fantasy becomes
the only way for infants to retain their ties to objects and
avoid this emotional threat. However, the connections
with objects in fantasies could be viewed as victimized or
persecuted, making one feel anxious and further splitting
the ego to withdraw and avoid anxiety (Ehrlich, 2009
41.
The final withdrawal represents a regression “into what
is probably an unconscious hallucinated reproduction of
the intrauterine condition” (Guntrip
10). This regressed ego
leaves the infant with an unrealized part of self and would
influence relationship building in adulthood.
For Guntrip, the power differential in the holding
situation forces the infant to seek dependence and
validation from others. However, insufficient mothering
inevitably directs it to the inner world for safety. Thus, the
requirements of validation by others and psychic survival
were also processed as a conflict, leading to a separation
between the self and environment (Ehrlich
41). Regression
then serves as a defensive mechanism against anxiety
and emotional threats by developing a less open self to
establishing new connections with others.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
Thus, the
requirements of validation by others and psychic survival
were also processed as a conflict, leading to a separation
between the self and environment (Ehrlich
41). Regression
then serves as a defensive mechanism against anxiety
and emotional threats by developing a less open self to
establishing new connections with others.
Thus, in order to achieve positive therapeutic outcomes,
Guntrip
11 argued that the therapeutic process should
create an environment that provides clients with a sense
of safety and allows the ego to regrow the unrealized part.
Psychological contact is created between a congruent
psychoanalyst and an incongruent analysand who
experiences anxiety and regression.
By revisiting his psychoanalytic experiences with
Fairbairn and Winnicott, Guntrip
11 concluded that analysts
should fill in the emptiness of a non-relating parent in
infancy. In therapy, the psychoanalyst functions as an
attending parent, compensating for the empathic failure
experienced in the past. This process provides a foundation
for the client to regrow the unrealized part of self and
develop a more integrated self.
From Guntrip’s perspective, human development
involves not only the expression of self but also the
dependence on the acceptance and support of significant
others. This perspective stresses the importance of
interaction between analyst and analysand. Guntrip
stated that it is crucial to allow the analysand to relate with
a genuine “good object” in one’s analyst. This perspective is
in line with the psychologist-client/patient relationship in
rehabilitation psychology. The rehabilitation psychologist
must develop a valuable therapeutic relationship and
create a safe ambiance in which the psychologist could fill
in feelings of emptiness resulting from empathic failure and
create a sense of “ego-relatedness” (Guntrip
10).
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
This perspective is
in line with the psychologist-client/patient relationship in
rehabilitation psychology. The rehabilitation psychologist
must develop a valuable therapeutic relationship and
create a safe ambiance in which the psychologist could fill
in feelings of emptiness resulting from empathic failure and
create a sense of “ego-relatedness” (Guntrip
10). For example,
negative societal attitudes could result in internalized
stigma among individuals with disabilities, leading to low
self-esteem and distrust in social relationships. Having
a genuine therapeutic relationship could help the client
relate with the good object in the rehabilitation practitioner
and address trust-related interpersonal issues.
D.W . Winnicott
Lastly, no discussion of the role of object relations
theory in rehabilitation would be complete without
mention of D. W. Winnicott’s foundational work on how
children develop and come to relate to the external world.
Winnicott was born in Plymouth, England, in 1896. He was
both a pediatrician and a psychoanalyst. His contributions
to psychoanalysis and child development greatly exceeded
any name recognition he might have had in the general
psychology literature. He was probably the most notable
of the members of the “Independent” group of the British
Psychoanalytic Society. The two other most notable
members of the Society were Anna Freud and Melanie
Klein.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
His contributions
to psychoanalysis and child development greatly exceeded
any name recognition he might have had in the general
psychology literature. He was probably the most notable
of the members of the “Independent” group of the British
Psychoanalytic Society. The two other most notable
members of the Society were Anna Freud and Melanie
Klein. Among Winnicott’s most famous publications
are The Child, the Family and the Outside World
14; Playing
and Reality16; The Maturation Processes and the Facilitating
Environment; Collected Papers 15; Through Paediatrics to
Psycho-Analysis12; Holding and Interpretation: Fragment of
an Analysis19; The Piggle: An Account of the Psychoanalytical
Treatment of a Little Girl 18; Therapeutic Consultations
in Child Psychiatry 17; Babies and their Mothers 20; and
Psychoanalytic Exploration21. He was also famous for his
extraordinary ability to simplify complex issues with pithy
phrases and sentences.
With such an expansive career, it is no surprise that
Winnicott’s body of work has numerous implications
for conceptualizing and helping people adjust to having
a disability (Thomas & McGinnis
28). The most relevant
ideas from Winnicott’s work on this topic include the
“holding environment,” the “good enough” mothering,
the true and false self, transitional objects, hate in the
countertransference, and environmental impingement.
One of the most vital aspects of helping a client adjust
to having a disability is ensuring the client’s needs are
met, which, as Winnicott (1958,
12) proposed, is linked to
their sense of self.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
One of the most vital aspects of helping a client adjust
to having a disability is ensuring the client’s needs are
met, which, as Winnicott (1958,
12) proposed, is linked to
their sense of self. Winnicott claimed that a child begins
his or her life psychologically in a state of undisturbed
isolation, being unfettered. Children will psychologically
adjust if the environment and their caretakers meet
their needs. If not, the child’s sense of self will collapse,
which they will attempt to reclaim by self-isolating.
In response, psychologists should aim to provide a
“holding environment,” otherwise called a “good enough”
psychological environment, in which the psychologist can
adapt to the client’s needs. This environment should enable
the client to develop more autonomously by increasing
their confidence and independence as well as rectifying
their developmental discrepancies. In a social model of
disability, which understands disability as the product of
environmental limitations (Thomas & McGinnis, 1991,
28),
a holding environment could help the client adjust to these
limitations.
According to Thomas and McGinnis (1991
28), two
factors determine the success of a holding environment in
helping a client with a disability adapt to any environmental
limitations. The first is the client’s adaptive and coping
abilities, and the second is the facilitating characteristics of
the environment. This approach must be conceptualized as
a flexible process during which medications can be made
available depending on the client’s type of disability and
related needs. For instance, clients with spinal cord injuries
may be uncomfortable sitting down in particular chairs or
couches, or a client with impaired vision may need Braille
or audio versions of texts.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
This approach must be conceptualized as
a flexible process during which medications can be made
available depending on the client’s type of disability and
related needs. For instance, clients with spinal cord injuries
may be uncomfortable sitting down in particular chairs or
couches, or a client with impaired vision may need Braille
or audio versions of texts. Beyond sensory and physical
impairments, psychologists should think carefully about
how to modify psychoanalytic psychotherapy for clients
with intellectual impairments and consider if the client is
likely to benefit from such treatment.
People born with a congenital disability may be less likely
to have difficulties in their relationship with caregiving
and personality development due to the presence of the
disability if psychologists apply a Winnicottian lens. If a
child, for example, is socially distant or withdrawn due to the
nature of the disability, such as autism, this characteristic
will affect the caregiver’s capacity to adapt to the
child’s needs. Such children are apt to develop a “false self,”
as Winnicott (1960
13) called it. A child with a “true self”
is a child who has sufficiently adapted to her or his needs;
the child with a false self is marked by inauthenticity, which
results in the child being overwhelmed by the environment
and the caregivers’ demands. The child’s true self is hidden
and cannot properly form due to the child’s attempt to
meet the expectations of others. While children with a
disability may be more prone to developing a false self,
certainly not every child with a disability will develop one.
Specific conditions will, however, increase the chances of
it happening. These include, first, when a caregiver cannot
satisfactorily adapt to the child’s disability.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
While children with a
disability may be more prone to developing a false self,
certainly not every child with a disability will develop one.
Specific conditions will, however, increase the chances of
it happening. These include, first, when a caregiver cannot
satisfactorily adapt to the child’s disability. Second, when
a caregiver has a negative attitude or reaction toward the
child because of the child’s disability. And third, when
a child, due to the disability, cannot successfully convert an
insufficient adaption into a good enough adaptation. Being
aware of these potential disruptions to a child with a
disability developing a “true self” can inform psychologists
in creating the best treatment plans for persons with
disabilities.
People who develop or acquire disabilities later in life
(i.e., adventitious disabilities) could still face psychological
effects from the conditions of the environment that would
ultimately hide their true selves. As such, psychologists
should design treatment plans similarly for clients
with adventitious disabilities, no matter what their
relationship has been with early caregivers.
Perhaps Winnicott’s most famous concept that has
bearings for the treatment of persons with a disability is
called transitional objects. These objects refer to literal
objects (e.g., a teddy bear) that come to symbolize the
mother and her breast. These objects are transitional in
that they help the child complete the process of separating
from the mother and becoming an individual (Mahler
42,
Mahler, Pine, & Bergman43). Depending on the impairment,
children with disabilities may have difficulty forming bonds
with transitional objects due to the nature of the object
(e.g., unsafe or inaccessible). With these objects, the child
is likely to have struggles in achieving a coherent sense of
self and /or developmental deficits.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
Depending on the impairment,
children with disabilities may have difficulty forming bonds
with transitional objects due to the nature of the object
(e.g., unsafe or inaccessible). With these objects, the child
is likely to have struggles in achieving a coherent sense of
self and /or developmental deficits. The child’s separationindividualization process could be further disrupted by
an overprotective caretaker who does not give the child
enough independence or, later in adulthood, persons
with disabilities may have separation-individualization
struggles deriving from reawakened dependenceindependence conflicts (Thomas
46). In either scenario, the
client could regain independence in a therapeutic holding
environment that makes the client feel safe and has the
appropriate ego supports.
Also relevant for helping clients with disabilities is the
concept of “hate in the countertransference,” which is a
child client’s capacity to process and accept the occasional
hate they receive from caregivers, including their clinical
providers and caregivers. Without accepting hatred from
objects, it is thought that the child or client cannot accept
love from an object either. This is not to say that caregivers
and providers are quick to hate those in their care, but
rather it is normal and healthy for them to express a range
of affects during the caregiving or treatment process. Since
children and clients with disabilities have alternative needs
and behaviors from those without disabilities, they are
more prone to receive negative reactions and affects, such
as hate and disgust, from other people, including providers
and caregivers. As a result, if the child or client is unable to
accept this hate, they may have difficulty or be unable to
love, which would affect their ability to develop positive,
supporting relationships.
Readers aware of Carl Rogers may see some similarities
between his work and that of Fairbairn and Winnicott.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
As a result, if the child or client is unable to
accept this hate, they may have difficulty or be unable to
love, which would affect their ability to develop positive,
supporting relationships.
Readers aware of Carl Rogers may see some similarities
between his work and that of Fairbairn and Winnicott.
It is important to emphasize that there are significant
differences between Rogers’s person-centered approach
and Fairbairn and Winnicott’s approaches, despite the
importance of empathy to all three therapists. Specifically,
Rogers
44,45 promoted the point of view that the caregiver
should provide a facilitating environment characterized by
empathy, unconditional positive regard, and genuineness,
which would allow the child or client to develop congruence
between self and experience. Fairbairn and Winnicott,
however, seem to require that the caregiver provide a
more active role in meeting the child or client’s needs that
go beyond just listening and responding empathically.
Moreover, as pointed out by one of the manuscript’s
reviewer, Fairbairn and Winnicott also advocated a more
active exploration of the internal conflicts and object
relational struggles that are acted out interpersonally and
externally, often through projective identification.
Summary and Recommendations
Five prominent object relations theorists were
discussed in this manuscript: Melanie Klein, W. R. D.
Fairbairn, Michael Balint, Harry Guntrip, and D. W.
Winnicott. Melanie Klein is known primarily for her work
with children, and her theories, while relatively complex,
can be used to understand both normal and pathological
personality development. Klein adopted Freud’s belief in
drives, especially the death drive, and the importance of
transference.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
Melanie Klein is known primarily for her work
with children, and her theories, while relatively complex,
can be used to understand both normal and pathological
personality development. Klein adopted Freud’s belief in
drives, especially the death drive, and the importance of
transference. Much of her theory concerns the relationship
of the child to the mother’s breast, and this relationship may
be especially significant clinically in the case of a child with
a physical disability. Two other notable beliefs of Klein’s
were that the superego was helped to develop by envy and
guilt prior to the phallic period and the primacy of four
defense mechanisms: introjection, projection, splitting and
fantasy. Klein’s most important theoretical contributions
were projective identification and the paranoid-schizoid,
and depressive positions. Rehabilitation psychologists
working with clients with more severe psychiatric
disorders such as borderline or narcissistic personality
disorders need to be on the alert for their clients’ use of
these defense mechanisms. Projective identification is an
especially troublesome defense mechanism. When clients
use this defense mechanism, a bad part of the client is
projected into the therapist, and the therapist may begin
to act accordingly. According to Kernberg et al.
30, these
issues could be treated by improving the client’s ability
to experience self and others as coherent, integrated,
realistic perceived human beings and reduce the need to
use defenses that weaken ego structures by reducing the
repertoire of available responses. Since object relations
psychotherapy and rehabilitation share common goals,
except typically for personality restructuring, Melanie
Klein’s object relations theory would probably be apt for
use in many rehabilitation settings.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
Since object relations
psychotherapy and rehabilitation share common goals,
except typically for personality restructuring, Melanie
Klein’s object relations theory would probably be apt for
use in many rehabilitation settings.
Another prominent object relations theorist was W. R.
D. Fairbairn, who is considered by some to be the father of
object relations. Fairbairn made the novel claim that humans
are not motivated by sexual and aggressive drives; instead,
humans are object-seeking. Later, he hypothesized that
pleasure-seeking resulted from unsuccessful relationships
with objects. He also gave strong attention to the role of
satisfaction and contended that the child is born with an
ego that is coherent, structured, and entirely operative.
The child grows restless by the frustrating and desirable
aspects of the non-satisfying object. Thus, the object is
split into two parts, an exciting object, and a frustrating
object. The child represses both objects, thus dividing the
ego, which may ultimately result in psychopathology and
internal conflict.
Despite its complexity, Fairbairn’s theory can inform
the treatment of persons with a disability. Specifically, it
is critically important that the rehabilitation psychologist
strives to become the satisfying, good object in the client’s
mind. The attention on the roles of caregiver, environment,
and desire for satisfaction in one’s social relations are all
uniquely related to helping a person with a disability gain
independence and trusting, positive attitudes toward
caregivers. Also, for Fairbairn, creating a safe environment
where the client feels loved and cared for is foundational
to helping the client break away from the bad object and
instead depend on real objects.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
Also, for Fairbairn, creating a safe environment
where the client feels loved and cared for is foundational
to helping the client break away from the bad object and
instead depend on real objects. Fairbairn’s work, like
Winnicott’s, implies that some type of dependence is
necessary for treatment and adult adjustment.
Finally, it is critical that rehabilitation psychologists
try to adapt to their clients’ needs and create an accepting
environment for their clients regardless of whether the
treatment situation is short-term or long-term. As Balint
advocated for positive therapeutic outcomes, psychologists
are responsible for creating a harmonious and safe
environment because this environment could allow clients
to regress to the basic fault level and have a new start to
relearn caring and love, which they lack (Balint
7). In order
to allow this process to happen, as Guntrip mentioned, the
development of therapeutic relationships should be based
on the needs of clients. The psychologist should serve as
a genuine “good object” who can fill in the emptiness in
clients due to empathic failure, leading to a sense of “egorelatedness” (Guntrip
10).
The final psychoanalytic approach discussed in this
paper is the one developed by D.W. Winnicott. Winnicott
was without question one of the most thoughtful,
brilliant, prolific, and until recently least appreciated of
the major theorists in psychoanalysis. His contributions
to psychoanalytic literature were both theoretically and
clinically groundbreaking. Many of these contributions
have implications for helping persons adjust to their
disability.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
Winnicott. Winnicott
was without question one of the most thoughtful,
brilliant, prolific, and until recently least appreciated of
the major theorists in psychoanalysis. His contributions
to psychoanalytic literature were both theoretically and
clinically groundbreaking. Many of these contributions
have implications for helping persons adjust to their
disability. The most relevant concepts from Winnicott’s
writings that could be used to help persons with a
disability include “the holding environment,” “good enough
mothering,” “the true and false self,” “transitional objects,”
“hate in the countertransference,” and “environmental
impingements.” One of the most vital aspects of helping a
person adapt to a disability is ensuring that the person’s
needs are met. Winnicott
12 proposed that having a person’s
needs met is closely linked to their sense of self. Thus, it
is the rehabilitation psychologist’s job is to facilitate the
client being able to meet as many of the client’s needs
as possible. If not, the client’s sense of self will collapse,
which the client will attempt to reclaim by self-isolating.
In response, psychologists should try to provide a “holding
environment,” which is otherwise called a “good enough”
psychological environment in which the psychologist can
adapt to the client’s needs.
According to Thomas and McGinnis
28, two factors
determine the success of the holding environment in
helping a client adapt to any environmental limitation.
The first is the client’s adaptive and coping skills, and the
second is the facilitating characteristics of the environment.
When treating children Winnicott used play as his primary
therapy technique. In fact, he believed that play was the
only way to work psychoanalytically with children.
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
The first is the client’s adaptive and coping skills, and the
second is the facilitating characteristics of the environment.
When treating children Winnicott used play as his primary
therapy technique. In fact, he believed that play was the
only way to work psychoanalytically with children. Two of
the games he played with his child patients were Squiggle
and Spatula. Rehabilitation therapists could use these same
or other games with their patients if they were properly
trained. One of Winnicott’s most famous books is titled
Playing and Reality. Moreover, several books are available to
facilitate playing Squiggle. Rehabilitation therapists could
adopt Winnicott’s theories and techniques to advance their
own therapy goals, especially when working with earlyaged patients. Such activities would clearly facilitate the
creation of a holding environment and meeting the child’s
need for attention.
People who develop or acquire a disability later in life
could still face psychological effects from the conditions
of the environment that would ultimately hide their true
selves. In these situations, rehabilitation psychologists
should design treatment programs that serve to adapt
to their client’s needs regardless of the client’s age. As
pointed out previously, several other of Winnicott’s
ideas and techniques have relevance in rehabilitation
settings, including “transitional objects” and “hate in the
countertransference.”
author: Kenneth R. Thomas; Kaiqi Zhou; David A. Rosenthal

text:
Introduction
The best way to approach such a complex topic as
psychoanalytic ego psychology (Pep) is to follow
the historical approach that Sigmund Freud himself
recommended in his 1923 contribution with the
title “Two encyclopedia articles ” as the best way to
understand psychoanalysis (Freud, 1923a). This is
exactly the type of definition that Otto Fenichel
(1897–1946) gave of psychoanalytic ego psychology
in 1935, that is:
The history of psychoanalysis brought it about that we
became acquainted with the unconscious before the
conscious and with the repressed before the ego.
Nowadays the psychology of the ego stands in the
center of our investigations. (Fenichel, 1935; 1953,
p. 348)
Such a general and wide definition is what stimulated me to distinguish Pep from Heinz Hartmann ’s
(1894–1970) particular version of it, which I will
call Ego Psychology (EP). In other words, I look at
Pep as a necessary phase of the whole work carried
out by Freud in his attempt to define the ways of
working of the unconscious, with particular regard
to the unconscious aspects of clinical phenomena
such as resistance and anxiety. These could not be
accounted for well enough on the basis of his original
model of the mind, the topographical model – originally formulated by Freud (1900 )i n “The interpretation of dreams ”. Such a definition of Pep, as a
specific phase in the development of psychoanalysis,
actually represents a rather recurrent theme in Otto
Fenichel’s second series of Collected papers .

North America. In other words, although only the

In fact, this is true also for Hartmann and his
group, whose original inspiration came from a book
which Hartmann published in 1927 with the title
Die Grundlagen der Psychoanalyse (The foundations
of psychoanalysis); this was never translated into
English, but it was translated into Italian, in 1981.
In this work, Hartmann presented psychoanalysis as
a natural science, and showed how important it was
to redefine it in such a way as to make of psychoanalysis a discipline capable of collaborating with general
psychology – and with the social sciences. Hartmann’s 1939 monograph Ego psychology and the
problem of adaptation (English edition, Hartmann,
1958) can be seen as his way of satisfying this priority
of his – which he later further articulated with his
closest collaborators Ernst Kris (1900 –1957) and
Rudolph Loewenstein (1898 –1976) (see Hartmann,
1964; Hartmann, Kris, & Loewenstein, 1964).
Such a priority and such a perspective became not
only a school, but even the dominant psychoanalytic
paradigm, between 1950 and 1970, but only in the
USA.
This was never the case in Europe, where the hegemonic agenda and the monolithic character of what
was also called “American Ego Psychology ” ended
up limiting the reception of Pep as a whole.

If, on the one hand, it is true
that the major texts of (North American) EP were
translated and published in Italy and Germany, it is
on the other hand also true that Pep survived in
Europe not only in the form given to it by Heinz
Hartmann and his collaborators, but also in the
form of a series of autonomous contributions (see
below), not to mention – as we will also see below –
Pep being still widely used today, in everyday clinical
practice, with particular regard to Germany.
In this context there also took place what we can
call the lack of reception of EP in France and the
Francophone analytic world, as we can gather from
the book La psychanalyse américaine published in
2005 by the serious French-Canadian scholar
Hélène Tessier. Judging EP not in terms of its
agenda (to develop psychoanalysis as a natural
science), but in terms of its results (in the first
place, pre-conflictual ego functioning and the conflict-free sphere), the author can easily demonstrate
how “cette vision s ’eloigne considérablement de la
perspective de Freud ” (such a perspective is considerably distant from the perspective of Freud)

(Tessier, 2005, p. 39). Elisabeth Roudinesco and

what in French psychoanalysis is called “le sujet,” it

and health” (see Roudinesco & Plon, 1997, p. 243).

The fact is that the Hartmann school remained confined to the United States. With the exception of
Anna Freud and Willi Hoffer, who may be regarded
as honorary members of this group, no thinker in
Europe or South America drew inspiration from Hartmann. (Bergmann, 2000a,p .7 )
Such a superficial point of view can be ascribed to
the deficits of international dialogue and exchange
which André Green (1927–2012) and Otto Kernberg
dealt with in two of their interventions to the same
volume (Green, 2000; Kernberg, 2000). Here is
what André Green says:
You can say everything in defense of Hartmann, but
you cannot say that he has been fostering dialogue.
Again, I come back to international conferences and
their failure. How is it that such an important endeavor
can take place … with no change at all in the literature?
After a congress each one went back home and continued to practice, to lecture and to write, as if nothing
happened! (Green, 2000, p. 136)
And here is how Otto Kernberg immediately
reacted to Green:
I think the last point is so important that we should

And here is how Otto Kernberg immediately
reacted to Green:
I think the last point is so important that we should
have it on the table very clearly. The German totschweigen means to silence to death. It is a way in which you
deal with thoughts that are not permitted to exist, and it
was the technique of the Communist party in the Soviet
Union. Even in photographs they eliminated those who
no longer existed. We must confess that there has been
such an unfortunate tendency in our literature, and
Hartmann certainly participated actively and leadingly
in eliminating from his statements anything going on
simultaneously in the international psychoanalytic
debate about all issues. That, I think, is tragic, and he
did it with the Kleinians, and the Kleinians did it
with the Anna Freudians. It was more a general
problem, but he certainly did not go beyond it. (Kernberg, 2000, p. 137)
Accurately studying the history of Pep can allow us
to define, for every single author who dealt with it –
with particular regard to Europe, before and after
World War II – a specific scientific agenda, and
thus overcome the monolithic character of its
North American configuration. The negative consequences of this for the analytic discourse in the
USA were clearly articulated also by the former
ego-psychologist (and IPA president) Robert Wallerstein (1921 –2014) in his 2002 article “The growth
and transformation of American ego psychology. ”
Indeed, in some cases it will even be possible to
connect such an agenda to a series of personal and
biographical reasons.

Indeed, in some cases it will even be possible to
connect such an agenda to a series of personal and
biographical reasons.
A good way to further document the possibility of
reconstructing the various approaches to Pep in
terms of the scientific agendas of the psychoanalysts
with whose contributions we will deal in this article
is to again go back to Otto Fenichel. I am here referring to the way in which he, in his 1941 paper “Psychoanalysis of character, ” talking about the “three
reasons why psychoanalysis could not fail to be
extended to ego psychology ” (Fenichel, 1941a;
1954, p. 200), presented the first one as having
been the clinical phenomenon of the patients ’resistance. This allowed him to very clearly state: “Thus it
was the necessity for analyzing the resistance which
in practice started psychoanalytic ego psychology ”
(p. 201). This is why we can say that the point of
view of clinical psychoanalysis and of psychoanalytic
technique was the specific perspective from which
Otto Fenichel dealt with and contributed to Pep.
Before going on with the other authors, here is a
further relevant fact worth mentioning: in the introductory chapter to the abovementioned book on
The Hartmann era (Bergmann, 2000b), Martin Bergmann only marginally mentioned the fact that Otto
Fenichel was an important pioneer of Pep before
Heinz Hartmann ’s branch of it dominated the field,
and that the former was critical of the way in which
the latter reformulated Freud ’s( 1923b) original
articulation of Pep (see Bergmann, 2000a, p. 4).

In, on the one hand, a historically well founded,
and, on the other hand, a selective reconstruction
of the major authors involved in the development of
Pep, that is, the 1958 article “A historical review of
psychoanalytic ego psychology ” (Rapaport, 1958),
David Rapaport (1911 –1960) overlooked the contribution of both Sándor Ferenczi and Paul Federn, but
formulated a scheme in four phases that can still be
very useful for our purposes.

He saw the first phase
as terminating in 1897, in connection with Freud ’s
renunciation of the seduction theory; the second
phase as terminating in 1923, with the publication
of Freud ’s “The ego and the id” (Freud, 1923b);
the third phase as associated with Freud ’s development of his own Pep, and lasting till 1937; and the
fourth phase as coinciding with books from not
only Anna Freud (1936) and Heinz Hartmann
(1939), but also Karen Horney (1937) and H.S. Sullivan (1940), and as being characterized by the
specific version of Pep formulated by Hartmann
around his own concepts of innate (pre-conflictual)
ego functioning and of ego autonomy. At the same
time, Rapaport also assigned to the abovementioned
third phase the work of post-Freudian authors such
as Hermann Nunberg (1894 –1970) and Robert
Waelder (1900 –1967), with particular regard to
their contributions on the synthetic functions of the
ego and the principle of multiple function. Of
course, not only Rapaport ’s conceptual research,
but also his diagnostically oriented clinical work is
an important part of North American EP – the
latter finding widespread use in Europe, with particular regard to the handbook on psychological testing
which he published together with Merton Gill
(1914-1994) and Roy Schafer (1922-2018) (see
Rapaport, Gill and Schafer, 1974). Last but not
least, it is also interesting to see how the ego-psychological character of some of H.S. Sullivan ’s work did
not escape Rapaport ’s attention.

And what about the specific European contributions to Pep? North American EP was an important source of inspiration for the unique and
multifaceted
work that Alexander Mitscherlich performed in West Germany until his death in 1982
aged 73, in order not only to help his people elaborate
the incredible disaster brought about by the twelve
years of the Nazi regime (1932 –1945), but also in
order to bring an enlightened and socially critical
psychoanalysis back to his country. From this point
of view, the common denominator of his work was
Freud’s 1928 plea to bring about such a stronger
ego as to be able to listen to and follow die Stimme
der Vernunft (the voice of reason; Freud, 1928).
The same is true for Paul Parin in terms of both the
ethnographic research work which he undertook in
West Africa together with his wife Goldy ParinMatthéy (1911 –1997) and with Fritz Morgenthaler
(1919–1984), and of the ego-psychologically based
social critique which he systematically developed in
Zurich. Furthermore, in his 1977 article “Das Ich
und die Anpassungs-Mechanismen “ (The ego and
the mechanism of adaptation) he gave a specific
new contribution to the point of view developed by
Heinz Hartmann and his collaborators in terms of
the concept of “role identification. ” The same is
true for the concept of the “scenic function of the
ego,” formulated by Hermann Argelander, a collaborator of Alexander Mitscherlich.

Although (North American) EP was critically
received by the colleagues of the Italian Psychoanalytic Society, and although its reception in terms of the
translation of its literature took place outside of it
(see below), we can look at Stefano Bolognini ’s clinical priorities in terms of the systematic attention he

of both the Italian Psychoanalytic Society and the
International Psychoanalytic Association (IPA).
But, of course, the major contribution to Pep
coming from Europe after World War II is represented by Joseph Sandler ’s (1927 –1998) integrative agenda, which allowed him – as Otto Kernberg
did in North America – to bring Pep closer to
object relations theories – and to the Kleinian tradition, with particular regard to the concept of “projective identification. ”
Last but not least, very interesting and inspiring for
the definition of the best approach to our topic is the
position evolved by Leo Rangell (1913 –2011), a
former president of both the American Psychoanalytic Association and the IPA.

Last but not least, very interesting and inspiring for
the definition of the best approach to our topic is the
position evolved by Leo Rangell (1913 –2011), a
former president of both the American Psychoanalytic Association and the IPA. As he explained in detail
in his 2004 book My life in theory , after having been
for many decades a protagonist of EP (see, for
example, Rangell, 1965), he ended up developing
the theoretical frame of what he called a “developed
Freudian,” that is, a frame both centered on EP and
also going beyond it, in terms of both interpersonal
Psychoanalytic
ego psychology: A European perspective 7
and objects relations, and self-object dynamics. In
other words, from this point of view we can speak
of Pep not only as a school, and as a phase in the
development of psychoanalysis, but also as a stable
and still relevant perspective from which to look at
the work we do in our field – what Leo Rangell
would call a stable component of his “composite
theory.”
Pep in Europe before World War II
Carlo Bonomi’s 2010 revisitation of the topic “Ferenczi and ego psychology ” centers around a good
demonstration of the crucial role played by the personal inclinations and interests of every single
analyst in shaping their unique approach to the
concept of the ego, and his formulation of his own
Pep. Only one year after his first meeting with
Freud, Ferenczi coined the term “introjection” (Ferenczi, 1909), which was thought of “as extension of
the ego” (Ferenczi, 1912, p. 317).

text:
Only one year after his first meeting with
Freud, Ferenczi coined the term “introjection” (Ferenczi, 1909), which was thought of “as extension of
the ego” (Ferenczi, 1912, p. 317). In 1913, following
Freud’s pioneering paper on the “Two principles of
mental functioning” (Freud, 1911), Ferenczi published the two important contributions to the psychoanalytic study of the ego: “Stages in the development
of the sense of reality ” (1913a) and “Belief, disbelief,
and conviction ” (1913b). The first deals with the
transition from the pleasure principle to the reality
principle, and the second reflects further on the
impediments to independent judgment, a necessary
instrument for engaging reality. In this paper, Ferenczi defined the sense of reality as not attainable
by relying on authority, and this anticipates and
explains an important aspect of his later opposition
to Pep based on the structural model. In fact, according to it, and at variance with Ferenczi’ s point of
view, the patient ’s sense of reality is considered to
be enhanced by the introjection of the analyst as an
auxiliary superego.
According to Bonomi, it was at the level of the
technical problems encountered by the analyst at
work with their patients that the mutual aversion
and estrangement which gradually developed
between Ferenczi ’s line of thought and the egopsychological concepts connected with the structural
model emerged most clearly. But behind such technical differences there was also a different psychopathological perspective concerning the basic
problems under which our patients suffer.
author: Marco Conci
file_name: Psychoanalytic ego psychology  A European perspective.pdf
source_document: Psychoanalytic ego psychology  A European perspective.pdf

text:
But behind such technical differences there was also a different psychopathological perspective concerning the basic
problems under which our patients suffer. According
to Ferenczi, our patients suffer from a dissociation or
lack of integration between the emotional and the
cognitive dimensions of their mental life. According
to, for example, Anna Freud, they suffer from the
ego’s primary antagonism or innate hostility
towards the instincts (see A. Freud, 1936; English
1946), that is, what David Rapaport called the
insufficient “control of structure over drive ” (see
Rapaport, 1957).
This is what explains, on the one
hand, the development of the so-called standard
technique centered around the analyst’ s abstinence
from any form of participation in the relationship
with the patient, and, on the other hand, Ferenczi’ s
gradual elaboration of an attitude of thoughtful participation in it. According to Bonomi, the crucial discovery behind these contrasting technical stances was
“the discovery that the analyst induced repetition ”
(Bonomi, 2010, p. 109), with Pep reacting to it in
terms of aiming at reducing or eliminating such a
problem, and Ferenczi taking it seriously.
Another paradox connected to the way in which
Ferenczi’s early interest in the ego ended up distancing him from the abovementioned direction taken
by Pep consists in the fact that Hanns Sachs (1925 )
considered Ferenczi ’s “active technique ” as being
founded upon Freud ’s structural model, as if the
analyst could determine a structural change by representing the ego-ideal (superego).
author: Marco Conci
file_name: Psychoanalytic ego psychology  A European perspective.pdf
source_document: Psychoanalytic ego psychology  A European perspective.pdf

text:
If this was the direction in which James Strachey moved, allowing him to
redefine the aim of therapy in terms of an “integral
change in the nature of the patient ’s superego” (Strachey, 1934, p. 279), and thus making the superego
the fulcrum of psychotherapy, such a “metapsychological solution ” of the problem of the relationship
between analyst and patient did not at all satisfy Ferenczi. From his point of view, such a solution, by pretending an unattainable objectivity, produced the
repression of the doubts and objections which naturally also accompany a therapeutic relationship, and
this is why he ended up giving up Freud ’s structural
model, and ended up looking at the relationship
between analyst and patient as “the fulcrum of psychotherapy” (see Bonomi, 2010, p. 121).
Already by 1927, Ferenczi had stopped clinging to
a preconceived model of therapy, embracing instead
the idea of a basic “elasticity” of technique (see Ferenczi, 1928). Later, in his Clinical diary (see Ferenczi,
1988), he would even wonder if one should not
abandon “technique” altogether. Having systematically worked with a whole series of traumatized and
dissociated patients, Ferenczi had come to view the
main problem of the ego as being not its autonomy
from instinctual pressures, as framed within Pep,
but the preservation of its boundaries and of the
feeling of oneself, that is, the Ich-Gefühl, as defined
by Paul Federn (see Bonomi, 2010, p. 126).

This new sensibility with respect to the ego – which first
appears in the paper ‘The unwelcome child ’(1929) –
further modified Ferenczi ’s understanding of the role
of the analyst in precipitating repetition. He suddenly
felt a great responsibility, and he began to stress that

the task of the analyst was to attenuate repetition. Once
again, he tried to manage the problem technically – that
is, by intentionally creating a benevolent and non-frustrating atmosphere. Yet he soon reached the conclusion that the quality of the relationship was not
defined by its exterior aspects, but rather involved a
more subtle participation that cannot be fully planned
and controlled in advance. This final conclusion put
an end to Ferenczi ’s hope to find the correct technique
and to the notion that there is an ultimate solution to
these problems that could be formulated in advance.
(Bonomi, 2010, p. 127)
In the Introduction, we have already seen how
Otto Fenichel welcomed Pep as a perspective
through which it would have eventually been possible
not only to better account for the clinical phenomenon of unconscious resistance, but also to more
exactly formulate the basic principles of the analytic
technique. Such a point of view was also shared by
his Viennese colleagues Hermann Nunberg and
Richard Sterba (1898 –1989), and by the pioneer of
the study and formulation of analytic technique
Franz Alexander (1891 –1964).

Such a point of view was also shared by
his Viennese colleagues Hermann Nunberg and
Richard Sterba (1898 –1989), and by the pioneer of
the study and formulation of analytic technique
Franz Alexander (1891 –1964).
“Few papers have been as frequently quoted and
have exerted an influence comparable to ‘The synthetic function of the Ego, ’”wrote Martin Bergmann
and Frank Hartmann in their introduction to Nunberg’s paper in their 1976 handbook The evolution
of psychoanalytic technique (Bergmann & Hartmann,
1976, p. 304). Going beyond Freud, Nunberg postulated the need for causality as a fundamental human
need, and described the synthetic function of the ego
as not merely unifying the entire personality, but also
simplifying and bringing economy into the ego ’s
mode of operation (see Nunberg, 1931, p. 129). In
the 1934 article “The fate of the ego in analytic
therapy”, Richard Sterba was the first analyst to
speak of what would later be called “the therapeutic
alliance,” and Bergmann and Hartmann consider
his pioneering article as “the first contribution of
this ego psychology to technique ” (Bergmann &
Hartmann, 1976, p. 361).
Very instructive in terms of the reception of
Freud’s structural model and in terms of the elaboration of its technical consequences are the two papers
by Franz Alexander which Bergmann and Hartmann
included in their abovementioned handbook, that is,
the 1925 paper “A metapsychological description of
the process of cure, ” and the 1935 paper “The
problem of psychoanalytic technique. ”

text:
In the
former paper, “one of the earliest responses of psychoanalytic technique to the structural theory ”
(Bergmann & Hartmann, 1976, p. 99), Alexander
was the first analyst to advance the idea that “psychoanalytic technique should center its energy on the
amelioration of the superego ” (Bergmann &
Hartmann, 1976, p. 99). In the second paper, we
find a very different point of view, strongly influenced
by Nunberg’s concept of the synthetic function of the
ego:
In analytic therapy our main allies are the striving of
unconscious forces for expression and the integrating tendency of the conscious ego . … Nunberg’s thesis that the
psychoanalytic treatment is not only an analytic but
simultaneously a synthetic process as well is fully
valid. … Through our interpretations, without fully
realizing it, we actually do help the synthesis in the
ego. (Alexander, 1935, pp. 610 –611; emphasis in the
original)
More theoretically than technically oriented is
another classical paper, the 1930 paper by Robert
Waelder “The principle of multiple function: observations on multi-determination” (Waelder, 2007).
In it, the author looks at Freud ’s new model of the
mind in terms of a whole mind, “whose interests”–
wrote Lawrence Friedman in 2007 –“are diagramed
as separate structures in the theory, but are simultaneously served in some proportion by every act of
the whole mind ” (Friedman, 2007, p. 129). From
this point of view, “id and ego are simply different
aspects of the same psychic event ” (p. 126).

129). From
this point of view, “id and ego are simply different
aspects of the same psychic event ” (p. 126). According to the principle of multiple function, “no
attempted solution of a problem is possible which is
not of such a type that it does not, at the same
time, in some way or other, represent an attempted
solution of other problems ” (Waelder, 2007, p. 78).
In his 1939 monograph Ego psychology and the
problem of adaptation , Heinz Hartmann repeatedly
mentioned Waelder ’s contribution to EP, and the
affinity of their points of view can be easily guessed
by the following words with which Lawrence Friedman revisited Hartmann ’s monograph in 1989:
Hartmann’s monograph is an argument for the
problem-solving value of all aspects of the mind and
for the subordination of intelligence to the organism ’s
larger, primarily social purposes. (Friedman, 1989,
p. 526)
That “ego psychology antedated the Hartmann era
by a number of decades ” and that “the leading ego
psychologist was Otto Fenichel ” (Bergmann,
2000a, pp. 4 and 67) is substantiated by a large
number of ego-psychological papers by Fenichel,
starting with his 1926 paper on “Identification.”

affects” (1941b). These are the clinically oriented
papers which accompanied and followed his
ego-psychological reformulation of analytic technique, as we can find in his paper “Concerning the
theory of psychoanalytic technique ” (originally published in German in 1935; Fenichel, 1935), and in
the lectures on analytic technique which he held in
Vienna in the fall of 1936. Translated into English
by David Brunschwick and published in the Psychoanalytic Quarterly in 1938 –1939 under the title Problems of psychoanalytic technique , they came out in
book form in 1941; only in 2001 did Michael
Giefer and Elke Mühlleitner publish these important
lectures in the original German.
“Concerning the theory of psychoanalytic technique” is the paper by Fenichel in which we find
the sentence “Nowadays the psychology of the ego
stands in the center of our investigations ” (Fenichel,
1935; 1953, p. 348), mentioned at the beginning of
the Introduction.

“Concerning the theory of psychoanalytic technique” is the paper by Fenichel in which we find
the sentence “Nowadays the psychology of the ego
stands in the center of our investigations ” (Fenichel,
1935; 1953, p. 348), mentioned at the beginning of
the Introduction. And here is how Fenichel formulates his ego-psychological redefinition of analytic
technique:
All those fine differences in the consciousness of man,
which have been studied by the non-analytic schools
… now come within the sights of analysis, too. No
doubt that psychoanalytic technique stands to gain
much from this through the refinement of ‘resistance
interpretation‘… But let us not forget, either, that the
preceding exploration of the unconscious makes it
possible for the psychoanalyst to approach the
phenomena of the ego, the differences of consciousness
and the phenomena of self-regard, in a fundamentally
different manner from other schools: psychoanalysis
must explain these phenomena too as arising from an
interplay between unconscious – and in the final analysis, biological – instinctual tendencies, and influences
of the external world. (Fenichel, 1935; 1953, p. 348)
And here is how Martin Bergmann and Frank
Hartmann introduced this important paper by Fenichel in their abovementioned handbook:
One can see from this paper how embattled the position of the early psychoanalytic ego psychologists was
in the 1930s. On the one hand, Fenichel argues
against Theodor Reik and Melanie Klein, who were
all too ready to make interpretations about the id
without regard to the readiness of the ego to absorb
these interpretations.

On the one hand, Fenichel argues
against Theodor Reik and Melanie Klein, who were
all too ready to make interpretations about the id
without regard to the readiness of the ego to absorb
these interpretations. On the other hand, ego psychologists argue against Reich, and even more against
Kaiser, who wished to limit all interpretations to resistance interpretations. … It is a forceful exposition of the
principles of analytic ego psychology in the field of
technique. (Bergmann & Hartmann, 1976, p. 448)
These last words by Bergmann and Hartmann are
even more appropriate for Fenichel ’s seven chapters
of Problems of psychoanalytic technique , in which we
find a whole series of formulations that we can consider
as being still relevant today. Towards the end of the first
introductory lecture, we can for example read:
Psychoanalytic technique is a complicated matter. Its
tool is the unconscious of the analyst which intuitively
comprehends the unconscious of the patient. Its aim is
to lift this comprehension out of intuition into scientific
activity. … The subject matter, not the method, of psychoanalysis, is irrational. (Fenichel, 1941c, pp.

text:
Its
tool is the unconscious of the analyst which intuitively
comprehends the unconscious of the patient. Its aim is
to lift this comprehension out of intuition into scientific
activity. … The subject matter, not the method, of psychoanalysis, is irrational. (Fenichel, 1941c, pp. 12 –13)
A high point in the formalization of his method is
what we find in the third lecture, “The first analytical
steps – Dynamics and economics of interpretation, ”
in which Fenichel formulates the following “generally known rules, ” which still characterize the egopsychological approach to technique:
(a) ‘One should always start the interpretation at the
surface’… (b) ‘The patient determines the subject
matter of the analytic hour ’… (c) ‘Interpretation of
resistance precedes interpretation of content ’… (d)
‘We should avoid too deep and too superficial
interpretations’. (Fenichel, 1941c, pp. 44 –45)
Even more interesting, from the point of view of
our topic, is the following lecture, dedicated to the
“Structural aspects of interpretation,” in which Fenichel shows how “the analyst works exclusively upon
the ego” (Fenichel, 1941c, p. 54; emphasis in the
original), and comes up with the following final
formulation:
That the analyst should carry on his work of interpretation from a position equidistant form ego, id, and
superego, is a rule suggested by Anna Freud (1936)
which can be paraphrased as meaning that the analyst
must see all three aspects of psychic phenomena and
in the struggle between them remain neutral.

text:
Essentially however, he begins always to work with the ego
and only through the ego can he reach the id and the
superego; in this sense he is always closer to the ego
than to the other two. (Fenichel, 1941c, p. 70)
Equally relevant for our contemporary daily clinical work is the ego-psychological approach of a phenomenological nature developed by Paul Federn in
connection with his life-long passion for helping
and therapeutically working with the sickest patients,
those that Freud defined as not amenable to treatment, or übertragungsunfähig, that is, incapable of
transference. On the basis of his very rich clinical
experience, Federn conceptualized psychosis, with
particular regard to schizophrenia, not in terms of
psychic conflict, but in terms of a psychological
deficiency connected with the patient ’s family
environment. Psychoanalytically speaking, a psychosis is for Federn a “sickness of the ego,” characterized
by an “insufficient cathexis of the ego ” and
accompanied by a “pathological or insufficient ego
feeling.” To such a phenomenological approach,
10 M. Conci
based on what the ego actually is, belong also the
concepts of “ego borders ” and “ego states,” aimed
at describing and possibly measuring a patient ’s subjective sense of unity in a way in which Freud ’s and
Hartmann’s genetic-functional approaches do not
allow us to do – concerned as they are with the
ego’s genesis and functions. According to Paul
Federn, the ego also originated together with the id,
but independently from it, and is already present at
birth.

According to Paul
Federn, the ego also originated together with the id,
but independently from it, and is already present at
birth.
Only in 1952 did Edoardo Weiss put together his
training analyst’ s papers connecting his clinical
work with psychotic patients with his study of
their ego in the anthology Ego psychology and the
psychoses, a very good document in Paul Federn ’s
legacy (Federn, 1972). Among them, we can
mention the 1926 paper “Some variations in egofeelings” and the 1931 paper “The analysis of psychotics,” both published in the International Journal
of Psychoanalysis .
Historically and conceptually very interesting is the
fact of how such a legacy was shaped by Federn ’s
great conflict between, on the one hand, his need to
stay as close as possible to Freud (of whom he,
together with Anna Freud, became the official representative in Vienna after 1923) and to his theoretical
and clinical orientation and, on the other hand, his
need to freely pursue his clinical interest with the
sickest patients and to develop his own theoretical
point of view, that is, his own branch of Pep. If
Edoardo Weiss played a crucial role in helping
Federn develop his own point of view, Federn ’s son
Ernest spent many years of his life writing about his
father’s life and work, in a way which is still worth
mentioning:
Federn had started out with trying to find a clinical
proof for Freud ’s theory of narcissism and in doing so
he developed a theory of narcissism and the ego
which differed from that of Freud.

The papers on this
subject are very hard to comprehend and suffer from
a desperate effort on the part of Federn to use Freudian
terms for observations Freud himself never made. …
During Freud ’s life-time Federn was not aware that
he had been contradicting Freud and according to a
personal communication of Hermann Nunberg,
neither did Freud. The latter, however, had not
found Federn ’s papers about ego feelings and narcissism particularly appealing and felt that they were complicating the problems rather than clarifying. Freud
remained cool also to the treatment of psychoses with
a modified psychoanalytic technique, in spite of
having suggested it earlier. … To the extent that
Federn could treat psychotics successfully and found
them appealing and treatable, he had differed from
Freud. Ultimately the majority of psychoanalytic psychiatrists have sided with Federn as expressed in a
number of books. (E. Federn, 1972, p.32)
One of the most important of these books was
Ping-Nie Pao ’s Schizophrenic disorders: Theory and
treatment from a psycho-dynamic point of view (Pao,
1979). As a director of the Chestnut Lodge Hospital
(Rockville, Maryland) and a heir of the tradition of
psychotherapeutic work with the sickest patients
inaugurated by H.S. Sullivan and Frieda FrommReichmann (1889 –1957), Pao was in the best position to summarize the various theoretical
approaches to schizophrenia developed by psychoanalysis, giving a prominent place to Federn ’s work
and legacy.

and legacy. Pao dedicated to this topic the twenty

Psycho-Analysis. In it he introduced the reader to
Federn’s basic terminology (ego feeling, ego boundaries, ego states and ego cathexis), and to his conceptualization of schizophrenia, coming to the
conclusion that “we may still be greatly benefited
by reading Federn ’s attempts at grappling for solutions half a century ago on problems which are
still very much with us” (Pao, 1975, p. 479).
Three authors active before and after World
War II
Not only Edoardo Weiss and Anna Freud, but also
Gustav Bally (1893 –1966) was active in the field of
Pep both before and after World War II. Bally was
a Swiss medical doctor who trained as an analyst at
the Berlin Psychoanalytic Institute, and worked as
an analyst in Berlin between 1926 and 1932 before
going back to Zurich, where he died in 1966. He
played a crucial role in the transmission of his egopsychological training and orientation to a whole
series of younger and important colleagues, who
kept it alive into the 1970s –1990s in Switzerland,
Germany and Italy.

He
played a crucial role in the transmission of his egopsychological training and orientation to a whole
series of younger and important colleagues, who
kept it alive into the 1970s –1990s in Switzerland,
Germany and Italy. In fact, after introducing the
German medical student Alexander Mitscherlich,
who had escaped Switzerland during the war, to psychoanalysis, Bally became a very close friend of his –
as we can read in Timo Hoyer ’s 2008 biography of
Mitscherlich. Furthermore, Bally was the training
analyst of Gaetano Benedetti (1920 –2013) and
Fritz Meerwein (1922 –1989) in the 1950s, and of
Johannes Cremerius (1918–2002) in the early 1960s.
As far as Bally’s contribution to Pep and to EP is
concerned, his 1933 article “Frühe Entwicklungsstadien des Ichs. Primäre Objektliebe ” (Early phases of
development of the ego. Primary object love) was
mentioned twice by Heinz Hartmann in his monograph Ego psychology and the problem of adaptation
(1958). Through the first one we can see Bally
work in the same direction as Anna Freud:
Psychoanalytic ego psychology: A European perspective 11
Bally (1933) has convincingly shown that the prerequisite of learning by play is a state in which ‘nourishment
and protection against enemies ’ are assured; and his
attempt to derive the phylogenesis of man ‘s mind
from the evolution of the motor apparatus led him to
believe that the protracted parental care is one of the
causes of this evolution.

The fact, stressed by Anna
Freud, that for the small child the external world is a
strong ally against his instinctual drives, is also
related to the extensive parental care. (Hartmann,
1958, pp. 29 –30)
In 1945, Bally was able to bring his research work
on early development and on the role of play to fruition through the publication of the book Vom
Ursprung und von den Grenzen der Freiheit: Eine
Deutung des Spiels bei Tier und Mensch (On the
origin and the limits of freedom: An interpretation
of play in animals and human beings).
In the fall of 1908, the young Edoardo Weiss left
his native Trieste to go to Vienna to study medicine,
and he immediately contacted Freud, who sent him
to his close collaborator Paul Federn, with whom
he underwent his training analysis, becoming a
member of the Vienna Society in 1913 – before
graduating from medical school. At the end of
World War I, he went back to his native Trieste,
working in the local psychiatric hospital until the
end of the 1920s. At this point, with Freud ’s encouragement, he moved to Rome, where he was eventually able to train his first pupils (Nicola Perrotti
and Emilio Servadio being the most important),
bring to life the Italian Psychoanalytic Society that
he had cofounded in 1925, and found the Italian
Rivista Italiana di Psicoanalisi . In it, he published
various ego-psychological papers, for example “Il
Super-io” (The super-ego; 1933), and “La parte
inconscia dell ’Io” (The unconscious part of the
ego; 1934).

In it, he published
various ego-psychological papers, for example “Il
Super-io” (The super-ego; 1933), and “La parte
inconscia dell ’Io” (The unconscious part of the
ego; 1934). Because of the Racial Laws promulgated
by Mussolini’s Regime in 1938, he left Italy for the
USA, going first to Topeka and then to Chicago.
He had a specific interest in agoraphobic patients,
whom he treated from an ego-psychological point
of view, and about whom he wrote before and after
the war (see Weiss, 1935, 1953).
Having kept in close touch all his life with not only
Paul Federn, but also Sigmund Freud (see Weiss,
1970), Weiss developed a unique capacity to see
and value both their points of view, and this
allowed him to write in 1957 what we can call the
first comparative ego-psychological paper, “A comparative study of psycho-analytical ego concepts.”
Taking into account not only such an openness,
but also the fact that Weiss ’s wife, the Slovenian
pediatrician Vanda Shrenger, worked along Jungian
lines (see Corsa, 2017), we can dare see in his tolerance and pluralism an important ingredient of the
ways in which psychoanalysis developed in Italy
after World War II (see Conci, 2019; David, 1990).

In addition, given the fact that Heinz Kohut was
exposed to Edoardo Weiss ’s teaching at the
Chicago Institute, we can also look at his self-psychology as an extension of Paul Federn ’s point of
view, and this in as much it made of the self (as
Federn had made of the ego) the main focus of our
attention and treatment.
Anna Freud ’s 1936 book The ego and the mechanisms of defense was the most important book on Pep
after Freud ’s “Inhibition, symptom and anxiety ”
(1926), and it antedated the original German
version of Hartmann ’s Ego
psychology and the
problem of adaptation by three years. Paul Gray
(1982) stressed the resistances that Anna Freud ’s
book evoked among analysts, not excluding Freud,
who referred to her work only once. In fact – as
Gray demonstrated – Freud, the founder of Pep,
was not himself an ego-psychologist. This is also
why, in his exposition of Anna Freud ’s contribution
to EP, Martin Bergmann stresses the way in which
Hartmann’s perspective represented the best theoretical framework for her own developmental research
work (see Bergmann, 2000a, pp. 46 –49). Anna
Freud herself did not fail to admit this in her
homage to Hartmann in the festschrift in his honor:
The child analyst ’s thinking, governed as it is by the
developmental aspects of the human personality, does
not thrive on the basis of drive psychology alone, but
needs to range freely in the whole theoretical field of
psychoanalysis, according equal significance to id,
ego, and superego, to depth and surface, as Hartmann
does.

This creates the specific links between his work
and the child analyst ’s thinking. … So far as I am convinced, I have tried to take care of this by establishing
the concept of developmental lines , contributed to both
from the side of the id and of the ego development;
these developmental lines lead from child ’s state of
immaturity to the gradual setting up of mature personality and are, in fact, the result of interaction between
maturation, adaptation, and structuralization. (A.
Freud, 1966, p.17 and p. 21; emphasis in the original)
In his 1985 biography of Anna Freud, the German
psychologist Wilhlem Salber was able to show how
her developmental viewpoint was closely connected
to a life full of conflicts, turning points, changes,
and developments (Salber, 1985). Since 2006 her
life and her close relationship with her father have
been documented through their voluminous correspondence, edited by Ingeborg Mayer-Palmedo and
translated into English in 2014 (Freud & Freud,
2014). In his recent revisitation of her legacy,
Thomas Aichorn (2016 ) aptly showed what a creative mixture of conservative and innovative (and
reformistic) aspects her legacy stands for.

institution for the training of child psychoanalysts
and psychotherapists. In the mid-1950s a major
research project was undertaken under the leadership

(see Bolland and Sandler, 1985).

text:
In the mid-1950s a major
research project was undertaken under the leadership
of Joseph Sandler – the Hampstead Index Project
(see Bolland and Sandler, 1985). Based on the
reports written by the therapists about their clinical
work, their findings were correlated under various
headings by a team of researchers, the project
aiming at a better integration between psychoanalytic
theory and direct clinical observation. As a result, a
large number of papers were published by Sandler
and his coworkers, most of them in the Psychoanalytic
Study of the Child and reprinted in Sandler (1987 ). A
very good recent document of this creative climate
and of Anna Freud ’s role in keeping it alive can be
found in the volume edited by Daniel Benveniste
Anna Freud in the Hampstead Clinic: Letters to Humberto Nágera (Benveniste, 2015), with particular
regard to her specific interest in the conceptual, diagnostic, developmental, and structural aspects of analytic work.
A unique integration of all these aspects characterizes Anna Freud’s 1965 book Normality and pathology
in childhood, “one of the most important books of the
Hartmann era ” (Bergmann, 2000a, p. 49). Going
beyond Karl Abraham ’s 1924 table of psychosexual
phases (see Abraham, 1948) Anna Freud ’s concept
of developmental lines allowed greater fluidity. In
certain children, ego developments go further than
their psychosexual development or their object
relations. Each individual was now seen as a unique
combination of various interacting lines of development.

Pep in Europe after World War II
The Zurich analyst Gustav Bally played a very important role in Alexander Mitscherlich ’s life starting in
the mid-1930 when, during the latter ’s exile, he
became for him “some kind of a provisional psychotherapist” (see Hoyer, 2008, p. 89). Well documented by his biographer Timo Hoyer is
Mitscherlich’s 1951 six-month study trip to the
USA and his “love relationship” with EP (p. 280).
In fact, as a medical doctor working in Heidelberg,
where he had graduated from medical school in
1941, he was one of the few German professionals
whom the American army could trust, due to his
opposition to the Nazi regime. An expert witness at
the Nuremberg Trials in 1946 –1947, also thanks to
North American donations, he was able to open in
Heidelberg the first German university department
of psychosomatic medicine and psychotherapy – a
dream
of his Doktorvater Viktor von Weizsäcker
(1886–1957).
